# Study

## Determine whether treatment is needed and what is driving the change
Characterise hallucinations, insight, delusions, distress, dangerous behaviour and the impact on care. Recognised, tolerated visual experiences may need explanation and observation rather than medication. Severe distress, loss of insight, persecutory/jealous delusions or unsafe behaviour change the decision. Sudden onset, fluctuating attention or physiological deterioration requires delirium/medical workup, including pain, sleep, sensory and medication contributors.

Review actual medicines and recent additions: anticholinergics, amantadine, dopamine agonists, other dopaminergic drugs and non-neurological psychoactive exposures. Correct reversible causes and improve lighting, sensory aids, sleep and communication. Any reduction in Parkinson medicines balances psychosis against mobility/swallowing and withdrawal; involve the specialist. There is no safe universal “stop all agonists” rule or rigid sequence applicable to every regimen.

## Antipsychotic choices are constrained by motor and cognitive risk
Strong D2 blockade can worsen parkinsonism and swallowing. Avoid treating this as ordinary schizophrenia. NICE’s UK pathway considers **quetiapine when there is no cognitive impairment**, then **clozapine when standard strategies are ineffective**; quetiapine’s evidence is weaker than clozapine’s, and convenience does not prove safety or efficacy. NICE advises against **olanzapine** for Parkinson hallucinations/delusions. Other dopamine-blocking drugs can also worsen motor function. PDD/DLB require additional sensitivity caution.

An inspected **UK clozapine oral label** starts Parkinson psychosis at **≤12.5 mg in the evening**, with 12.5 mg increments at most twice weekly initially; usual effective treatment is much lower than schizophrenia dosing, commonly **25–37.5 mg/day**. It should only exceptionally exceed **50 mg/day**; labelled maximum **100 mg/day**. Confirm the actual product and specialist protocol before prescribing. Monitor orthostasis, sedation, constipation, cardiac/systemic adverse effects and required blood counts. Current Greek monitoring rules must be verified; do not import an older UK WBC/ANC timetable as a current universal protocol.

**Pimavanserin** has a US indication for hallucinations/delusions associated with Parkinson psychosis. # Study

## Classify symptoms by their relation to seizures
**Ictal symptoms** are part of the seizure: sudden stereotyped fear, experiential/olfactory phenomena, altered awareness/responsiveness or automatisms. Persistent apparent psychiatric disturbance can represent non-convulsive status; urgent neurological assessment and EEG may be needed. “No convulsion” does not mean “no seizure”.

**Pre-ictal/peri-ictal** mood or behavioural changes occur around seizures but are not necessarily the seizure discharge itself. **Postictal confusion** begins soon after a seizure, with impaired cognition/arousal during recovery. **Postictal psychosis** often follows a seizure cluster after recovery/a lucid interval, with hallucinations, delusions and affective symptoms arising later—hours to a week, often 1–3 days. The upstream 12–72-hour interval is common teaching shorthand, not a compulsory boundary. Distinguish delirium, ongoing seizures, medication toxicity and intoxication/withdrawal; suicide or aggression risk can require urgent care.

**Interictal** depression, anxiety or psychosis occurs between seizures and need not track immediate events. Interictal psychosis can resemble schizophrenia; preserved affect or fewer negative symptoms may occur, but “negative symptoms never occur” is false. Comorbidity needs ordinary syndrome assessment rather than attribution to a stereotyped epilepsy personality. Temporal-lobe epilepsy does not diagnose hyperreligiosity, hypergraphia or a Gastaut–Geschwind syndrome in every patient.

## Assess illness, treatment and psychosocial contributors together
Ask about seizure control, sleep, adherence, medication starts/titration, cognitive effects, stigma, driving/work restrictions and family impact. Levetiracetam and some other antiseizure drugs can contribute to irritability or mood/behaviour changes; drug exposure does not prove causation in every case. Review new symptoms promptly with neurology and avoid abrupt unsupervised cessation. Depression and suicidality deserve direct assessment; no single multiplier predicts individual risk.

“Forced normalisation” describes emergence of psychiatric disturbance associated with improved seizure control/EEG reduction; it is an uncommon clinical association, not proof that controlling seizures is harmful or an instruction to provoke them.

## Terminology has changed
Older “simple/complex partial” terminology maps broadly onto later focal aware/impaired-awareness language. The **ILAE 2025** framework uses focal, generalised, unknown whether focal/generalised and unclassified classes, and **consciousness** assessed through awareness and responsiveness. Record observable chronology and semiology rather than forcing an old label onto an uncertain event. Routine normal EEG does not exclude epilepsy; atypical recurrent events may need prolonged/video-EEG. Functional seizures can coexist with epilepsy and require positive assessment, not diagnosis by exclusion alone.

# Study

## A short stereotyped sequence is more informative than the symptom label
Temporal-lobe seizures can produce sudden fear, an epigastric rising sensation, autonomic change, déjà vu/jamais vu, olfactory/gustatory experiences or altered familiarity. A seizure aura is itself an ictal event, not necessarily a separate psychological warning. Symptoms may progress to impaired consciousness, behavioural arrest, oroalimentary/manual automatisms and post-event confusion or amnesia. Many events last around **one to two minutes**, but duration varies and is not a strict diagnostic cutoff.

Ask for the sequence, abruptness, reproducibility, responsiveness, recall and recovery; obtain eyewitness accounts/video where feasible. A recurrent identical smell, brief fear and lip-smacking followed by amnesia carries a different probability from prolonged variable worry. Focal seizures may occur without collapse or a bilateral convulsion. No single experiential symptom uniquely localises the temporal lobe or proves epilepsy.

## Compare common mimics positively
Panic attacks typically crescendo over minutes and can include autonomic symptoms and derealisation; ictal fear is often briefer, stereotyped and associated with impaired responsiveness/automatisms. Either can coexist. Dissociation/functional seizures require positive clinical evidence and specialist event assessment; trauma history or emotional triggers alone do not establish them. Syncope often has a relevant posture/prodrome and haemodynamic explanation, but can include jerks. Sleep events, substances, cardiac rhythm disorders and migraine enter the differential according to the history.

Persistent voices or delusions over days are not automatically an ictal hallucination. Consider interictal/postictal psychosis and ordinary psychiatric comorbidity. Recurrent brief waking amnesia can suggest transient epileptic amnesia; a single prolonged isolated episode with preserved identity has a different TGA differential. New late-onset seizures with subacute memory/behaviour change raise structural or inflammatory causes.

## Investigate the event, not just an interictal tracing
Neurological assessment, EEG and appropriate structural imaging help establish seizure type/cause. A **normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy**. Sleep-deprived, ambulatory or inpatient video-EEG may be needed to capture typical events; an isolated nonspecific abnormality does not prove that every spell is epileptic. Deep focal events can be difficult to record, so interpretation needs semiology and specialist judgement.

Sudden prolonged impairment, recurrent events without recovery or new focal deficits need urgent care. Review antiseizure adherence, sleep and exposure changes. Management should not consist of escalating benzodiazepines or antipsychotics for an unexplained recurrent spell. Document the working event formulation and uncertainty; psychiatric assessment and neurological investigation can proceed together.

# Study

## Huntington: inherited degeneration with psychiatric and executive change
Huntington disease is an **autosomal-dominant HTT CAG-repeat expansion on chromosome 4**. GeneReviews categories are ≤26 normal, 27–35 intermediate, 36–39 reduced penetrance and ≥40 full penetrance within a typical lifespan. Repeat length influences onset but does not precisely predict an individual course; sequence/context modifiers matter. Anticipation, particularly with paternal transmission, can produce younger onset in descendants. Predictive testing requires specialist genetic counselling and consent, not opportunistic testing of relatives during an acute crisis.

Psychiatric/behavioural manifestations—irritability, depression, apathy, disinhibition, compulsive behaviour or psychosis—can precede motor recognition. Cognitive change often involves executive function, processing speed and flexible action, with progressive dependence. Chorea is irregular, flowing involuntary movement; later rigidity/bradykinesia can dominate, and juvenile disease may be relatively rigid. Caudate/striatal atrophy supports the pattern but does not replace genetic/clinical assessment. Assess suicide risk, swallowing, falls, family impact and decision-specific capacity. Do not propagate a fixed “10% suicide” claim as an individual forecast.

## Sydenham: a different acquired inflammatory context
Sydenham chorea is associated with the post-group-A-streptococcal/rheumatic-fever spectrum, typically in children/adolescents. Emotional lability, obsessive-compulsive symptoms, anxiety and behavioural change can accompany chorea, hypotonia and motor impersistence. The time lag means active throat symptoms or positive acute testing may be absent. Consider cardiac/rheumatic assessment and the wider neurological differential, not simply primary OCD. The exact diagnostic workup and secondary prevention require paediatric/neurological protocols; Sydenham chorea is not synonymous with every proposed PANDAS/PANS presentation.

## Characterise movement and choose a cause-directed differential
Distinguish chorea from suppressible tics with premonitory urge, rhythmic tremor, sustained dystonia and medication-related akathisia/tardive dyskinesia. Review dopamine-blocking drugs, dopaminergic exposure and timing; psychiatric symptoms plus abnormal movement do not always mean one neurodegenerative disorder.

Consider **Wilson disease** in a relevant young person with psychiatric, hepatic and movement abnormalities; it is a treatable copper-metabolism disorder requiring specialist assessment. Sudden chorea may reflect vascular, autoimmune, metabolic or exposure causes. New dyskinesia with seizures, language decline, catatonia or autonomic instability raises autoimmune encephalitis. Coordinate neurological diagnosis and targeted symptom care; a sedating drug that hides movement can worsen falls/swallowing without treating the cause. Genetic counselling, nutritional support and family planning are substantive parts of Huntington care.

# Study

## Reconstruct injury severity and the recovery timeline
Document mechanism, loss/alteration of consciousness, post-traumatic amnesia, neurological findings and imaging, using witnesses/records when memory is impaired. **Post-traumatic amnesia** is the period before continuous new memories return, not simply retrograde loss of the accident. Historical mild-TBI teaching uses **GCS 13–15**, loss of consciousness no longer than about **30 minutes**, and PTA no longer than **24 hours**; classification conventions and timing matter. A mild label or normal conventional scan does not mean trivial symptoms or no injury.

Early confusion, fluctuating arousal and disorientation require acute medical care; worsening headache, repeated vomiting, new focal signs, seizure or decreasing consciousness needs urgent reassessment. Do not attribute deterioration to frustration or anxiety without checking structural and physiological complications. Persistent symptoms need a new formulation rather than indefinite extension of the acute diagnosis.

## Link deficits to networks without rigid localisation
Attention, processing speed, working memory, executive control and new learning can be affected by diffuse axonal and focal injury. Orbitofrontal-related injury may impair inhibition/social judgement; dorsolateral networks executive organisation; medial frontal systems initiation. These are associations, not a reliable one-lesion/one-behaviour map. Fatigue, sleep disruption and pain can worsen performance independent of structural burden.

Depression, anxiety/PTSD, irritability, emotional lability, apathy, aggression or psychotic symptoms may occur. Compare sustained mood with involuntary laughing/crying, disinhibition with mania and cognitive fatigue with lack of motivation. Consider premorbid functioning, substance use, psychosocial loss, medications, seizures and endocrine complications when indicated. Psychiatric symptoms after injury may be caused, precipitated or merely temporally associated; chronology alone does not prove direct physiological causation.

## Persistent post-concussion symptoms are multifactorial and real
Headache, dizziness, sensory sensitivity, poor sleep, fatigue and cognitive complaints may persist. Neither normal imaging nor psychological contributors establish fabrication. Conversely, every later symptom is not automatically irreversible brain damage. Assess mood, vestibular/visual function, pain, sleep and environmental demands; use targeted neuropsychology and specialist rehabilitation when needed. Repeated concussions and chronic traumatic encephalopathy research do not establish a definite CTE diagnosis from current symptoms alone.

Care combines education, graded activity/return to roles, compensatory strategies and targeted treatment of the identified drivers. Coordinate occupational and neurological assessment for real-world safety. Prescribing needs cognitive, seizure, fall and interaction consideration; avoid a universal stimulant/sedative solution. Set functional goals and track change. Long-term family/relationship strain and suicide risk deserve assessment even when motor recovery is good.

# Study

## Recognise a subacute evolving brain syndrome
New psychosis can be the first phase of autoimmune encephalitis, but psychiatric symptoms alone do not establish it. Red flags include rapid progression, prominent new memory/attention impairment, seizures, language reduction/mutism, catatonia, abnormal movements, altered consciousness, autonomic instability or central hypoventilation. A flu-like prodrome may occur; fever is not required. Anti-NMDAR disease is associated with IgG against the **GluN1** receptor subunit, causing receptor dysfunction/internalisation; it is not identical to schizophrenia’s NMDA hypothesis.

Anti-NMDAR illness often progresses from psychiatric/behavioural change to speech dysfunction, seizures, dyskinesia/rigidity, reduced consciousness and autonomic/respiratory problems. It affects all sexes/ages; ovarian teratoma is an important association in the relevant population, not a compulsory cause. Severe apparent antipsychotic intolerance/NMS-like deterioration should prompt reconsideration, while still treating actual medical emergencies.

## Clinical criteria precede antibody certainty
The Graus possible-AE framework requires **subacute onset <3 months** of memory deficits, altered mental state or psychiatric symptoms, plus at least one of new focal CNS signs, unexplained new seizures, **CSF pleocytosis >5 cells/mm³**, or suggestive MRI, with reasonable exclusion of alternatives. This is a threshold for an AE differential, not proof of anti-NMDAR disease.

Probable anti-NMDAR criteria use rapid onset of **≥4 of six groups**: psychiatric/cognitive change; speech dysfunction; seizures; movement disorder/rigidity/abnormal postures; reduced consciousness; autonomic dysfunction/central hypoventilation. They additionally require abnormal EEG or inflammatory CSF/oligoclonal bands and exclusion of alternatives; three groups can qualify with a systemic teratoma. Definite disease requires at least one of these symptom groups plus IgG anti-GluN1 antibodies and reasonable exclusion of other disorders; antibody studies should include CSF because serum-only testing can give false positives or negatives.

## Investigate and stabilise in parallel
Urgently coordinate neurology/medical care, EEG, MRI and CSF studies including infectious assessment and paired serum/CSF antibody testing as indicated. MRI may be normal; EEG slowing is nonspecific, while extreme delta brush is suggestive but neither necessary nor uniquely decisive. Serum positivity alone, especially low-specificity testing, can mislead; a negative serum result does not categorically exclude disease.

Exclude infection, toxic/metabolic causes, ongoing seizures and other encephalitides; tumour screening follows syndrome, age and sex. Stabilise seizures, breathing, autonomic instability and nutrition. Immunotherapy/tumour treatment requires specialist judgement after appropriate exclusion; do not wait passively for antibodies in a deteriorating compatible syndrome or prescribe an unverified universal steroid regimen. Psychiatric symptom care is supportive and needs particular adverse-effect vigilance.

# Study

## Think in interacting neurological, psychiatric and treatment pathways
Multiple sclerosis (MS) can affect mood, cognition, affective expression and behaviour in addition to producing focal neurological disability. **Depression and anxiety are common**, but a psychiatric presentation should not be attributed automatically to demyelination: disability, pain, sleep disturbance, social loss, medication effects and an independent psychiatric disorder may all contribute. Conversely, NICE cautions that fatigue or depression alone should not usually trigger suspicion of MS without a history or evidence of focal neurological symptoms.

Fatigue is especially important because it overlaps with depressive vegetative symptoms. Ask whether low energy varies with heat, exertion or other MS symptoms; assess sleep, pain, bladder problems, infection, anaemia, thyroid disease, medication and mood. Treating “fatigue” without defining the mechanism risks missing depression or a medical contributor.

## Cognitive and affective syndromes
MS-related cognitive impairment often involves **processing speed, attention, learning/memory and executive function** rather than a uniform global dementia. A person may retain conversational fluency while becoming slower, distractible or inefficient at complex work. NICE recommends cognition as part of comprehensive review and stresses that anxiety, depression, sleep difficulty, fatigue and medication can worsen performance; persistent impairment may justify neuropsychological assessment.

**Pseudobulbar affect** is episodic, involuntary laughing or crying that is excessive or incongruent with the person's internal mood. It is an affect-expression disorder, not synonymous with depression. Euphoria or behavioural disinhibition can occur in advanced cerebral disease but are far less useful diagnostically than a careful syndrome description.

## Mania, psychosis and treatment effects
Mania and psychosis occur in MS but are much less common than depression or cognitive/fatigue syndromes. New psychosis, marked activation or major personality change requires a broad differential: primary mood/psychotic illness, delirium, seizures, substance use, infection/metabolic disturbance, medication effects and active neurological disease. High-dose corticosteroid treatment for relapse can itself produce insomnia, euphoria, irritability, mania or psychosis.

Management therefore follows the **identified syndrome and cause**: standard evidence-based treatment of depression/anxiety where appropriate, correction of fatigue/sleep/medical contributors, and coordination with neurology when symptoms coincide with relapse, new focal findings or treatment changes. Avoid assuming that every psychiatric symptom is a direct lesion effect or that a psychiatric diagnosis excludes active MS.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## Separate common post-stroke syndromes
Stroke can produce focal cognitive deficits, disorders of awareness and emotional/behavioural syndromes. **Post-stroke depression (PSD)** is one of the most frequent complications; the AHA/ASA scientific statement estimates that roughly one third of survivors are affected at a given time. Diagnose a depressive syndrome rather than inferring it from disability alone: aphasia, fatigue, sleep disruption and neurological slowing can obscure the interview.

**Apathy** is different. Its core is reduced goal-directed activity, initiation or interest, often without the negative emotional tone, guilt, hopelessness or pervasive sadness of depression. The two can coexist. Emotionalism/pathological laughing or crying is another separate phenomenon: brief involuntary affective expression may be disproportionate to the underlying mood.

Post-stroke mania and psychosis occur, but they are uncommon and should trigger review for delirium, seizures, medication/substance effects and pre-existing illness rather than a reflex localization claim.

## High-yield focal syndromes
A lesion in the **dominant hemisphere**, usually the left, can produce aphasia; a right-hemisphere lesion classically produces visuospatial neglect and can produce anosognosia. Neglect is failure to attend/respond to contralesional space that is not explained by primary sensory loss. Anosognosia is impaired awareness of a deficit such as hemiplegia and may create major safety and rehabilitation problems.

These are exam-useful patterns, not absolute rules. Neglect can occur with either hemisphere depending on the task/reference frame, and anosognosia reflects distributed awareness networks involving cortical and subcortical structures. Likewise, older claims that left-sided strokes “cause depression” and right-sided strokes “cause mania” are too crude for modern clinical reasoning.

## Assessment and rehabilitation implications
Ask about onset relative to the stroke, prior psychiatric history, cognitive/language limitations, pain, sleep, medication, substance use and social loss. Test attention, language, visual fields, neglect, executive function and awareness of deficit rather than relying only on a verbal mental-state examination.

Aphasia can mimic confusion or non-cooperation; neglect can be missed if examination is purely conversational; anosognosia can look like denial. Depression and apathy each predict poorer engagement and outcomes, so identifying the actual syndrome matters for rehabilitation. Treatment is multidisciplinary: manage the psychiatric syndrome, optimize vascular/neurological care and adapt communication and rehabilitation to the patient's focal deficits.

# Study

## When a “psychiatric” presentation should prompt structural thinking
Intracranial tumours, subdural collections, hydrocephalus and other mass/structural lesions can present with apathy, depression, disinhibition, personality change, psychosis, cognitive decline or delirium. Psychiatric symptoms may rarely precede obvious focal neurology. The diagnostic mistake is not “failing to scan every psychiatric patient”; it is missing **atypicality and neurological context**.

Red flags include new-onset or rapidly changing symptoms at an unusual age, progressive cognitive/personality change, seizures, headache with neurological features, focal deficits, gait disorder, papilloedema, endocrine abnormalities, reduced consciousness or an unexpectedly atypical course/poor treatment response. Acute or subacute change also raises haemorrhage, hydrocephalus, infection and metabolic disease.

## Localization is a clue, not a diagnosis
Frontal lesions can produce abulia/apathy, impaired judgement, disinhibition or personality change; temporolimbic lesions can produce memory disturbance, seizures and occasionally hallucinations, affective or psychotic symptoms. Hypothalamic/pituitary-region lesions may present through endocrine and behavioural consequences.

However, systematic review of tumour presentations shows that psychiatric phenomenology is heterogeneous and **location does not reliably predict a specific syndrome**. Network disruption, oedema, seizures, raised intracranial pressure, treatment and premorbid vulnerability all matter. Do not reverse-engineer a tumour site from a psychiatric symptom.

## Normal-pressure hydrocephalus
Idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (iNPH) is classically associated with **gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary dysfunction** plus ventriculomegaly. The Japanese third-edition guideline defines possible iNPH as more than one triad symptom unexplained by another disorder and without an obvious preceding cause of secondary hydrocephalus. Probable disease additionally requires appropriate CSF findings plus characteristic DESH imaging with gait disturbance or improvement after CSF drainage testing; “definite” iNPH is demonstrated by objective improvement after shunting.

Clinically, gait impairment—small steps, shuffling, instability and difficulty turning—often appears early and is particularly useful. Cognitive change commonly has frontal-subcortical features such as slowing, inattention and executive dysfunction rather than an isolated amnestic syndrome.

The practical rule is to **image when the psychiatric/cognitive story has structural red flags**, then interpret imaging in clinical context. Incidental abnormalities do not prove causation, and treatment of a structural lesion belongs in a neurological/neurosurgical pathway.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## A visual-release syndrome, not automatically psychosis
Charles Bonnet syndrome (CBS) describes recurrent **visual hallucinations in a person with significant visual impairment** without a broader syndrome that better explains them. Images may be formed—people, faces, animals, objects or scenes—or patterned/simple visual phenomena depending on the definition used. Reduced visual input is thought to produce a release/deafferentation phenomenon in visual association cortex.

The high-yield distinction is that cognition is otherwise relatively preserved and the person has **insight that the images are not real**, at least after explanation. Insight can be incomplete at first, so a frightened initial reaction does not by itself exclude CBS. Hallucinations are characteristically visual; persistent auditory/tactile hallucinations, fixed delusional interpretation, marked cognitive fluctuation or impaired consciousness should push the differential elsewhere.

## Differential diagnosis
Do not label every visual hallucination in an older visually impaired person as CBS. Consider delirium, dementia with Lewy bodies/Parkinson disease, occipital seizures, migraine aura, medication/substance effects, sleep-related hallucinations and structural visual-pathway disease. Ask about timing, duration, stereotypy, visual-field relationship, other sensory modalities, insight, cognition and neurological symptoms.

Ophthalmological assessment identifies the cause and potentially reversible components of visual loss. Neurological assessment or imaging is appropriate when features are atypical—for example focal signs, seizures, new cognitive decline, poor insight that persists despite explanation, or hallucinations not plausibly linked to sensory loss.

## Management
The first intervention is **explanation and reassurance**: the experience is a recognized consequence of impaired visual input and does not in itself mean schizophrenia or dementia. Patients often conceal symptoms because of that fear. Optimise vision where possible—correct refractive error, treat cataract/retinal disease when indicated, and use low-vision support.

Environmental and behavioural measures may help: better lighting, visual engagement, blinking or shifting gaze during an episode, reducing isolation and treating sleep/anxiety problems. Recent reviews emphasise that there is **no standardized, reliably effective pharmacological treatment**. Case reports describe several drug classes, but evidence is too weak to justify routine antipsychotic treatment simply because hallucinations are vivid.

CBS is therefore a diagnosis that prevents harm: recognize a benign release phenomenon when the pattern fits, but actively investigate loss of insight, multimodal hallucinations, cognitive decline or neurological red flags.

# Study

## Recognise infection before calling it “psychiatric”
CNS infection can first appear as agitation, psychosis, mood change, personality change, cognitive decline or delirium. **Acute/subacute behavioural change plus fever/recent infection, altered consciousness or cognition, new seizures, meningism or focal neurological signs** should trigger an encephalitis/meningitis pathway rather than routine psychiatric disposition.

HSV encephalitis has a particular tendency to involve temporal/limbic systems, so memory disturbance, behavioural change, dysphasia, seizures and psychotic symptoms can dominate early. Normal early tests do not justify complacency when clinical suspicion remains high. Current infectious-disease guidance emphasizes prompt empiric antiviral treatment for suspected encephalitis while diagnostic studies proceed; exact regimens belong to the medical/infectious-disease protocol, not a psychiatry memory rule.

## Neurosyphilis
Treponema pallidum can invade the CNS **at any stage of syphilis**. Early neurological presentations include meningitis, cranial-nerve dysfunction, acute altered mental state and meningovascular disease/stroke. Late disease can include general paresis with progressive cognitive, personality, affective and psychotic change, and tabes dorsalis.

CDC guidance recommends CSF evaluation when a person with syphilis has clinical neurological involvement such as cognitive dysfunction, motor/sensory deficits, cranial-nerve signs, meningitis or stroke. Ocular and otologic syphilis have their own examination pathways. A positive serology does not prove that every psychiatric symptom is neurosyphilis; integrate history, neurological examination and CSF/other findings.

## HIV and neurocognitive change
In the ART era, severe HIV-associated dementia is less common, but milder neurocognitive impairment persists. Problems may involve **attention, processing speed, executive function, memory and motor function**. NIH guidance stresses that cognitive impairment in people with HIV is often multifactorial: vascular disease, mood disorder, substances, medication burden, ageing and independent neurodegeneration can all contribute.

Do not use older “HAND” research labels as automatic clinical explanations. Progressive or functionally important cognitive symptoms warrant neurological/neuropsychological assessment and investigation for HIV control/CSF escape where indicated, opportunistic CNS infection, metabolic disease and other causes.

The exam principle is temporal and syndromic: **rapid change = infection/encephalitis emergency; chronic cognitive/behavioural change = define the syndrome, immune/infectious context and competing causes before attribution.**

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## Metabolic disease usually announces itself as encephalopathy
A new “psychiatric” presentation caused by an electrolyte or systemic metabolic disturbance usually has **inattention, fluctuating cognition, altered arousal or global slowing** somewhere in the syndrome. Agitation, hallucinations, suspiciousness, emotional lability or bizarre behaviour can occur, but isolated stable psychosis is less typical. The practical move is therefore to look for delirium physiology: acute/subacute onset, fluctuation, reduced attention, abnormal vital signs, dehydration, organ failure, medication changes and new laboratory abnormalities.

**Sodium and osmolality** are high-yield. Both hypo- and hypernatraemia can produce lethargy, irritability, confusion, seizures and coma. Severity depends on the **rate as well as magnitude** of change because cerebral adaptation takes time. Acute hyponatraemia is therefore more likely to cause dangerous cerebral oedema than a similar chronic value. Hypernatraemia causes brain-cell dehydration; severe/rapid rises can progress from weakness and confusion to seizures or coma. Psychiatric interpretation never substitutes for urgent medical correction, and correction itself must be controlled because overly rapid shifts can injure the brain.

## Organ failure produces mixed, non-specific brain syndromes
**Hepatic encephalopathy (HE)** is brain dysfunction associated with liver insufficiency and/or portosystemic shunting. It ranges from subtle attention/psychomotor abnormalities to disorientation, somnolence and coma. The diagnosis is clinical and alternative causes of altered mental state must be sought. Ammonia contributes mechanistically but a concentration alone neither defines nor grades every episode; infection, gastrointestinal bleeding, constipation, dehydration, sedatives and electrolyte disturbance may precipitate deterioration.

**Uremic encephalopathy** occurs with severe renal dysfunction and can range from impaired concentration, fatigue and apathy to delirium, seizures and coma. There is no single diagnostic laboratory or imaging finding. Improvement after renal replacement may retrospectively support the attribution, while persistent symptoms demand another explanation.

Other metabolic clues include hypoxia/hypercapnia, acid–base disturbance and major calcium or magnesium abnormalities; endocrine and glycaemic syndromes are covered separately. The exam principle is to **recognise the brain-failure syndrome first, identify the physiological disturbance second, and avoid claiming causation from one abnormal laboratory value in isolation**.

# Study

## Thyroid disease can resemble primary mood or cognitive illness
**Overt hypothyroidism** commonly produces slowing, fatigue, reduced attention, memory difficulty and depressive symptoms. Severe disease may rarely produce agitation or psychosis (“myxoedema madness”). Look for cold intolerance, constipation, weight gain, dry skin, bradycardia and delayed reflex relaxation, but remember that symptoms are neither necessary nor specific.

**Hyperthyroidism/thyrotoxicosis** more often produces anxiety, irritability, insomnia, restlessness, tremor and impaired concentration; hypomania/mania or psychosis can occur. Older adults may instead look apathetic. Thyroid storm is a medical emergency in which marked systemic decompensation—typically fever/tachycardia plus agitation, delirium or coma—distinguishes it from uncomplicated anxiety or mania.

## Cortisol and calcium/PTH
**Cushing syndrome** is strongly associated with depression and anxiety, with cognitive problems in attention, memory and executive function; mania and psychosis are less common. The body phenotype—proximal weakness, bruising, striae, hypertension, diabetes and characteristic fat distribution—should trigger endocrine consideration rather than psychiatric attribution alone.

**Adrenal insufficiency** can produce fatigue, depression and cognitive complaints; crisis may cause hypotension, volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia, confusion or coma. Psychiatric symptoms in that physiological context are part of a medical emergency.

**Primary hyperparathyroidism/hypercalcaemia** may be accompanied by fatigue, low mood, anxiety, sleep or cognitive complaints, but these are nonspecific. Severe hypercalcaemia is more likely to cause confusion/encephalopathy. Confirm the biochemical disorder rather than using the old “psychic groans” mnemonic diagnostically.

## Glycaemia
Hypoglycaemia can initially produce adrenergic symptoms—sweating, tremor, palpitations, hunger—and then **neuroglycopenia**: irritability, behavioural change, confusion, focal deficits, seizures or loss of consciousness. ADA defines level 2 hypoglycaemia as **<54 mg/dL (<3.0 mmol/L)**, a level at which neuroglycopenic symptoms become important and immediate action is required.

Severe hyperglycaemic crises can also cause altered mental status through dehydration, hyperosmolality and metabolic derangement. The bedside rule is simple: in acute psychiatric or cognitive change, especially with autonomic/systemic signs, **check glucose and consider endocrine physiology before diagnosing a primary psychiatric relapse**.

# Study

## Vitamin B12: neurological disease can precede the blood count
Vitamin B12 deficiency can present with **cognitive difficulty, depression, anxiety or psychotic symptoms**, peripheral neuropathy, sensory ataxia or myelopathy. NICE explicitly warns not to exclude B12 deficiency solely because anaemia or macrocytosis is absent. Risk factors include autoimmune gastritis, gastric/ileal surgery, malabsorption, dietary deficiency and relevant medication/exposure contexts.

The neurological pattern is especially useful: impaired vibration/proprioception, gait imbalance, paraesthesiae and posterior-column/myelopathic signs should push the differential beyond primary depression or dementia. Biochemical testing and cause assessment matter because treatment can stop progression, but established neurological damage may not fully reverse.

## Wernicke encephalopathy: do not wait for the classic triad
Thiamine deficiency causes Wernicke encephalopathy (WE), classically associated with confusion, ocular abnormalities and gait/cerebellar dysfunction. The complete triad is often absent. EFNS guidance therefore recommends, in people with alcohol-related risk, diagnosis when **two of four** are present: dietary deficiency, eye signs, cerebellar dysfunction, or altered mental state/mild memory impairment. WE should also be suspected in **any condition causing thiamine deficiency**—for example prolonged vomiting, malnutrition or bariatric surgery—not only alcohol dependence.

Untreated WE can progress to persistent amnestic **Korsakoff syndrome**, with severe anterograde learning impairment and variable retrograde memory loss; confabulation may occur but is not required. Suspected WE is a medical emergency: thiamine treatment should not be delayed for imaging or laboratory confirmation.

## Less common but examinable deficiencies
**Niacin deficiency (pellagra)** is classically remembered by dermatitis, diarrhoea and dementia/encephalopathy, with death as the historical fourth “D.” It is now uncommon in well-nourished populations but remains possible with severe malnutrition, malabsorption and particular metabolic/drug contexts.

**Copper deficiency** can mimic B12-related subacute combined degeneration, producing sensory ataxia and spastic myelopathy; gastric surgery, malabsorption and excess zinc are important clues. Folate, vitamin E and other nutritional disorders may also contribute to neurological disease, but vague psychiatric symptoms alone are poor evidence.

The exam rule is to connect **risk context + neurological phenotype + targeted testing**, rather than ordering or interpreting vitamins as nonspecific explanations for every psychiatric symptom.

# Study

## Aphasia: test language, not just “speech”
**Aphasia** is an acquired disorder of language, usually from dominant-hemisphere brain disease. It can affect spoken output, comprehension, naming, repetition, reading and writing. A bedside assessment therefore samples **fluency, comprehension, repetition and naming**, then reading/writing. Dysarthria is impaired articulation with language formulation/comprehension preserved; dysphonia is impaired voice production.

Classical syndromes remain exam-useful: Broca/non-fluent aphasia has effortful reduced output with relatively better comprehension; Wernicke/fluent aphasia has fluent but poorly comprehended/paraphasic speech; conduction aphasia has disproportionately impaired repetition; global aphasia severely affects both production and comprehension. Real lesions often produce mixed patterns, and modern language networks are broader than a simple Broca–Wernicke diagram.

## Apraxia: the idea or execution of skilled action fails
**Apraxia** is an acquired inability to perform learned purposeful actions despite adequate strength, sensation, coordination, comprehension and cooperation. Test imitation and pantomime, transitive tool-use gestures, intransitive symbolic gestures and multistep actions.

In **ideomotor apraxia**, the person knows the act but makes spatial/temporal errors when asked to pantomime or imitate it. **Ideational/sequencing apraxia** disrupts the ordered sequence of a multistep task; **conceptual apraxia** disrupts knowledge of tool/action meaning. Terminology varies, so describe the error rather than relying only on the label.

## Agnosia: perception reaches the brain but recognition fails
**Agnosia** is failure to recognize an object, person or sound within one sensory modality despite sufficiently intact primary sensation, attention, memory and language. Visual agnosia is the classic form. In **apperceptive** visual agnosia, perceptual integration itself fails, so copying/matching is impaired. In **associative** visual agnosia, perception is adequate enough to copy an object but its meaning cannot be accessed visually.

**Prosopagnosia** is impaired recognition of familiar faces and is commonly linked to right or bilateral ventral occipitotemporal/fusiform networks. Recognition from voice, gait or other cues may remain possible.

These syndromes matter in psychiatry because aphasia may look like thought disorder, apraxia like refusal/incompetence, and agnosia like confusion. Always establish what basic sensory, motor, language and attentional functions are intact before naming a higher cortical deficit.
chunks.title: Aphasia, apraxia, agnosia and cortical neuropsychological syndromes

# Study

## Frontal syndrome is a circuit disorder
“Frontal lobe syndrome” is not one personality type. Damage to prefrontal cortex, its white matter or connected **frontal–subcortical circuits** can disturb planning, inhibition, motivation, social judgement and emotional regulation. Causes include stroke, traumatic brain injury, tumour, neurodegeneration, infection/inflammation and toxic-metabolic disease. Similar behaviour can therefore arise from lesions outside the frontal cortex when the relevant network is disconnected.

Three classic circuit patterns are useful for exams. **Dorsolateral prefrontal** dysfunction produces a dysexecutive syndrome: impaired working memory, planning, set-shifting, abstraction, verbal fluency and problem solving, often with perseveration and stimulus-bound behaviour. **Orbitofrontal/ventromedial** dysfunction produces disinhibition: impulsivity, tactlessness, poor social judgement, emotional lability, reward-driven behaviour and loss of normal restraint. **Anterior cingulate/medial frontal** dysfunction produces reduced initiation and motivation—apathy, abulia and, at the extreme, akinetic mutism.

These patterns overlap. A focal lesion can affect several circuits, and distributed degeneration or white-matter disease often creates mixed syndromes. Avoid inferring exact lesion location from a single behaviour.

## Examine executive function and behaviour separately
Executive assessment samples initiation, working memory, inhibition, cognitive flexibility, planning and sequencing. Bedside tasks may include verbal fluency, alternating sequences, abstraction, response inhibition and the Luria three-step motor sequence. Primitive “frontal release” reflexes can occur but have limited specificity, particularly with ageing.

The behavioural history is equally important. Ask family or colleagues about change from baseline: impulsive spending, sexual/social disinhibition, loss of empathy, poor judgement, reduced initiative, neglect of responsibilities, perseveration or environmental dependency. Insight may be impaired, so self-report can underestimate change.

A key problem is the **frontal paradox**: a person may perform adequately on a structured test yet fail badly in unstructured real life, where they must generate goals, prioritize, switch plans and monitor consequences independently. Neuropsychological scores therefore do not substitute for collateral and functional evidence.

## Psychiatric differential
Apathy can resemble depression but lacks obligatory sadness, guilt or hopelessness; disinhibition can resemble mania but may lack sustained elevated/irritable mood, reduced sleep need and episodic course. New personality change should prompt neurological context—onset, focal signs, seizures, cognition, imaging and systemic causes—rather than automatic personality-disorder labeling. Management targets the underlying disease, safety and rehabilitation first; behavioural medication is syndrome- and aetiology-specific.
chunks.title: Frontal and executive syndromes and behavioural change from focal brain lesions

# Study

## Wilson disease: psychiatric symptoms can precede the diagnosis
Wilson disease is an autosomal-recessive disorder of copper handling that affects liver, brain and other organs. Psychiatric manifestations are broad—personality/behavioural change, depression, irritability, cognitive decline, psychosis and other syndromes—and can precede obvious hepatic or neurological diagnosis. Suspect it particularly in a **young person** with otherwise unusual psychiatric change plus tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, parkinsonian features, unexplained liver disease or haemolysis.

Kayser–Fleischer rings support neurological Wilson disease but are not a universal screening substitute. Diagnosis is **multimodal**: clinical phenotype, slit-lamp examination, serum ceruloplasmin/copper interpretation, 24-hour urinary copper and sometimes genetic/hepatic assessment. A low ceruloplasmin supports but does not by itself prove Wilson disease, and a normal value cannot be used as a single definitive exclusion. Psychiatric symptoms may be intrinsic to Wilson disease or independent; response to copper-directed treatment is not a diagnostic test.

## Acute hepatic porphyrias: a neurovisceral mimic
Acute hepatic porphyrias—including acute intermittent porphyria—produce attacks of severe, often poorly localised **abdominal pain** with autonomic and neurological features. Tachycardia, hypertension, vomiting/constipation, hyponatraemia, neuropathic weakness, seizures, anxiety, agitation, insomnia, confusion or psychotic symptoms may accompany an attack. The combination is much more informative than “psychosis plus abdominal pain” in isolation.

AGA best-practice advice recommends initial biochemical testing with **random urine porphobilinogen (PBG), δ-aminolevulinic acid (ALA) and creatinine**, ideally during symptoms. Urine porphyrins alone are not an adequate screening test and can cause overdiagnosis. Genetic testing confirms the specific acute hepatic porphyria after biochemical evidence.

## SLE: attribution is the difficult step
Systemic lupus erythematosus can be associated with seizures, cerebrovascular disease, acute confusional state, cognitive dysfunction, mood symptoms and psychosis. However, infection, metabolic disease, medication effects—including glucocorticoids—vascular disease and primary psychiatric illness are often more plausible explanations.

EULAR therefore recommends that a new neuropsychiatric event in SLE first be **evaluated as it would be in a patient without SLE**; only then should attribution to inflammatory or thrombotic lupus mechanisms be made. That distinction determines treatment. The broader lesson applies to systemic disease generally: a medical diagnosis expands the differential; it does not automatically explain the mental state.
chunks.title: Wilson disease, porphyrias, SLE and other systemic diseases with psychiatric presentations

# Study

## First define the question
Consultation-liaison (C-L) psychiatry works at the interface of mental and physical health in medical, surgical and increasingly outpatient settings. A referral such as “depressed,” “confused,” “capacity?” or “difficult patient” is not yet a clinical question. Clarify **what decision or problem the team needs help with**: diagnosis of delirium versus primary disorder, suicide risk, capacity for a specified treatment, medication safety, behavioural management, unexplained symptoms, adjustment to illness or discharge planning.

Before the bedside interview, review the chart: current medical diagnoses and trajectory, observations, laboratory/imaging data, procedures, pain, sleep, medication changes, substances/withdrawal risk and the reason for admission. Speak to the primary team and obtain collateral when needed. This often reveals that the referral question and the true problem differ.

## Integrate psychiatric and medical formulation
The assessment still requires psychiatric history and mental-state examination, but it must be adapted to illness severity, communication limitations and fluctuating cognition. Establish baseline cognition/function and **screen for delirium early** when onset is acute or behaviour has changed. Examine risk to self/others, ability to engage with essential care, substance withdrawal, medication adverse effects and relevant capacity.

Formulation should connect rather than silo:
1. the psychiatric syndrome;
2. medical/neurological contributors;
3. treatment/medication effects;
4. psychological response to illness;
5. social/support factors;
6. immediate risks and barriers to care.

C-L psychiatry also has a **liaison** function: understanding team dynamics, clarifying communication, reducing conflict, supporting staff and coordinating with other services. Modern proactive C-L models add systematic screening, early targeted intervention, team-based care and integration with the primary medical team rather than waiting for crisis referrals.

## A consultation is not finished until it is actionable
Document a concise impression that answers the question asked and states uncertainty explicitly. Prioritize recommendations: urgent safety/medical actions first, then investigations, medication changes, behavioural/environmental measures, communication strategy, capacity/risk conclusions and follow-up.

Avoid vague notes such as “continue medical management.” Specify **who should do what, why, and what should trigger reassessment**. Discuss important recommendations directly with the referring team, especially when they affect observation level, treatment refusal, discharge, medication interactions or urgent medical investigation. Good C-L work changes the patient's overall care plan; it is not simply a psychiatric diagnosis added to the chart.
chunks.title: Consultation-liaison psychiatry: role, clinical question and assessment structure

# Study

## Start with medical trajectory, not the psychiatric label
A medically hospitalized patient may be referred for agitation, withdrawal, low mood, refusal, hallucinations, “non-compliance” or capacity. Before diagnosing a psychiatric disorder, establish **what changed, when, and alongside which medical events**. Review admission diagnosis, operations/procedures, observations, oxygenation, pain, infection, organ dysfunction, laboratory trends, sleep, nutrition, bowel/bladder issues, current and recently stopped drugs, substance use and withdrawal risk.

In hospital, **delirium is the default high-stakes exclusion** when cognition or behaviour changes acutely. NICE recommends looking for recent fluctuation in concentration, response speed, confusion, perception, mobility, agitation/withdrawal, sleep and social behaviour; hypoactive delirium is particularly easy to miss. When delirium indicators are present, use an appropriate validated assessment such as the 4AT in general hospital settings and identify the underlying cause or causes.

## Adapt the psychiatric interview
Pain, dyspnoea, fatigue, hearing/visual impairment, aphasia, intubation and medication effects can make a standard interview misleading. Keep questions brief, establish attention and orientation early, repeat key information if cognition fluctuates, and use interpreters or communication aids when required.

Collateral is often essential: baseline cognition and personality, independent functioning, psychiatric history, alcohol/drug use, adherence, previous capacity or safety problems and the exact time course of the current change. Examine the mental state but interpret it in the context of the physical examination, neurological findings, observations and investigations.

The formulation should separate:
- delirium/other medical or neurological causes;
- medication or withdrawal effects;
- primary psychiatric disorder;
- psychological response to illness;
- pre-existing cognitive/neurodevelopmental vulnerability.

## End with decisions relevant to the ward
Assess acute safety and behavioural risk, but also **medical-care risk**: falls, absconding, interference with essential treatment or inability to follow restrictions. Capacity is assessed for the specific treatment decision when relevant; a psychiatric diagnosis does not itself remove capacity.

Disposition requires medical and psychiatric reality to match. “Psychiatrically cleared” is not a useful conclusion if oxygen, IV treatment, mobility, cognition or nursing needs make a psychiatric setting unsafe. State what needs to happen next, what can be managed on the current ward, and what change should trigger repeat psychiatric review.
chunks.title: Psychiatric assessment of the medically hospitalized patient

# Study

## Diagnose an iatrogenic syndrome by chronology
When psychiatric symptoms appear during medical treatment, ask: **What started, stopped or changed? When? Is the syndrome pharmacologically plausible? Are there stronger competing causes? What happened after a safe dose reduction or withdrawal?** A product label can generate a hypothesis; it does not prove causality.

Review prescriptions, PRN drugs, over-the-counter agents and recent omissions. Risk rises with polypharmacy, renal/hepatic impairment, dehydration, drug–drug interactions, high doses and rapid changes. Abrupt withdrawal from a dependence-forming drug can be as important as starting one.

## High-yield syndromic patterns
**Delirium/cognitive toxicity:** cumulative anticholinergic burden, benzodiazepines/Z-drugs, opioids and multiple CNS-active medicines are important contributors, especially in older or medically vulnerable patients. The 2023 AGS Beers Criteria links these classes to delirium risk in older adults. Rather than naming one culprit automatically, reduce unnecessary burden while correcting concurrent illness, pain, hypoxia, dehydration or sleep disruption.

**Dopaminergic treatment:** levodopa and especially dopamine agonists can contribute to hallucinations/delusions and **impulse-control disorders** such as gambling, hypersexuality, binge eating and compulsive shopping. NICE emphasizes that these behaviours may be concealed. If problematic, specialist-led review of dopaminergic therapy—usually addressing a dopamine agonist first—is preferred to simply layering on psychotropics.

**Levetiracetam** can produce irritability, aggression, agitation and, less commonly, psychotic symptoms. This is a useful example of why the psychiatric history should always include recent antiseizure-drug changes and why a new behavioural syndrome in epilepsy is not automatically “postictal” or a primary psychiatric disorder.

## Management: remove harm without creating another problem
First assess severity, delirium and the patient's ability to receive essential care. Then coordinate with the treating specialty to stop, reduce or substitute the suspected treatment **when medically safe**, while treating the psychiatric syndrome and competing medical causes.

Document the temporal relationship and outcome. Improvement after dechallenge strengthens causality but is not always possible; rechallenge is rarely justified solely for diagnostic certainty. The central C-L task is balancing treatment benefit, withdrawal risk and psychiatric toxicity rather than treating every adverse effect with an additional psychiatric drug.

# Study

## Corticosteroids produce several psychiatric phenotypes
Systemic glucocorticoids can produce insomnia, irritability, euphoria, hypomania/mania, depressive symptoms, psychosis and behavioural change. Recent systematic evidence supports **different time-course patterns rather than one “steroid psychosis” syndrome**: during early treatment, activation/manic symptoms are relatively prominent, whereas depressive symptoms are also associated with corticosteroid exposure and may be more evident with longer treatment. Psychotic reactions occur in a minority.

Symptoms often begin within days to weeks of starting or increasing treatment, but timing is variable and delayed presentations occur. A prior psychiatric history may increase vulnerability, yet reactions are unpredictable and can occur without previous mental illness.

## Dose matters, but not as a diagnostic cutoff
Higher daily exposure is associated with greater psychiatric risk in several studies, but the evidence is heterogeneous. The traditional **40 mg/day prednisone-equivalent** teaching is best understood as an older risk signal, not a safe/unsafe boundary: clinically important reactions can occur below it, while many patients tolerate higher doses.

When a patient becomes activated, depressed or psychotic during corticosteroid treatment, assess chronology, dose changes and previous exposures, but also exclude **delirium, infection, metabolic disturbance, CNS disease and the underlying inflammatory/autoimmune illness itself**. In SLE, for example, psychosis may reflect lupus, corticosteroids, infection or a primary disorder; temporal association alone is not enough.

## Management is a medical–psychiatric balance
First determine severity and whether urgent medical or behavioural intervention is required. If symptoms are plausibly corticosteroid-induced, discuss with the treating specialty whether the dose can be **reduced, shortened or discontinued safely**. Do not abruptly stop chronic systemic corticosteroids simply because psychiatric symptoms emerged: adrenal suppression and loss of control of the underlying disease may make this dangerous.

When the steroid cannot be reduced sufficiently or symptoms are severe, treat the actual psychiatric syndrome using standard principles while continuing to reassess causality. Evidence for a single preferred prophylactic or treatment drug is limited; avoid memorising one universal regimen.

Other immune treatments can also affect mood. **Interferon-alpha** is the classic exam example, especially for treatment-emergent depressive symptoms, although its use has narrowed substantially. The general rule is to establish temporal association, competing medical causes and reversibility rather than attributing psychiatric symptoms to treatment by name alone.
chunks.title: Corticosteroids and other medical treatments causing psychosis, mania or depression

# Study

## Refusal starts with consent, not with psychiatry
Under Greek law, medical treatment normally requires the patient’s prior informed consent. The Ministry of Health also states that the hospital patient has the right to **consent to or refuse** diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Therefore, refusal of a treatment that clinicians consider highly beneficial or even potentially life-saving does not itself prove psychiatric illness or incapacity.

Before judging capacity, make the decision genuinely informed. Explain the diagnosis or uncertainty, proposed intervention, material risks and expected benefits, alternatives—including no treatment—and the likely consequences of refusal in clear language. Correct communication barriers, sensory impairment, pain, sedation, intoxication, delirium and other reversible factors where possible. Check for coercion or threat. Article 12 requires consent to be informed, voluntary and specific to the medical act and timing.

## Assess capacity for this decision, now
Greek Article 12 requires **ικανότητα για συναίνεση** but does not codify the UK Mental Capacity Act’s four-part statutory test. Clinically, explore whether the patient can understand the relevant health situation and proposed intervention, appreciate the consequences for their own situation, compare the options in a reasoned way and communicate a voluntary choice. These are assessment domains, not imported Greek statutory wording.

Capacity is **decision-specific and time-sensitive**. A psychotic, depressed or cognitively impaired person may retain capacity for a particular decision; a person without a psychiatric diagnosis may lack it during delirium or severe encephalopathy. An apparently “unwise” choice, disagreement with doctors or refusal based on different values is not enough. Document the information given, the patient's own explanation, relevant psychopathology/cognition, efforts to support decision-making and the conclusion for the specific treatment.

## If valid consent is absent
Article 12 specifies who may consent when a patient lacks capacity: a judicial supporter when appropriately appointed, otherwise the patient's relatives under the statutory framework, while the physician should still seek the patient's voluntary participation as far as possible.

The emergency exception is narrower than “doctors think treatment is best.” Consent is not required when suitable consent cannot be obtained and there is an **immediate, absolute and urgent need** for medical care; Article 12 also contains other specified exceptions. These should be documented and applied to the concrete circumstances.

Do not assume that involuntary psychiatric admission automatically authorizes unrelated medical treatment. General medical consent rules and the separate statutory framework for compulsory psychiatric care answer different questions. When consequences are grave or the legal pathway is uncertain, involve the treating consultant, hospital legal/ethics structures and appropriate senior decision-makers rather than converting uncertainty into a global “no capacity” label.
chunks.title: Refusal of life-saving medical treatment: capacity, risk and ethics

# Study

## “Unexplained” describes our current knowledge, not the cause
Persistent physical symptoms are common across medicine. Some occur with established disease, some remain incompletely explained, and some fit positive functional syndromes. The term **medically unexplained symptoms (MUS)** is increasingly avoided because it can imply that normal investigations prove a psychological cause. They do not. A patient can also have functional symptoms **and** structural disease.

DSM-5/DSM-5-TR **somatic symptom disorder (SSD)** deliberately removed the requirement that symptoms be medically unexplained. Its centre of gravity is clinically significant somatic symptoms accompanied by excessive or disproportionate symptom-related thoughts, anxiety or behaviours. Thus, a person with cancer, inflammatory disease or another established diagnosis can meet SSD criteria; conversely, unexplained symptoms alone do not establish SSD.

## Functional neurological disorder is a positive diagnosis
Functional neurological disorder (FND) illustrates the modern approach. Diagnosis is supported by **positive internal inconsistency or incongruence** with recognized neurological disease—for example Hoover's sign in functional weakness or entrainment/distractibility in functional tremor—not simply by normal imaging, unusual behaviour or recent stress. Psychological stressors are common but neither necessary nor sufficient.

Positive functional findings do not abolish the ordinary differential. Epilepsy can coexist with functional seizures; Parkinson disease can coexist with functional movement symptoms. New red flags or a changed phenotype require reassessment.

## Assessment and management
Take the symptoms seriously and define their chronology, triggers, disability and meaning to the patient. Review prior investigations rather than repeatedly restarting them; look for unresolved red flags, medication effects, sleep, pain, autonomic symptoms and psychiatric comorbidity. Ask what the patient fears and how healthcare use, avoidance, deconditioning and attention to symptoms may be maintaining disability without implying conscious production.

Communication is part of treatment. Give a coherent, non-dualistic explanation: the symptoms are **real**, the diagnosis is based on recognizable patterns where possible, and altered functioning can occur without structural damage detectable on routine tests. For FND, demonstrate positive signs when appropriate.

Management is coordinated and functional: scheduled follow-up rather than crisis-driven repeated testing; treatment of genuine comorbid disease; physiotherapy/occupational rehabilitation when relevant; and psychological interventions such as CBT when symptom-related beliefs, avoidance, anxiety or coping are treatment targets. Avoid promising that every symptom is reversible or using a functional diagnosis to dismiss future medical change.
chunks.title: Medically unexplained symptoms and functional somatic syndromes

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## Distress is common; disorder requires formulation
Cancer produces uncertainty, loss, pain, altered roles and treatment burden, so fear and sadness are not automatically psychiatric disorders. ESMO nevertheless emphasizes that **anxiety and depression are common and under-recognised** across the cancer trajectory. Assessment should ask about severity, persistence, functional impact and the patient's own concerns rather than infer disorder from a screening score alone.

Somatic depressive symptoms are difficult to interpret because cancer and treatment can independently cause fatigue, anorexia, weight change, poor sleep and reduced activity. Give particular weight to **pervasive low mood, anhedonia, hopelessness/guilt, cognitive depressive themes and loss of psychological reactivity**, while still assessing the full syndrome. Also review pain, anaemia, infection, endocrine/metabolic disturbance, brain disease and treatment effects such as corticosteroids.

## Depression, adjustment and demoralization are not interchangeable
**Demoralization** describes a state of helplessness, perceived inability to cope, loss of meaning/purpose and feeling trapped or defeated. It overlaps with depression but is not identical. A demoralized patient may still experience pleasure when circumstances allow, whereas pervasive anhedonia is more characteristic of major depression. Demoralization can coexist with depression or adjustment disorder, and severe hopelessness or statements about wanting life to end always require careful exploration rather than semantic reassurance.

Adjustment disorder links disproportionate distress/impairment to an identifiable stressor without another disorder better accounting for the syndrome. Normal grief, fear of recurrence and existential distress remain important even when no formal psychiatric diagnosis is met.

## Palliative psychiatry is integrated care
In advanced cancer, first control physical suffering: pain, breathlessness, nausea, insomnia and medication adverse effects can drive distress. **Delirium** is common near the end of life and should be suspected with acute fluctuation, impaired attention/arousal, perceptual disturbance or reversed sleep–wake cycle; do not misdiagnose it as anxiety or psychosis.

Treatment should fit goals, prognosis and burden. Evidence-based psychotherapy—including CBT and supportive/meaning-focused approaches—and pharmacological treatment can help anxiety/depression, but expected time to benefit, interactions, swallowing, organ function and patient preference matter increasingly as illness advances. Communication about prognosis and goals should be clear, paced and preference-sensitive.

Psychiatry also contributes to decision-specific capacity assessment, family/team communication, pre-existing severe mental illness and complex behavioural symptoms. The endpoint is not simply symptom reduction: it is preserving agency, comfort, relationships and concordance between psychiatric care and the patient's oncology/palliative goals.
chunks.title: Psychiatry in oncology and palliative care

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## Chronic physical and mental illness modify each other
Depression and anxiety are disproportionately common in people with chronic physical disease and multimorbidity, particularly when illness causes pain, disability, role loss, uncertainty or treatment burden. The association is **bidirectional and cumulative**: physical illness can precipitate or sustain psychiatric symptoms, while depression/anxiety can worsen activity, sleep, cognition, self-care, adherence and engagement with medical treatment. Social deprivation, isolation and fragmented care can amplify both.

Do not reduce this to “depression is a reaction to being ill.” Shared biological pathways, medications, direct CNS effects, behavioural changes and independent psychiatric disorders may all contribute.

## Diagnose the syndrome despite somatic overlap
Fatigue, sleep disturbance, appetite/weight change, poor concentration and reduced activity can come from either depression or the medical condition. NICE therefore recommends a **comprehensive assessment rather than symptom counting alone**, including duration, functional impairment, previous mood episodes, comorbid psychiatric/physical disorders, relationships and social context.

Ask whether loss of interest/pleasure, persistent low mood, guilt/hopelessness and negative cognitive themes exceed what would be expected from physical limitation. At the same time, avoid “diagnostic overshadowing” in both directions: a known psychiatric disorder must not explain away new physical symptoms, and chronic disease must not make clinicians dismiss a treatable depressive or anxiety disorder.

## Treatment must fit the medical context
Treat the psychiatric disorder using evidence-based psychological and pharmacological approaches, but modify the plan around **organ function, frailty, polypharmacy and drug–disease/drug–drug interactions**. For example, side effects that are minor in a healthy adult—sedation, orthostasis, anticholinergic effects, bleeding tendency, QT effects or hyponatraemia—may become clinically important with particular comorbidity or co-medications.

Rehabilitation, sleep, pain control, activity pacing and social/occupational support may be treatment targets alongside formal psychiatric therapy. If physical illness prevents standard face-to-face intervention, adapt delivery rather than abandoning psychological treatment.

## Integrated care beats parallel silos
NICE recommends coordinated care when depression coexists with chronic illness. Contemporary meta-analysis of mental–physical multimorbidity supports **collaborative care**—structured follow-up, case management, measurement-based review and communication between primary/medical and mental-health clinicians—as producing modest improvements in depression and quality of life, with some sustained benefit.

Set goals in terms of both symptoms and function: mood, adherence, activity, sleep, disease self-management and quality of life. The psychiatric plan should make the medical plan easier to live with, not become another disconnected treatment burden.
chunks.title: Psychiatric morbidity in chronic physical illness

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study

## ADHD is neurodevelopmental, not a simple “dopamine deficiency”
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a **neurodevelopmental disorder** with onset in development and clinically important impairment that can persist across the lifespan. Family, twin and genomic evidence supports substantial heritability and a predominantly **polygenic** architecture: many genetic variants of small effect interact with environmental and developmental influences. There is no single ADHD gene or single environmental cause.

Catecholamine systems and frontostriatal/frontoparietal networks are relevant to mechanisms and treatment, but “ADHD = dopamine deficiency” is an oversimplification. Group-level studies find small average differences in brain structure/function and in tests of executive function, attention and reward processing. These findings overlap extensively with controls and **cannot diagnose an individual**.

## Core phenotype
The diagnostic core comprises **inattention** and **hyperactivity-impulsivity** that are excessive for developmental level and produce meaningful impairment in everyday settings. Inattention includes difficulty sustaining/selecting attention, organizing and completing tasks, remembering obligations and resisting distraction. Hyperactivity-impulsivity includes excessive activity or restlessness, difficulty remaining still or waiting, interrupting and acting before consequences are adequately considered.

Executive dysfunction—time management, working memory, task initiation, planning and self-monitoring—is clinically prominent in many adults but is not synonymous with ADHD. Emotional dysregulation, sleep problems and motivational variability are common associated features, not independent proof of the diagnosis.

## The phenotype changes with age
ADHD does not simply disappear at puberty. Longitudinal evidence shows that many people with childhood ADHD continue to have **impairing symptoms in adulthood even when they no longer meet full categorical criteria**. Persistence estimates vary depending on definition and follow-up method, so distinguish persistence of some symptoms/impairment from persistence of the full syndrome.

Overt running/climbing and constant motor activity commonly lessen with age; adults may describe **inner restlessness**, excessive talking, impatience or difficulty tolerating inactivity. Inattention, organization and executive-demand problems often remain prominent as life becomes less externally structured. Impairment shifts from classroom behaviour toward higher education, work performance, household administration, relationships, driving and financial/time management.

NICE therefore treats adult ADHD as a continuation of a developmental disorder: symptoms should trace back to childhood and persist, with impairment across relevant domains. Apparently new adult-onset attentional symptoms require careful review for mood/anxiety disorders, sleep deprivation, substances, medication effects, neurocognitive disease and environmental overload rather than automatic retrospective labeling.

The exam principle is **developmental continuity plus current impairment**, while recognizing that symptom expression, compensatory strategies and environmental demands change across life.
chunks.title: ADHD: neurodevelopmental model, core symptoms and lifespan course
