chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Stress biology: adaptive regulation and cumulative burden are different

## The hormonal cascade

Hypothalamic corticotropin-releasing signalling stimulates pituitary ACTH, which drives adrenal-cortical glucocorticoid production. Cortisol feeds back through receptor-dependent regulation at several levels. Circadian and pulsatile activity, acute demands and connected neural systems influence the resulting pattern; one sample is not a complete measurement of HPA function.

Hippocampal, prefrontal and threat-related circuitry can modulate the axis, but their roles should not be reduced to an identical inhibitory arrow for every limbic region. Hormonal output, receptor sensitivity and feedback responsiveness are different mechanisms. A normal basal concentration does not establish that all dynamic regulation is normal.

## Stress responses are not inherently pathological

Acute adjustments can help maintain function under changing demand. Allostasis describes regulation through such changes; allostatic load concerns cumulative burden from repeated or poorly regulated adaptations across systems. It is not simply another name for high cortisol.

Autonomic, immune, metabolic and cardiovascular changes can contribute alongside endocrine measures. Composite load indices use different components and thresholds, so one score is not a universal psychiatric diagnostic test. An association with later illness can also reflect confounding and reciprocal effects of existing disease.

## Psychiatric findings vary

HPA abnormalities have been reported in subsets of depression and other stress-related presentations, but phenotype, timing, medical illness, treatment and exposure history matter. Do not teach that every depressed patient has high cortisol or that one endocrine direction defines PTSD. Group variation does not establish a useful individual classifier.

Endocrine disease can itself produce psychiatric symptoms and belongs in clinical differential assessment. That is different from using a research HPA model to explain all distress. Sleep disturbance, chronic adversity and behaviour may influence the measurements as well as being outcomes.

## Mechanistic hypotheses need calibrated interpretation

Proposed links between stress, plasticity, inflammation and brain structure do not prove inevitable irreversible neuronal loss in an individual. Interpret exposure, mediator and outcome separately. No cortisol cutoff, suppression-test rule or allostatic-load panel is supplied as psychiatric diagnostic practice; those would require a specific validated clinical indication and protocol.
chunks.title: HPA axis, stress response and allostatic load

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Plasticity models: a downstream change is not automatically the clinical mediator

## Plasticity has several meanings

Synaptic plasticity includes changes in synaptic strength, number or structure; neurogenesis and survival of cells are related but distinct processes. Learning, stress and treatment may influence different components over different time scales. The word plasticity does not mean that every observed change is beneficial or that lost function has been restored.

BDNF participates in growth-factor signalling supporting neuronal and synaptic functions. Its production, location, receptor signalling and downstream pathways qualify an effect. A peripheral BDNF concentration is not a direct count of brain synapses or a patient-specific measure of hippocampal repair.

## Monoamine and rapid-action hypotheses

Stahl describes monoamine-related signalling leading to transcriptional and growth-factor changes as one explanation for delayed antidepressant effects. Immediate transporter occupancy and later clinical response are different levels of the account. A compatible time course does not establish that one adaptation is necessary and sufficient for benefit.

Ketamine-related models propose NMDA-mediated disinhibition, AMPA signalling and downstream neurotrophin/synaptic effects. The cascade is a candidate explanation, not proof that all rapid improvement results from new synapse formation or that every NMDA antagonist shares clinical efficacy. Preclinical cellular findings require careful translation to human illness.

## Disease models are heterogeneous

Stress-related reductions in trophic support or altered connectivity have been proposed in depression. Such models do not establish uniform neuronal degeneration, inevitable irreversibility or one biological cause in every patient. Severity, duration, subtype, other illness and treatment can affect observed brain or blood measures.

An improvement in symptoms, a biomarker change and a mechanistic intervention are not interchangeable evidence. Showing mediation requires more than observing that both outcome and marker changed; alternative pathways and confounding still matter.

## Use the model without a repair promise

Plasticity provides a useful account of adaptation beyond immediate neurotransmitter levels. It can generate testable predictions about timing and context, but does not replace evidence for treatment selection, maintenance or safety. No BDNF cutoff, imaging-repair test or guarantee of neuroprotection is supplied. Clinical assessment remains based on meaningful symptoms, functioning and risk rather than declaring success from a plausible molecular story.
chunks.title: BDNF, synaptic plasticity and antidepressant-action models

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Genetic liability: population variance is not an individual's genetic percentage

## Heritability needs a population and a model

Heritability concerns the proportion of variation in a phenotype or liability attributed to genetic differences within the studied population and conditions. It is not the percentage of an individual's illness caused by genes, nor a statement that environmental intervention cannot help. Change the environment, measurement or population and the estimate may change.

Family aggregation can reflect shared genes and shared environment. Twin/adoption designs help separate influences but rely on assumptions and selection/measurement quality. Concordance is the observed agreement in phenotype between paired individuals; it is not interchangeable with heritability. Estimates from different genetic-study methods need not measure identical components.

## Penetrance and variable expression

Penetrance is the probability that a phenotype is expressed among carriers of a defined genotype, under the relevant conditions. It differs from how severely the phenotype is expressed and from the population frequency of the genotype. A risk-associated variant is not necessarily a deterministic cause or a diagnostic result.

## Polygenic architecture

Many common variants with small effects can contribute to liability, alongside rarer variants with larger effects in some cases. Polygenic does not mean every variant has the same size or acts through the same pathway. Pleiotropy allows one variant or biological pathway to contribute to more than one phenotype; diagnostic categories need not map one-to-one onto genes.

Gene–environment interaction means the association/effect of one factor differs according to the other under a specified model or scale. Gene–environment correlation is a different possibility: genetic influences may be associated with exposure to particular environments. Neither is proved by simply observing both a genetic risk and an adverse experience.

## Clinical communication

Explain absolute risk, uncertainty, family context and the purpose of testing without genetic fatalism or blame. A high population estimate cannot predict one person's outcome. Molecular findings, family history and clinical phenotype provide different information; test interpretation and counselling require appropriate expertise. No disorder-specific inheritance percentage or product-style predictive claim is invented here.
chunks.title: Psychiatric genetics: heritability, penetrance and polygenicity

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# GWAS and PRS: statistical association is not an individual diagnosis

## What a GWAS identifies

A genome-wide association study tests variants across the genome for statistical relationships with a phenotype. Large samples, multiple-testing control, ancestry/structure assessment and replication matter. A significant marker may tag correlated variation rather than identify the causal variant, gene or biological mechanism.

Phenotype definition affects the result: broad categories, symptom measures and selected clinical samples do not answer identical questions. Association with a disorder does not mean that a variant codes for that diagnosis or predicts it with certainty. Population structure, relatedness and sample overlap can complicate interpretation.

## A polygenic score aggregates estimated effects

A PRS usually combines many variant dosages weighted by estimated associations from a discovery dataset. The result is relative genetic liability under that construction, not the sum of deterministic disease genes. It does not include every rare variant, environmental factor or clinical observation.

Training/discovery performance is not independent predictive validation. Evaluate an external target sample, overlap/leakage, discrimination, calibration and the incremental value over existing clinical information. A high score's absolute meaning depends on baseline risk and how the score was calibrated; rank ordering is not the same as an accurately estimated probability.

## Portability and clinical utility

Discovery ancestry, variant frequencies/linkage patterns, phenotype ascertainment and context can change performance elsewhere. A score should not be assumed portable merely because the same calculation runs. Nor should differences be explained by race as a biological substitute for the actual genetic, environmental and social variables.

Clinical usefulness requires an appropriate decision, validated benefit and consideration of harm, not only statistical significance or a promising area under a curve. A psychiatric PRS is not by itself a diagnostic criterion or proof of treatment response. This unit does not declare a universal ban or approval for every genomic application.

## Communicate the boundary

Explain uncertainty, consent, privacy and familial implications. Separate a research finding from a specific clinically validated test and avoid fatalistic or embryo-selection conclusions. The retrieved ISPG and NHGRI material supports careful interpretation; complete current guidance and Greek implementation remain approval gates.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Epigenetics: regulation without a DNA-sequence change

## Define the level of change

DNA methylation, histone modification and chromatin organisation can influence gene activity without changing the underlying nucleotide sequence. Their effects depend on genomic location, cell type, developmental stage and context. One label such as methylation should not be treated as uniformly silencing every gene in every tissue.

Epigenetic regulation can participate in differentiation and adaptation as well as illness-associated processes. It is not synonymous with environmental damage, and it does not mean that genetic sequence is irrelevant. A measured regulatory change and the cause of a psychiatric syndrome are separate claims.

## Environment, interaction and correlation

Stress, substances, treatment and other exposures may be associated with regulatory patterns. Such findings can provide candidate mechanisms for gene–environment relations, but interaction is a statistical/biological question that requires evidence; it is not established merely by naming an epigenetic pathway.

Gene–environment correlation and shared social or biological factors may also explain exposure patterns. Reverse causation is possible when illness or treatment changes the measured marker. Longitudinal timing, relevant controls and experimental evidence help distinguish alternatives but do not automatically remove every confounder.

## Tissue and cell composition matter

Blood measurements do not directly describe the same gene regulation in a specific brain cell. Differences in cell mixtures, smoking, medication, age and sampling conditions can produce or modify associations. Ask whether a finding reflects a change within cells, a change in their composition or both.

Likewise, a post-mortem brain result needs consideration of terminal illness, tissue handling and prior treatment. A plausible pathway is not proof that a marker records one particular life event or can establish recovered trauma history.

## Inheritance and reversibility require care

Stable regulation within a cell lineage is not equivalent to proven transgenerational inheritance of an acquired psychiatric trait in humans. Animal evidence and human observational associations answer different questions. Modifiability also does not establish that a treatment can safely reverse the relevant pattern or guarantee recovery.

Use epigenetic models to generate testable hypotheses while separating molecular measurement, exposure association, mediation and clinical utility. No epigenetic psychiatric diagnostic test, personal-trauma assay or targeted treatment promise is supplied.
chunks.title: Epigenetics and gene–environment relations in psychiatry

questions.modelAnswer: Structural MRI describes anatomy; diffusion assesses tissue microstructure/tract-related properties. BOLD fMRI indirectly reflects activity through blood oxygenation, not direct firing. PET/SPECT tracers assess selected molecular/physiological processes; MRS measures metabolite signals rather than release at every synapse. Spatial, temporal and interpretation limits differ, and correlated activity does not establish a causal pathway.
questions.prompt: What do structural, functional, molecular and spectroscopic imaging measure, and which signals are indirect?

questions.modelAnswer: Case–control averages may overlap despite statistical significance, limiting individual sensitivity/specificity and predictive value. Regions participate in multiple processes, making reverse inference unreliable. Normal structural imaging does not exclude psychiatric illness, and incidental findings may not explain symptoms. Clinically indicated neurological investigation differs from diagnosing a psychiatric disorder from a research activation map.
questions.prompt: Why can a significant group difference or region activation not automatically diagnose an individual?

questions.modelAnswer: Review selection, motion, medication, physiological state, task performance and analytic choices. Check leakage, small samples and site effects, then independent validation, calibration, reproducibility and incremental decision benefit. Longitudinal changes may reflect illness, treatment, development or other exposures; similarity to healthy averages does not prove repair or causal mediation.
questions.prompt: Which confounders and validation requirements matter before an imaging result changes clinical decisions?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- MRI, BOLD, tracer and spectroscopy signals measure different things.
- Group differences and reverse inference do not establish individual diagnoses.
- External validation and decision benefit are separate from internal accuracy.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Imaging evidence: a group difference is not a patient-level classifier

## Distinguish modalities and signals

Structural MRI describes anatomy; diffusion methods assess properties related to tissue microstructure/tract organisation. Functional MRI commonly uses a blood-oxygenation-dependent signal linked indirectly to neural activity. PET/SPECT methods use tracers to study selected molecular or physiological processes. MRS measures selected metabolite signals, not neurotransmitter release at every synapse.

Each method has spatial, temporal and interpretative limits. A BOLD change is not a direct electrical firing measurement, and correlated activity is not proof of a causal anatomical pathway. A normal structural image cannot exclude a psychiatric syndrome, while an incidental finding need not explain its symptoms.

## Clinical investigation and research classification differ

Imaging can identify or assess relevant neurological/structural explanations when clinically indicated. That purpose is different from diagnosing depression, psychosis or personality disorder from a research activation map. Consider history, examination, clinical trajectory and the actual question for the scan; no universal routine-imaging policy is implied here.

Case–control averages may overlap substantially. A statistically significant difference can be biologically informative without having sufficient sensitivity, specificity or predictive value for an individual. Reversing the inference from an active region to a particular mental state is also unreliable when that region participates in many processes.

## Evaluate a proposed biomarker

Check sample selection, motion, medication, physiological state, task performance and analytic choices. Internal model accuracy can be inflated by leakage, small samples or site-specific patterns. External validation, calibration, reproducibility and incremental decision value are separate requirements; successful computation does not establish clinical usefulness.

Longitudinal change may reflect illness, treatment, ordinary development or other exposures. A treatment-associated change is not necessarily its causal mediator, and visual resemblance to a healthy average is not proof of brain repair.

## Use findings proportionately

Describe what was measured, in whom, against which comparator and with what uncertainty. Preserve the difference between anatomy, physiological proxy, association, prediction and clinical decision benefit. The unit supplies interpretative discipline, not an approved psychiatric imaging classifier or a complete indication-specific investigation guideline.
chunks.title: Psychiatric neuroimaging: what it measures and cannot diagnose

questions.modelAnswer: Scalp EEG records voltage patterns mainly from coordinated cortical activity, with high temporal resolution but limited direct localisation, especially deep sources. Wake/sleep state, medicines, artefact and recording duration shape findings; one sampled trace is not whole-day brain activity. Diffuse slowing may support encephalopathy in context without identifying a specific cause.
questions.prompt: What does scalp EEG measure, and why do state, artefact and sampling limit interpretation?

questions.modelAnswer: NICE states EEG must not exclude epilepsy: normal routine interictal recording cannot settle suspicious events. An isolated abnormal waveform also needs a compatible history rather than explaining every symptom. Use event timing, precipitants, recovery and video/collateral evidence, considering syncope, functional events, intoxication/metabolic causes and specialist sleep/ambulatory/event-capture assessment where appropriate.
questions.prompt: Why must neither a normal recording nor an isolated abnormal waveform settle epilepsy without the clinical event account?

questions.modelAnswer: ERP averaging identifies stimulus-linked components; amplitude and latency are distinct and depend on attention, task and other conditions. P300 changes reported in schizophrenia also occur in other disorders and relatives, so neither a stand-alone diagnosis nor deterministic future prediction follows. Interacting systems generate the signal, not one uniquely identifiable cognitive operation.
questions.prompt: How do amplitude/latency and specificity limits qualify P300 findings in psychiatric research?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- A normal routine EEG does not exclude epilepsy.
- Electrical patterns require clinical/event and recording context.
- P300 research associations are not specific psychiatric diagnostic tests.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# EEG: electrical timing is not a psychiatric diagnosis

## Signal and recording context

Scalp EEG records voltage patterns arising largely from coordinated cortical activity. It has high temporal resolution but limited direct localisation, especially for deep sources. Recording conditions, wake/sleep state, medication, artefact and the sampled period affect interpretation. One trace is not a complete record of all brain activity throughout the day.

Diffuse slowing can support an encephalopathic process in the right clinical setting but is not specific to one cause. Epileptiform findings need interpretation with event history and examination; an abnormality is not an automatic explanation for every behavioural or psychiatric symptom.

## Epilepsy assessment is clinical

NICE NG217 states that EEG should not be used to exclude epilepsy. A normal routine interictal recording therefore cannot settle recurrent suspicious events. Conversely, a waveform without a compatible clinical account can mislead. Further sleep, ambulatory or event-capture work addresses different diagnostic questions and requires an appropriate specialist plan.

Video/event documentation, timing, precipitants and recovery belong alongside the EEG result. Syncope, functional events, intoxication, metabolic causes and other explanations require assessment rather than assuming a seizure whenever there was an unusual movement or loss of awareness.

## Evoked and event-related potentials

Averaging stimulus-linked responses can reveal components with characteristic timing, such as P300-related processing in target-detection tasks. Amplitude and latency are different measures and depend on task/attention and other conditions. These signals reflect activity from interacting systems rather than one uniquely identifiable cognitive operation.

Oxford describes reduced P300 measures in schizophrenia-related research but also in other disorders and relatives. That lack of specificity prevents using the pattern as a stand-alone psychiatric diagnostic test. A possible trait-related association is not a deterministic prediction of future illness.

## Keep measurement and clinical purpose aligned

Separate investigation of suspected neurological events or encephalopathy from research on information processing and vulnerability. Assess the actual clinical question, pretest context and recording limitations. No routine EEG screening programme, psychiatric subtype classifier or treatment-response guarantee is supplied; complete current event-assessment procedures require specialist review.
chunks.title: EEG and evoked potentials: psychiatric applications and limits

questions.modelAnswer: Incidence proportion is new cases divided by initially at-risk people over a defined interval, estimating risk under follow-up assumptions. Incidence rate uses new cases/person-time at risk, with rate units rather than probability. Point prevalence counts existing cases at one time; period prevalence covers an interval with specified denominator conventions. First-event time stops at onset, loss or observation end.
questions.prompt: Contrast incidence proportion, incidence rate and point/period prevalence with their time/denominator requirements.

questions.modelAnswer: One-year incidence proportion is 20/1,000 = 2%. At-risk time is 980 × 1 year plus 20 × 0.5 year = 990 person-years because first-onset cases stop contributing at onset. Incidence rate is 20/990 ≈ 0.0202 per person-year, or 20.2 per 1,000 person-years. This is hypothetical teaching arithmetic, not a disease estimate.
questions.prompt: Calculate one-year risk and person-time rate when 20 of 1,000 people develop first illness halfway through complete one-year follow-up; reconstruct the at-risk time denominator.

questions.modelAnswer: Prevalence depends on occurrence and duration, including recovery/survival. Detection, access, diagnostic definitions and population composition can alter recorded burden without equivalent biological-onset change; clinic attendance is not population prevalence. The prevalence ≈ incidence rate × duration approximation needs stable conditions and appropriate assumptions, not a universal identity or causal inference.
questions.prompt: Why can detection, duration or case-definition changes alter prevalence without the same change in incidence?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Incidence proportion is interval risk; incidence rate uses person-time.
- Point/period prevalence describes existing burden with an explicit denominator.
- Ascertainment, duration and population composition qualify comparisons.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Frequency measures: define who, what and when before dividing

## Incidence is new occurrence

Incidence proportion is new cases during a defined interval divided by people initially at risk of becoming cases. It estimates risk over that interval under the relevant follow-up assumptions. Incidence rate divides new cases by accumulated person-time at risk; its units are events per person-time, not a probability.

For a first-event analysis, a person stops contributing at-risk time after the event, loss to follow-up or the end of observation. Recurrent-event measures require a different defined counting scheme. Unequal observation time cannot be handled by silently treating every participant as followed for the same duration.

## Prevalence is existing case burden

Point prevalence counts current cases at a specified time over the corresponding population. Period prevalence covers cases present during an interval and must state its population/period convention. Neither is the same as the proportion of previously unaffected people developing illness.

Prevalence depends on occurrence and duration, including recovery and survival. The approximation prevalence ≈ incidence rate × average duration needs stable conditions and appropriate assumptions; it is not a universal identity or a way to infer a cause from one survey.

## Precision example and ascertainment

In an explicitly hypothetical first-onset cohort, 20 new cases among 1,000 initially unaffected people followed completely for one year gives 2% one-year incidence proportion. If the 20 cases occur halfway through the year, at-risk time is 980 full years plus 20 half-years: 990 person-years. The rate is approximately 20.2 per 1,000 person-years. The two denominators answer different questions.

Specify case definition, age/time frame, sampling and ascertainment. Clinic attendance is not automatically population prevalence. Changes in diagnostic criteria, access, detection or survival can alter recorded burden without an equivalent change in biological onset.

Report the population and uncertainty alongside the estimate. Comparisons across places or periods require compatible definitions and age/other composition, with suitable standardisation where needed. The measure describes frequency; it does not establish causation or individual prognosis by itself.
chunks.title: Incidence, prevalence and epidemiological frequency measures

questions.modelAnswer: Risk is an outcome probability; odds are p/(1−p). RR compares risks and OR compares odds, diverging when outcomes are common. Both ratio nulls are 1; risk-difference null is 0. State comparator, outcome and follow-up. Case–control sample case fraction is not population risk, and hazard ratios describe another time-to-event quantity rather than RR.
questions.prompt: How do risk, odds, RR and OR differ, including null values and sampling context?

questions.modelAnswer: Using treatment risk 0.10 and comparator risk 0.20: RR = 0.10/0.20 = 0.5; OR = (0.10/0.90)/(0.20/0.80) ≈ 0.444; ARR = 0.20−0.10 = 0.10; NNT = 1/0.10 = 10 over six months. These hypothetical values demonstrate different measures and provide no actual treatment evidence.
questions.prompt: Calculate RR, OR, ARR and six-month NNT for the hypothetical 20% versus 10% risks.

questions.modelAnswer: Identical relative effects can yield different absolute benefits with baseline risk. NNT/NNH are reciprocals of absolute risk differences for defined outcomes, populations and durations, not individual probabilities or interchangeable rankings; conventional whole-person NNT rounds up. Report uncertainty/harms, particularly when risk-difference intervals cross zero and simple finite reciprocal intervals mislead.
questions.prompt: Why must baseline risk, outcome, duration and uncertainty qualify reciprocal effect measures?

questions.modelAnswer: A strong observed ratio or small NNT cannot eliminate confounding, bias or design limitations and therefore does not establish causality. Individual selection also requires baseline risk, relevant outcome/time horizon, uncertainty, harms and preferences. An impressive estimate for one population or outcome cannot alone establish the best treatment for another person.
questions.prompt: Why can neither an impressive ratio nor a small NNT establish causality or the best individual treatment?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- RR compares risks; OR compares odds and is not automatically equivalent.
- Absolute effect and time horizon determine NNT/NNH.
- A ratio or reciprocal alone does not establish causality or individual response.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Effect measures: relative magnitude is not absolute benefit

## Risk and odds differ

Risk ratio is risk in one group divided by risk in the comparator. Odds are p/(1−p); an odds ratio compares those odds, not the probabilities. An OR can differ materially from an RR when outcomes are common. Its interpretation also depends on design and sampling; a case–control sample's case fraction is not the source population's risk.

Both ratios have a null value of 1. Risk differences have a null value of 0. Specify direction, outcome, comparator and follow-up before calling a value beneficial. A hazard ratio is a different time-to-event quantity and must not be relabelled a risk ratio.

## Absolute effects and reciprocal measures

For an undesirable outcome, ARR = comparator risk − treatment risk. NNT for one additional avoided event is 1/ARR when ARR is expressed as a proportion, with a stated time horizon; whole-person presentation conventionally rounds up. For increased undesirable events, NNH uses the reciprocal of the absolute increase. Neither is the chance that a particular individual will benefit or be harmed.

## Hypothetical calculation

Suppose six-month risks are 20% without and 10% with an intervention. Treatment/comparator RR = 0.5; odds ratio = (0.10/0.90)/(0.20/0.80) ≈ 0.444. ARR = 0.10, giving NNT = 10 over six months. This invented teaching example is not evidence for any actual treatment.

The same relative effect can yield different absolute benefit when baseline risk changes. NNTs from different outcomes, populations or durations are therefore not directly interchangeable rankings.

## Uncertainty and causality

Report uncertainty and relevant harms alongside benefit. If a risk-difference interval includes zero, a simple finite NNT interval can mislead across benefit/harm regions. An observed association or small NNT does not establish causality without an adequate design. Treatment selection requires clinical relevance, baseline risk and patient priorities, not one impressive number.
chunks.title: Relative risk, odds ratio, absolute effects, NNT and NNH

questions.modelAnswer: Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN), positivity among reference-positive people; specificity = TN/(TN+FP), negativity among reference-negative people. PPV = TP/(TP+FP) and NPV = TN/(TN+FN) condition on test results. Thus sensitivity is not the chance a positive is correct; predictive values depend on prevalence/pretest context, reference quality and threshold.
questions.prompt: Define sensitivity, specificity, PPV and NPV using TP/FN/FP/TN and their different denominators.

questions.modelAnswer: LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity); LR− = (1−sensitivity)/specificity. Convert pretest probability p to odds p/(1−p), multiply by the relevant LR, then convert updated odds o to probability o/(1+o). Multiplying probability directly by LR is incorrect; interpretation still depends on suitable accuracy estimates and the clinical context.
questions.prompt: How are LR+/LR− calculated and used to convert pretest to post-test probability?

questions.modelAnswer: At 1% prevalence, 100 of 10,000 have the condition: 90 TP and 10 FN. Of 9,900 without it, 90% specificity gives 8,910 TN and 990 FP. PPV = 90/(90+990) ≈ 8.3%; low prevalence makes false positives numerous. LR+ = 9 updates odds 1/99 to 1/11, giving probability 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. This is hypothetical arithmetic.
questions.prompt: Reconstruct the 10,000-person example and explain why PPV is about 8.3% despite 90% sensitivity/specificity.

questions.modelAnswer: Accuracy can vary with spectrum, threshold and verification/reference methods, rather than remain fixed across settings. Correlated tests cannot be combined by assuming conditional independence without justification. Evaluate uncertainty, false-result costs and what decisions change; favourable accuracy or AUC alone does not prove beneficial screening or an appropriate diagnostic pathway.
questions.prompt: Why must case spectrum, reference standard, correlated tests and decision consequences be reviewed?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Sensitivity/specificity condition on disease status; PPV/NPV on test results.
- Likelihood ratios update odds, not probability directly.
- Prevalence, spectrum and reference standard qualify accuracy and clinical value.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Diagnostic accuracy: condition on the right denominator

## Four cells, different questions

Against a defined reference standard, label true positives (TP), false negatives (FN), false positives (FP) and true negatives (TN). Sensitivity = TP/(TP+FN): positivity among those with the condition. Specificity = TN/(TN+FP): negativity among those without it.

PPV = TP/(TP+FP) and NPV = TN/(TN+FN) instead condition on the test result. They answer post-test questions and depend on prevalence/pretest context. High sensitivity is not the probability that a positive result is correct. Reference-standard quality and the selected threshold also affect interpretation.

## Likelihood ratios update odds

LR+ = sensitivity/(1−specificity); LR− = (1−sensitivity)/specificity. Post-test odds = pretest odds × the applicable LR. Convert probability p to odds p/(1−p), then updated odds o back to probability o/(1+o). Do not multiply probability directly by the LR.

## Hypothetical low-prevalence example

In 10,000 people with 1% prevalence and a test with 90% sensitivity/specificity, expected TP = 90, FN = 10, FP = 990 and TN = 8,910. PPV is 90/1,080 ≈ 8.3%. LR+ = 9: pretest odds 1/99 become 1/11, giving post-test probability 1/12 ≈ 8.3%. This is constructed arithmetic, not a real screening recommendation.

## Accuracy is not context-free utility

Sensitivity/specificity can change with case spectrum, threshold and verification methods; they are not guaranteed constants across settings. Avoid assuming conditional independence when combining correlated tests and thereby overstating certainty.

Report clinically meaningful accuracy and uncertainty, then ask what the result changes and what false results cost. A threshold or favourable area under a curve does not establish a beneficial screening programme. Diagnostic labels still require an appropriate population, reference and clinical decision pathway.
chunks.title: Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values and likelihood ratios

questions.modelAnswer: Cohorts define entry/exposure and examine subsequent outcomes; prospective versus retrospective describes data-collection timing, not whether exposure logically precedes the studied outcome. Known at-risk populations and adequate follow-up permit risk/incidence or person-time rates. Confounding, measurement, missing records and differential loss still matter; temporal ordering alone does not prove causation.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes prospective/retrospective cohort work, and which denominators make risk or incidence estimable?

questions.modelAnswer: Case–control studies sample by outcome, then compare prior exposure; controls should represent the relevant source population. Convenient controls can distort association, and investigator-selected case/control counts do not measure population risk. OR meaning/approximation depends on sampling and assumptions; recall/selection biases remain, so a retrospective label cannot substitute for analysing participant selection.
questions.prompt: Why do control selection and sampling scheme matter, and why is the sampled case fraction not population risk?

questions.modelAnswer: Cross-sectional designs measure exposure/outcome near one sampling occasion and can estimate prevalence and associations. They usually cannot determine which came first, leaving reverse causation and differential participation central. Larger sample size improves neither temporal ordering nor automatic causal identification; case definition and sampling still qualify the result.
questions.prompt: What can a cross-sectional study measure, and why is exposure–outcome timing uncertain?

questions.modelAnswer: Randomisation balances baseline causes on average; concealment prevents enrolment manipulation through foreknowledge; blinding reduces post-allocation behavioural/measurement biases. ITT retains allocation-based grouping irrespective of compliance when appropriately implemented. None automatically resolves missing outcomes, adherence, attrition or selective reporting, and ITT does not answer exactly the same question as per-protocol analysis.
questions.prompt: How do randomisation, concealment, blinding and intention-to-treat differ, and what problems remain?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Sampling by exposure, outcome or a snapshot produces different estimands.
- Randomisation, allocation concealment and blinding have different roles.
- A design label does not eliminate bias or guarantee applicability.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Study design: the sampling direction determines what can be estimated

## Cohort designs

Select or define a population by exposure or another entry condition and establish subsequent outcomes. Prospective and retrospective refer to the timing of data collection, not whether exposure logically precedes the outcome being studied. Incidence, risks and rates may be estimated when denominators and follow-up permit.

Confounding, exposure/outcome measurement and differential follow-up still matter. A temporal sequence supports interpretation but does not by itself prove causality. Existing records may improve feasibility while introducing missingness or ascertainment problems.

## Case–control designs

Sample cases and controls according to outcome status, then compare prior exposure. Controls should represent the relevant source population, not merely anyone convenient without the diagnosis. This design is useful for rare outcomes or long latency, but selected case/control numbers do not directly estimate population risk.

Odds ratios are common effect measures; when and what they approximate depends on control sampling and assumptions. Recall/selection bias can distort exposure comparisons. Calling the design retrospective does not replace an analysis of how participants were selected.

## Cross-sectional designs

Measure exposure and outcome at approximately the same sampling occasion. They can describe prevalence and associations but usually cannot settle whether exposure preceded outcome. Reverse causation and differential participation are therefore central concerns. A large sample does not remove this temporal limitation.

## Randomised controlled trials

Random allocation aims to balance known and unknown baseline causes on average. Allocation concealment prevents foreknowledge influencing enrolment; blinding addresses behaviour or measurement after allocation. These are different protections, and not every trial can blind participants or staff.

Attrition, adherence, outcome selection and analysis still affect validity. Intention-to-treat preserves the allocation-based comparison when implemented appropriately; it does not automatically repair missing data or answer the same question as a per-protocol effect. Precision, harms and applicability require review.

## Match design to the question

No label supplies a universal hierarchy for every causal, prognostic, diagnostic or rare-harm question. Examine sampling, timing, comparator, measurement and analysis before accepting an inference. Replication and generalisability are separate from a statistically significant result in one selected population.
chunks.title: Cohort, case–control, cross-sectional and randomised trial designs

questions.modelAnswer: Random error is sampling variation affecting precision. Selection bias distorts comparisons through recruitment/participation/follow-up; information bias distorts measurement; confounding reflects common causes of exposure and outcome. Larger samples may make biased results precisely wrong, while confidence intervals/p-values do not protect against all biases or establish causality. Nondifferential measurement does not guarantee harmless or always nullward bias.
questions.prompt: How do random error, selection/information bias and confounding differ?

questions.modelAnswer: A confounder is a common cause, a mediator lies on a proposed causal pathway, and a collider is a common consequence. Adjustment changes the question when blocking mediation and can introduce bias by conditioning on colliders. Choose variables against a defined causal question/timeline rather than everything available; causal diagrams express assumptions rather than verify them.
questions.prompt: Why should a mediator or collider not be treated as just another confounder to adjust away?

questions.modelAnswer: Check sampling/comparator, measurement, losses, analysis choices, reverse causation, common causes and sensitivity to alternatives. Longitudinal ordering, dose–response and plausible mechanisms support context without replacing adequate comparisons; repeated designs can replicate bias. Randomisation still faces deviations/missingness/reporting problems. State estimate, uncertainty and assumptions separately before claiming an intervention will change the outcome.
questions.prompt: What must be checked before turning a precise, temporally plausible association into a causal claim?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Larger samples reduce random error, not all bias.
- Confounders, mediators and colliders have different causal roles.
- Timing, plausibility and significance do not individually prove causation.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Causal interpretation: precise results can still answer the wrong question

## Random error and systematic error differ

Sampling variation can make estimates imprecise; confidence intervals express uncertainty under the model, not protection against every bias. Increasing sample size usually reduces random error but can make a biased estimate very precise. A small p-value does not establish representative sampling, correct measurement or causality.

Selection bias arises when recruitment, participation or follow-up creates a distorted comparison. Information bias concerns exposure/outcome measurement, including recall, observer expectations or misclassification. Nondifferential measurement is not a guarantee of harmless bias or movement only towards the null in every design.

## Confounding is an alternative causal explanation

An association can reflect common causes of exposure and outcome rather than an exposure effect. Specify the causal question and timing before choosing adjustments. Restriction, matching, randomisation and statistical adjustment provide different protections; none automatically removes unmeasured or poorly measured common causes.

A mediator lies on a proposed causal pathway and is not interchangeable with a confounder. Conditioning on a common consequence of exposure and another cause can introduce collider-related bias. “Adjust for every available variable” is therefore not a general solution. A causal diagram can clarify assumptions, but a well-drawn diagram cannot verify them by itself.

## Reverse causation and temporal evidence

Illness may change the apparent exposure: depression can affect activity, sleep, diet and treatment, which in turn affect measured biomarkers. Longitudinal timing helps but does not settle all shared causes or time-varying processes. A dose–response or plausible mechanism is supporting context, not a substitute for an adequate comparison.

## Interpret an effect claim proportionately

Check sampling, comparator, measurement, losses, analysis decisions and the sensitivity of conclusions to plausible alternatives. Replication of the same design can reproduce the same bias. Random allocation supports a causal treatment comparison, but deviations, missing outcomes and selective reporting still matter.

State the estimate, uncertainty and assumptions separately. An association can justify further research or surveillance without proving an intervention will change the outcome. The purpose is disciplined inference, not declaring every observational study useless or every trial automatically true.
chunks.title: Bias, confounding, random error and causal interpretation

questions.modelAnswer: Test–retest assesses consistency across suitable occasions; inter-rater reliability compares assessors; internal consistency relates items. Validity concerns support for the intended interpretation/use, including content, structure and criterion relationships. Responsiveness detects meaningful construct change, not treatment causation. Stable bias can be reliable, true clinical change can reduce stability, and item correlation alone proves neither dimensionality nor validity.
questions.prompt: Contrast test–retest/inter-rater reliability, internal consistency, validity and responsiveness.

questions.modelAnswer: Association shows analysed co-variation; prediction forecasts outcomes in a target setting; causation asks effects of specified changes/interventions. A noncausal marker may predict well, while a causal factor may add little discrimination because of distribution or measurement. These claims require different evidence, so reliability or correlated marker/outcome change cannot validate them interchangeably.
questions.prompt: How can association, prediction and causation diverge for the same marker?

questions.modelAnswer: Specify intended purpose/population/language, measurement validity and responsiveness, then evaluate external performance, calibration, clinical consequences and incremental decision value. Reproducibility or prediction alone does not show that acting on a score improves health or supports screening. Selection and disease spectrum alter performance; report the actual tested claim rather than use validated as universal endorsement.
questions.prompt: What is needed before a reproducible or externally predictive measure supports a clinical decision?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Reproducibility, content/construct validity and responsiveness differ.
- Association, prediction and causation answer different questions.
- A validated use in one population does not certify every new decision or setting.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Measurement and inference: five different claims

## Reliability concerns reproducibility

Test–retest reliability asks whether measurement is consistent across appropriate occasions; inter-rater reliability concerns different assessors. Internal consistency concerns relationships among items intended to measure a construct. These are not interchangeable, and a high item correlation does not by itself establish one dimension, correct content or a useful decision threshold.

Interpret repeatability against expected true change, measurement conditions and error. A stable bias can be highly reproducible. Conversely, poor stability during a genuinely changing clinical state may not indicate a defective instrument. The intended population, language and context matter.

## Validity concerns the intended interpretation

Content coverage, structural/construct relationships and comparison with an appropriate criterion provide different evidence. A scale labelled depression does not automatically measure all depressive phenomena or diagnose a disorder. There may be no adequate gold standard for the construct, and a correlation with another imperfect measure is not complete validation.

Responsiveness concerns detecting change in the intended construct; it does not mean that a changing score proves treatment caused improvement. The COSMIN framework distinguishes these measurement questions. Validity is attached to purpose and use, not a permanent badge earned by one study.

## Association, prediction and causation

Association means variables vary together under the analysis. Prediction asks how well information forecasts an outcome in the relevant target setting. Causation asks what would happen under a specified change or intervention. An associated factor can be a useful predictor without being causal, and a causal factor can add little predictive value when its distribution or measurement limits discrimination.

## Translation into decisions

Evaluate external performance, calibration, clinical consequences and incremental value rather than discovery accuracy alone. Reproducible score differences do not establish a beneficial screening programme or prove that acting on a marker improves health. Language, selection and disease-spectrum changes can alter performance.

Choose methods and claims that match the question. A strong relationship–outcome correlation, an internally consistent questionnaire and a successful treatment trial answer different propositions; none validates all the others. Report what was tested and what remains uncertain instead of using “validated” as an undifferentiated endorsement.
chunks.title: Reliability, validity, association, prediction and causation

questions.modelAnswer: Clarify requester, legal question, jurisdiction, material time and recipients; explain evaluator role and confidentiality limits. Forensic assessment is not automatically treatment or advocacy, and dual-role/objectivity limitations must be stated. Responsibility, proceeding participation, current capacity/treatment need and risk are distinct mandates governed by applicable law, not foreign textbook tests.
questions.prompt: Which mandate and role questions distinguish forensic evaluation from routine treatment?

questions.modelAnswer: Compare authorised collateral, records, communications and contemporaneous observations with the interview, noting timing, purpose and reliability. Differences may reflect memory, misunderstanding, context or deception rather than automatically malingering. Separate present findings from material-time state, assess substances/medical factors and demonstrate symptom-to-function links with supporting and contrary evidence instead of diagnosis alone.
questions.prompt: How should collateral discrepancies and material-time mental state be reconstructed without automatic deception conclusions?

questions.modelAnswer: Identify instructions, materials, methods, relevant history, mental-state/functional findings, formulation and an explicit answer. Distinguish observed/reported facts, inference and uncertainty; explain alternatives, limitations and missing evidence that could change conclusions. State expertise and jurisdiction boundaries; expert opinion supports rather than replaces the court’s determination, and AAPL methods do not supply Greek procedural authority.
questions.prompt: What must a report disclose so that its legal-question answer and uncertainties can be examined?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Define the mandate, role and confidentiality before evaluation.
- Present state, material-time function and legal questions differ.
- Separate facts, inference, alternatives and limits in an auditable report.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Forensic assessment: answer a defined legal question with traceable clinical reasoning

## Clarify the mandate

Establish who requested the assessment, the question, relevant jurisdiction, time period and intended recipients. Explain the evaluator role and confidentiality limits; this is not automatically a treatment relationship. Avoid dual-role conflicts where they compromise objectivity, and state any material limitation rather than quietly acting as an advocate.

Legal responsibility, ability to participate in proceedings, treatment need and risk are different questions. A current diagnosis does not answer them all. The referral wording and applicable law determine which functional findings are relevant; another country's legal test must not be imported because a textbook describes it clearly.

## Reconstruct evidence, not only an interview account

Review records, contemporaneous observations, relevant communications and collateral information where authorised. Compare the examinee's account with other sources, noting differences in timing, purpose and reliability. A discrepancy may reflect memory, context, misunderstanding or deception; it is not automatically proof of malingering.

For retrospective questions, separate mental state at the material time from the present examination. Substance exposure, neurological/medical illness, previous episodes and treatment history may matter. Demonstrate the proposed link between symptoms and function rather than merely attaching a diagnostic label to the alleged act.

## Make the report auditable

Identify instructions, materials reviewed, assessment methods, relevant history, mental-state/functional findings, formulation and the answer to the question. Distinguish observed facts, reported facts, professional inference and uncertainty. Explain alternative accounts and which missing evidence would change the conclusion.

The AAPL framework stresses collateral information and limitations to objectivity. It provides methodological support, not Greek procedural authority. Report boundaries of expertise and avoid numerical certainty that the method cannot support. The court's legal decision and the clinician's evidence-based opinion remain distinct.

## Continue ethical responsibility

Acute illness or risk identified during an evaluation still requires an appropriate safety response and referral. Document what was done without turning the assessment into undisclosed treatment or promising an outcome. Current Greek instructions on expert appointment, disclosure and report procedures require separate legal verification; no complete court-report template or procedural rule is encoded here.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Greek imputability: diagnosis must be linked to function at the time of the act

## A bounded enacted-text anchor

In the inspected 2019 Gazette text of Penal Code Article 34, non-imputability requires that a mental/intellectual disorder or disturbance of consciousness at the material time removed the ability to appreciate the wrongfulness of the act or act according to that appreciation. The alternatives are important: a diagnosis alone is insufficient, and the test is not simply whether the person could name a legal prohibition.

Article 36 addresses significantly reduced, but not completely absent, capacity and refers to reduced punishment under Article 83. Its second paragraph excludes culpably induced reduction within Article 35. Do not convert intoxication into either an automatic defence or a blanket clinical conclusion without the relevant legal analysis.

These are dated enacted-text anchors, not a certified 2026 consolidation. The Ministry-hosted PDF inspected separately retained legacy wording and was not used as current authority. Complete subsequent amendment and case-law review remains pending before operational use.

## Reconstruct the material-time link

Assess symptoms, cognition, reality testing, intoxication, neurological/medical factors and the timeline using contemporaneous evidence and collateral sources. Explain how the relevant disturbance affected appreciation or control, including evidence against that account. Later recovery, planning behaviour or amnesia should not be treated as a single decisive shortcut.

## Keep neighbouring questions separate

Present decision-specific treatment capacity, ability to participate in proceedings, criminal responsibility and current risk are different evaluations. A person may be ill yet retain the function relevant to one question. An expert clinical opinion supports, but does not replace, the court's legal determination.

Non-imputability also does not mean that no further legal/treatment question exists. Therapeutic/security measures have separate statutory conditions and procedures; no current duration or placement recipe is supplied. Do not substitute ordinary civil involuntary-admission criteria for criminal-law provisions.

## Document the limits

State the evidence, functional reasoning, date/jurisdiction and unresolved legal source checks. Avoid importing an insanity test from another country or presenting a score as the legal answer. Independent Greek legal and clinical approval remains required, with no release-validity date assigned.
chunks.title: Criminal responsibility and mental disorder: Greek framework

questions.modelAnswer: Specify harm type, potential victims, setting and time horizon.
