chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Violence-risk assessment: formulate a scenario and a response, not a certainty score

## Define the outcome and horizon

Specify the type of harm, potential victims, setting and time period. A short-term ward-aggression measure and a longer-term forensic reoffending assessment answer different questions. Risk of self-harm, general violence and sexual offending must not be merged into one undifferentiated danger label.

Gather history of relevant behaviour, current mental state, substance use, access to people/weapons, stressors and available support. Compare current circumstances with earlier incidents and note what has changed. Static history, dynamic factors and protective resources have different roles; absence of one recognised factor does not establish safety.

## Structured approaches differ

Actuarial tools combine specified information according to a defined algorithm and reference sample. Structured professional judgement organises relevant factors and supports a reasoned formulation/scenario and management plan. HCR-20 illustrates the latter; its summary judgement should not be represented as a simple probability read from a total score.

NICE NG10 discusses BVC/DASA-IV for inpatient monitoring rather than unstructured judgement alone. This setting-specific guidance is not authorisation to use a ward checklist as a complete forensic community prediction instrument. Training, version, population, evidence access and the manual qualify every tool.

## Management is part of the assessment

Describe plausible escalation pathways, warning signs and interventions: substance treatment, symptom care, contact/support, access restriction or an appropriate placement. Assign responsibilities and review triggers. A record saying high risk without an actionable plan provides little protection; a reassuring score without examining the scenario can be equally misleading.

## Prediction remains uncertain

Base rates, sensitivity and false positives affect the meaning of a risk category. Predictive performance in a group does not settle what one person will do, and restricting everyone above a cutoff can create substantial harm. Explain uncertainty and alternatives to the decision-maker.

Review after changes in exposure, state or setting, using collateral and team information. Protective planning and evidence-informed structure can improve communication without establishing zero risk or unlimited predictive accuracy. Complete instruments and Greek legal/disclosure procedures require specialist review; no copyrighted item list or automatic detention threshold is supplied.
chunks.title: Forensic violence risk: structured assessment and management

questions.modelAnswer: Convictions depend on detection and justice-system processes; self-report and institutional aggression measure different behaviours in different samples and settings. Follow-up and comparators also differ. Absolute risk gives the event probability behind a relative association: a large relative estimate may still accompany low absolute risk, and offender proportions cannot be reversed into patient risk.
questions.prompt: Why are conviction, self-reported violence and inpatient aggression not interchangeable, and what does absolute risk add?

questions.modelAnswer: Substance use, prior violence, antisocial behaviour and adversity complicate attributing violence to diagnosis alone. Attenuation with sibling rather than general-population comparators suggests familial confounding, not proof of a genetic cause: shared environment and selection remain alternatives. Neither substance-use findings nor statistical adjustment establish a sufficient cause for an individual act.
questions.prompt: How do substance-use and sibling-comparator findings qualify a diagnosis–violence causal claim?

questions.modelAnswer: Use group evidence to identify modifiable problems, then assess this person’s mental state, threat content, past pattern, access, exposure and protective supports. Address substance needs, distress and practical prevention while considering victimisation and exploitation. Diagnosis alone should neither label the person dangerous nor establish that treating one associated marker guarantees prevention.
questions.prompt: How should group findings inform an individual prevention plan while considering victimisation and protective factors?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Outcome definitions and absolute/relative measures matter.
- Substance use and familial/social factors complicate causal attribution.
- Diagnosis is not an individual violence forecast; victimisation also requires attention.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Violence evidence: relative association is not a diagnosis-based forecast

## Specify what the study counted

Interpersonal violence, recorded convictions, self-report and institutional aggression are different outcomes. Follow-up, sampling and comparator population also matter. A clinical forensic cohort is not representative of all people with the same diagnosis, and recorded offending reflects detection and justice-system processes as well as behaviour.

Compare absolute risk with relative association. A larger relative estimate can coexist with a low event probability, and a proportion among selected offenders cannot be reversed into risk among all psychiatric patients. Avoid pooling every disorder, substance exposure and violent outcome into one causal statement.

## Comorbidity and shared causes

Substance intoxication/dependence, prior violence, antisocial behaviour and adverse circumstances can change risk and complicate attribution. The schizophrenia–violence literature identifies important substance-use effects, but not a rule that substances explain every incident or that a diagnostic label alone makes someone dangerous.

Fazel's population study found that changing from general-population to sibling comparisons attenuated part of the association, illustrating familial confounding. This is not proof of one genetic cause; shared early environments and other selection factors are alternatives. Adjustment for measured variables also cannot eliminate every unmeasured cause.

## Clinical interpretation remains individual

Assess the actual mental state, threat content, access, exposure, past pattern and protective factors. A specific persecutory or jealous belief may matter in a particular scenario without every delusion implying aggression. Social circumstances and victim relationship can be as important as syndrome labels.

Patients can also experience victimisation and exploitation. Risk assessment should not frame them only as possible perpetrators or reinforce an unwarranted assumption that most people with severe illness are violent. Care must address safety, distress and substance-related needs rather than exclusion based solely on diagnosis.

## Evidence guides prevention, not a categorical verdict

Use findings to identify modifiable problems and appropriate support. Do not infer that an associated diagnosis is the sufficient cause of an act or that treating one marker guarantees prevention. Explain study age, outcome and generalisability when discussing evidence. No universal violence percentage, causal fraction or individual probability is supplied; the next decision still requires a specific formulation and current legal framework.
chunks.title: Mental disorder, substance use and violent offending: interpreting evidence

questions.modelAnswer: A paraphilia is an atypical interest, not automatically a disorder or an offence. DSM-5-TR paraphilic disorder requires the relevant interest pattern plus that disorder’s specified distress/impairment or harm/risk consequences. Sexually harmful conduct may occur with or without such a disorder; an allegation alone establishes neither diagnosis nor guilt.
questions.prompt: How do paraphilia, paraphilic disorder and sexually harmful conduct differ under the supplied DSM framework?

questions.modelAnswer: Establish alleged versus adjudicated events and obtain authorised collateral/contemporaneous evidence. Review previous behaviour, victim characteristics and access, fantasies, substances, disinhibition, relationships, opportunities, current supports and protective change. Investigate denial or inconsistency without treating it as automatic diagnosis, and keep examiner disgust or sympathy out of the risk formulation.
questions.prompt: What collateral, dynamic and victim/access information supports an individual sexual-risk formulation?

questions.modelAnswer: Static-99R is an actuarial sexual-recidivism instrument for adult males with a relevant charge or conviction. It does not test guilt or transfer automatically to women, adolescents or other populations. Coding version, training, norms and horizon qualify estimates; a category supplies no universal percentage and cannot replace dynamic assessment and management.
questions.prompt: What population/outcome does Static-99R address, and why must its score not be used as guilt or a universal probability?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Allegation, conduct, atypical interest and paraphilic disorder differ.
- Specific diagnostic criteria and risk scenarios must be assessed independently.
- Static-99R is population/outcome-qualified, not a guilt test or universal score.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Sexual-risk assessment: conduct, interest and disorder are separate questions

## Do not diagnose from an allegation alone

Sexually harmful conduct can arise in different clinical and social circumstances, with or without a paraphilic disorder. Conversely, an atypical sexual interest does not by itself establish criminal conduct. Establish the facts available, alleged versus adjudicated events, the referral question and the person's account without acting as an advocate or interrogator.

DSM-5-TR distinguishes a paraphilia from a paraphilic disorder: the latter requires the relevant interest pattern plus the specific consequences involving distress/impairment or harm/risk to others. Apply the particular disorder's criteria rather than assuming one general checklist supplies every diagnosis. A benign interest does not require a disorder label merely because it differs from a norm.

## Reconstruct the risk scenario

Review history, victim/access characteristics, fantasies/behaviour, substance exposure, disinhibition, relationships, current supports and opportunities. Obtain authorised collateral and contemporaneous evidence. A denial, minimisation or inconsistency requires investigation, not an automatic diagnostic conclusion; the examiner's disgust or sympathy must not determine the formulation.

Differentiate enduring history from current change and protective resources. Assess potential victims and practical access, not only severity of a label. General violence and sexual recidivism are different outcomes and may require different methods.

## Use tools within their scope

The Static-99R developer describes an actuarial sexual-recidivism tool for adult males with a relevant charge/conviction. It is not a general population test, a measure of guilt or a score that can be transferred automatically to women, adolescents or every clinical presentation. Norms, coding version and training determine interpretation.

A static estimate does not replace current dynamic assessment or a management plan. Explain the horizon, comparator, uncertainty and which changes could alter the scenario. Do not invent a percentage from a category without the applicable reference data.

## Specialist and safeguarding boundaries

Coordinate clinical care, victim safeguarding and authorised legal processes. Treatment selection must consider the actual disorder, consent and risks; no anti-libidinal dose or court-disclosure rule follows from this overview. Complete current tools, Greek procedural requirements and specific diagnostic/prescribing review remain necessary.
chunks.title: Sexual offending: psychiatric risk assessment and paraphilic disorders

questions.modelAnswer: Assess symptoms, physical health, risk, housing, income, relationships/supports, substances, occupation, access and the person’s goals. Case management coordinates assessment, treatment, follow-up and revision, with a named contact and explicit team/agency responsibilities. Community care is more than post-discharge prescribing or repeated assessments without ownership.
questions.prompt: What belongs in community assessment and case management beyond outpatient prescribing?

questions.modelAnswer: An effective handover confirms that the receiving service accepts responsibility, conveys medicines, pending investigations, warning signs and crisis contacts, and verifies follow-up. Explain the transition and failed-contact contingency to the person and chosen supporters. Sending a referral alone does not establish continuity or ownership.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes an effective handover from sending a referral?

questions.modelAnswer: Investigate missed contact for symptoms, transport, language, distrust or competing demands, offering proportionate outreach rather than automatic administrative discharge. Match intensity to changing symptoms, function, safety, engagement, physical health and patient priorities, and to actual service capacity. Diagnosis alone does not mandate escalation; local Greek pathways and implementation remain to verify.
questions.prompt: How should missed contact, changing needs and service capacity inform intensity without automatic discharge or escalation?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Continuity requires an accepted plan and accountable contacts.
- Multidisciplinary work must integrate expertise and next actions.
- A referral or appointment count does not establish accessible, effective care.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Community care: continuity must survive changes of setting

## A shared plan with identifiable responsibilities

Community psychiatry integrates symptom treatment, physical health, risk, social circumstances and personally meaningful goals. It is not simply outpatient prescribing after discharge. Housing, income, family/supports, substance use, occupation and practical access can determine whether a clinical plan is usable.

Case management provides assessment, coordination, follow-up and revision across this work. Clarify the named contact, what the wider team delivers, what other agencies provide and who responds to deterioration. A nominal coordinator without authority, access or a clear plan does not establish continuity.

## Integrate rather than duplicate expertise

Psychiatric, nursing, psychological, social and occupational contributions overlap but are not interchangeable in competence or responsibility. Shared information should help a formulation and agreed action, not produce repeated histories with no owner of the next step. Team review can identify changing need, missed tasks and conflicting advice.

Discuss the patient's understanding and priorities, identify obstacles to engagement and offer proportionate outreach. Missed appointments may reflect transport, symptoms, language, distrust or competing needs. Administrative discharge for non-attendance can remove care precisely when vulnerability is greatest.

## Handover is a clinical intervention

Transitions between inpatient, community, primary care and specialist services require current medicines, unresolved investigations, warning signs, crisis contacts and confirmed follow-up. Sending a referral is different from verifying that responsibility was accepted. Explain the change to the person and chosen supporters, including what happens if contact fails.

## Match intensity and review outcomes

Some people need stable long-term support, others temporary intensive input. Review symptoms, function, physical health, engagement and patient-defined outcomes rather than counting appointments alone. Escalation should reflect clinical need and feasible service capacity, not a single diagnosis or an assumption that community care is always preferable.

WHO's rights-based service framework emphasises connected, person-centred networks. It does not certify the local Greek team's staffing, availability or statutory powers. Document the actual service configuration and gaps; complete Greek pathway and confidentiality implementation requires separate review.
chunks.title: Community psychiatry: continuity, case management and team care

questions.modelAnswer: EIP aims at timely assessment and coordinated early psychosis care; untreated duration is a service concern, not proof that a delay caused an individual outcome. NICE CG178’s first-presentation access principle is independent of age or untreated duration, not a universal youth cutoff. Greek eligibility and availability need separate local verification.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes early-intervention access and delay concerns from an individual causal claim or universal age cutoff?

questions.modelAnswer: Combine pharmacological, psychological, family, social and occupational/educational work with physical-health, substance, trauma and safety assessment. Support study/work, relationships and personally chosen roles through realistic goals. A prescription alone is not EIP, and the model does not guarantee premorbid functioning or justify discouraging needed benefits.
questions.prompt: Which integrated interventions and realistic functional goals belong in an EIP model?

questions.modelAnswer: Escalate crises beyond team capacity to appropriate crisis/home-treatment or inpatient assessment while retaining clear EIP links and medication/follow-up ownership. Review symptoms, function, engagement, physical health, relapse and patient/family experience, recognising fidelity and comparator effects. Transition through a confirmed receiving service according to need, not an unexplained deadline.
questions.prompt: How should escalation, outcome review and eventual transition preserve care rather than a service label alone?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Timely access and coordinated early-course care are both parts of EIP.
- The package extends beyond medication and symptom response.
- Crisis and later transfer must preserve accepted responsibility and realistic recovery goals.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Early intervention: timely access plus integrated treatment

## Access is part of the intervention

An early-intervention service aims to reduce delays in assessment and provide coordinated care during the early course of psychosis. Duration of untreated psychosis is a relevant service concern, not proof that a particular delay caused an individual's outcome. Diagnostic uncertainty should prompt a careful pathway rather than leaving the person between services.

NICE CG178 recommends access for first episode/first presentation irrespective of age or untreated duration and assessment without delay. These source-qualified principles must not be replaced by an unsupported universal youth cutoff. A local programme may have different eligibility, so describe the actual route and avoid presenting a foreign service rule as Greek entitlement.

## Preserve the whole treatment package

The model includes pharmacological, psychological, social, occupational/educational and family-oriented work. Address physical health, substances, trauma and safety as well as psychotic symptoms. A rapid prescription alone does not reproduce the service intervention; neither does engagement without an adequate treatment plan.

Maintain roles, study/work and relationships where feasible, with realistic support and review. Do not promise every patient a return to premorbid functioning or discourage needed benefits merely to preserve optimism. Recovery goals should not be set by the team's assumptions alone.

## Outreach, crisis and continuity

Offer accessible contact and proportionate outreach when symptoms or practical barriers impede attendance. In an acute crisis exceeding service capacity, arrange urgent crisis/home-treatment or inpatient assessment as needed, retaining a clear link to the early-intervention team. Changing setting should not sever continuity or leave medication and follow-up ownership unclear.

## Evaluate benefit and transition

Review symptoms, functioning, engagement, physical health, relapse and patient/family experience. The package, implementation fidelity and comparator care matter to outcome evidence; the label EIP does not guarantee equivalent effects everywhere. Plan transfer or continuation according to need and confirmed receiving services, not an unexplained administrative deadline.

Complete current Greek eligibility, duration, referral and crisis arrangements remain to be checked. This unit defines the model and source-qualified access principles, not a promise of local availability or an automatic discharge timeline.
chunks.title: Early intervention in psychosis as a community-care model

questions.modelAnswer: Capacity is ability demonstrated under assessment conditions; performance is what happens consistently in everyday circumstances. Environment, symptoms, cognition, physical limitations and available support can separate them. Positive-symptom improvement does not itself establish independent functioning, and clinical, functional and personal recovery may progress at different rates.
questions.prompt: How do task capacity, everyday performance and symptom response differ?

questions.modelAnswer: Agree personally meaningful goals, assess abilities and environmental barriers, practise realistic skills and check transfer. Housing needs safety, stability, autonomy, preferred location and feasible support; work/education needs suitable demands, accommodation and practical/financial consideration. Independence is not a compulsory endpoint, nor does supported employment guarantee a job or establish Greek benefit rules.
questions.prompt: What must a housing/skills/employment plan address beyond a claim that the person is ready for independence?

questions.modelAnswer: Assess daily activity, quality of life, housing/work stability, participation, burden and relapse, not just completed exercises or placement. Name implementation support, confirm follow-up and service coordination, and plan responses to changing needs. Continued support can be appropriate; a move or clinic skill score alone does not show sustainable real-world benefit.
questions.prompt: Which outcomes and continuity arrangements establish sustainable rehabilitation rather than completed exercises or placement alone?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Capacity, performance and symptom improvement differ.
- Rehabilitation combines skills with opportunity and appropriate enduring support.
- Housing, work and inclusion goals should be personally meaningful and sustainable.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Rehabilitation: symptom response and real-world participation are different

## Assess function in context

Determine daily-living skills, cognitive/physical limitations, symptoms, motivation, social supports and environmental barriers. A person may perform a task in a clinic yet struggle to do it consistently at home; measured capacity and actual performance are not interchangeable. Improvement in positive symptoms does not establish independent functioning.

Agree personally meaningful aims rather than one mandatory destination. Some people need continuing support despite adequate symptom treatment. NICE NG181 recognises graded accommodation and long-term needs; independent tenancy is not the only legitimate outcome or a test of moral effort.

## Combine skill and opportunity

Practise relevant tasks in realistic settings, with prompts, environmental adaptation and feedback as appropriate. Cognitive rehabilitation, occupational work and social support can contribute, but a completed exercise is not proof of transferred benefit. Assess the everyday outcome the person values.

Housing plans should consider safety, stability, location, autonomy, support level and the person's preferences. Moving from intensive support requires a feasible plan and follow-up; retaining support can be appropriate rather than evidence of treatment failure. Administrative placement availability should not be disguised as a purely clinical recommendation.

## Work and education

Supported employment aims to help people who want work obtain and sustain it with appropriate support. NICE CG178 recommends offering supported employment in psychosis; the recommendation is not a guarantee of a job or a requirement that everyone be judged ready by a long preparatory course. Education and other meaningful activity also matter.

Consider workplace demands, accommodation, benefits/financial implications and the person's own priorities without imposing an unverified entitlement or benefit-withdrawal rule. Meaningful participation is broader than paid employment alone.

## Review sustainable outcomes

Evaluate quality of life, daily activity, housing/work stability, participation and burden alongside relapse. Identify who supports implementation, what happens when needs change and how services coordinate. Functional gains, clinical recovery and personal recovery can progress at different rates. Complete local housing, employment and social-support pathways require current Greek review; no universal independence or work target is encoded.
chunks.title: Psychosocial rehabilitation: function, housing, work and inclusion

questions.modelAnswer: Clinical recovery concerns symptoms and functioning under a stated framework; personal recovery concerns meaning, identity, agency, direction and participation. Personal recovery can improve despite residual symptoms, without making effective illness treatment unnecessary. Realistic hope and personally meaningful goals should coexist with clinical care, not promise cure or excuse inadequate services.
questions.prompt: How can personal recovery and clinical recovery differ without making symptom treatment irrelevant?

questions.modelAnswer: Define the decision, discuss feasible options including no change where relevant, explain benefits/burdens/uncertainty and relate them to the person’s priorities. Provide manageable information, check understanding and offer communication or advocacy support. Involve others by preference without replacing the person’s voice; a signature or agreement alone does not establish collaboration.
questions.prompt: What distinguishes shared decision-making from agreement to the clinician’s recommendation?

questions.modelAnswer: Record options, reasons for unavailable/inappropriate choices, service limitations, communication support, priorities, understanding, the agreed plan and review arrangements. Diagnosis or disagreement alone does not establish inability to decide. Emergencies or inability to participate require separately verified lawful processes; NICE shared-decision guidance is not a complete Greek capacity or emergency-consent protocol.
questions.prompt: How should unavailable options, supported participation and future review be documented without importing foreign capacity rules?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Personal and clinical recovery are distinct but compatible.
- Shared decisions connect feasible options with the person’s priorities and understanding.
- Constraints, emergencies and capacity require transparent, lawful separate handling.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Recovery orientation: a life worth living is not a symptom score alone

## Personal and clinical recovery

Clinical recovery concerns symptoms and functioning under a stated framework. Personal recovery concerns the person's direction, meaning, identity and participation, which may improve despite continuing symptoms. Neither should be used to erase the other's importance: treating serious illness and respecting a person's life goals can coexist.

Ask what matters now, what has helped before and which roles or relationships the person wants to preserve. Hope should remain realistic, not a promise of complete cure or an instruction to accept inadequate care. Peer support and chosen social resources can contribute without replacing needed clinical treatment.

## A shared decision is more than consent to a recommendation

Describe the actual decision and feasible options, including no change where relevant, with benefits, burdens and uncertainty. Discuss how each option fits the person's aims. NICE NG197 recommends manageable information and checking understanding, rather than presenting a lengthy menu and assuming the person has decided.

Offer communication, interpreter or advocacy support as needed and ask whether the person wishes to involve others. Family involvement can help but can also involve undue influence; it is not an automatic substitute for the person's voice. Diagnosis or disagreement alone does not establish inability to decide.

## Constraints must be transparent

Shared decision-making does not require clinicians to promise unavailable or inappropriate treatments. Explain service limitations, clinical reasoning and the possibility of further discussion or review. Immediate life-saving emergencies and inability to participate require their own lawful decision processes; the general NICE shared-choice guideline is not a complete Greek capacity or emergency-consent protocol.

## Document and revisit

Record options discussed, priorities, understanding, the agreed plan and when it will be reviewed. A signed form or apparently compliant answer is not evidence of a collaborative process. Decisions can change as symptoms, preferences or circumstances change.

WHO's community guidance supports person-centred and rights-based care, not a specific local entitlement. Review meaningful outcomes, agency, access and harms alongside clinical measures. No universal recovery endpoint, compulsory peer programme or foreign legal rule is imported into this educational framework.
chunks.title: Recovery-oriented care and shared decision-making

questions.modelAnswer: ACT uses multidisciplinary shared responsibility and caseloads, outreach in the person’s environment, direct integrated treatment, practical housing/occupation/substance support and crisis arrangements. This reduces reliance on one clinician or appointment attendance. Ordinary brokerage mainly connects the person to separate agencies; an ACT label alone does not establish actual coverage or model fidelity.
questions.prompt: How do shared caseloads, direct community provision and integrated support differ from ordinary appointment-based brokerage?

questions.modelAnswer: Examine mistrust, symptoms, communication and practical barriers, explain contact and agree preferences where possible. Persistence must remain proportionate and person-centred, not intimidation or authority for compulsion. Share a coherent formulation and agreed responsibilities so different staff do not repeat fragmented assessments; compulsory action requires the applicable legal framework.
questions.prompt: How should persistent outreach avoid becoming coercion or repeated fragmented assessments?

questions.modelAnswer: Check whether shared caseloads, community delivery and integrated support were implemented, and what comparator care already offered. Effects depend on population needs and baseline hospital use, not the service name. Review safety, function, housing, crises and patient experience; reduced admission alone is not success, and step-down requires supported continuity.
questions.prompt: Why do fidelity, comparator care and continuity matter before claiming that an intensive model is effective?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- ACT shares team responsibility and integrates outreach/practical treatment.
- Assertiveness is not automatic coercion or identical contact for everyone.
- Fidelity, population and comparator care qualify outcome claims.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# ACT: an intensive shared-team model, not compulsory contact by another name

## Match the model to persistent need

ACT provides comprehensive multidisciplinary care in the person's environment for people with substantial ongoing needs and difficulty obtaining effective support through usual services. Outreach, integrated treatment and practical housing/occupation/substance work distinguish it from simply increasing appointment frequency.

The team shares responsibility and caseload work, reducing dependence on one clinician's availability. Frequent review and accessible crisis arrangements support continuity. SAMHSA's current description includes integrated community and crisis response; these are model features, not a guarantee that every local team supplies the same coverage.

## Assertiveness must remain person-centred

Address missed contact by examining symptoms, mistrust, communication or practical barriers and offering proportionate engagement. Persistence is not authorisation for intimidation or coercion. Explain the purpose of contact, agree preferences where possible and use the applicable legal framework for any compulsory intervention.

Direct provision of services differs from brokerage to other agencies. Even an integrated team must coordinate with primary care, housing and social services, with identifiable responsibilities and information-sharing limits. A person should not have to retell the entire story simply because a different team member visits.

## Fidelity and comparator influence evidence

Staffing, shared caseloads, community delivery and integrated practical support matter to whether the model was actually implemented. A service label alone does not establish fidelity. Outcomes also depend on what usual care already provides, population need and baseline hospital use; an effect seen against weak comparator care is not guaranteed in another system.

FACT and other intensive variants change arrangements for fluctuating needs. Their terminology should not be treated as proof of identical structure, evidence or eligibility. No historical universal caseload ratio or traffic-light contact schedule is encoded.

## Review useful intensity

Assess housing/function, engagement, crises, hospital use, substance needs and patient experience. Reduced admission is not success if safety or quality of life worsens. Step-down requires a supported handover rather than loss of service for apparent improvement. Current Greek model availability, staffing and crisis procedures remain to verify; outreach alone cannot replace an adequate integrated care plan.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Acute community care: an alternative needs real capacity and a contingency plan

## Assess what makes home care feasible

Clarify urgency, suicide/violence risk, mental state, substances, medical causes, self-care and available support. Housing safety, victim access, ability to engage and the capacity of the actual service matter. A wish to avoid admission does not alone establish that home treatment is safe; neither does severe diagnosis alone require admission in every circumstance.

Immediate medical or psychiatric danger needs the appropriate emergency route. A crisis assessment should not be replaced by a routine appointment, a reassuring score or a safety agreement the person cannot use. Evaluate both what is needed and whether it can be delivered now.

## Consider appropriate alternatives

Crisis resolution/home treatment can provide frequent assessment, treatment and practical support, with crisis houses or acute day services where suitable. NICE CG178 considers community acute options before admission in psychosis and to support timely discharge. This is a source-qualified service recommendation, not a rule that every episode must first be managed at home.

Distinguish a supported crisis placement from unsupervised accommodation. Confirm staffing, access, observation capability, medication responsibility and escalation arrangements. Inform the person and chosen supporters about what the service can and cannot provide.

## Make ownership and review explicit

Document who is leading care, planned contacts, warning signs, out-of-hours response and thresholds for reassessment or admission. Sending messages across teams without accepted responsibility can create a dangerous gap. Supporters should not be assigned an unmanageable surveillance role merely because a service lacks staff.

Reassess after state, exposure or support changes. Home care can become unsuitable when engagement, safety or practical conditions deteriorate. Admission or increased support is a revised response to need, not proof of failure or noncompliance.

## Balance outcomes and rights

Avoid unnecessary institutionalisation while maintaining effective, lawful care. Patient experience, function and safety are more informative than a reduced admission count alone. Greek emergency contacts, service availability, involuntary pathways and discharge procedures require current local verification; no foreign statutory threshold or universal home-treatment duration is supplied.
chunks.title: Community crisis management and alternatives to hospital admission

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Neuropsychological evaluation: interpret a pattern against the referral question

## Screening is not the full evaluation

A brief cognitive screen can identify concern but does not provide the same detail as a formal assessment. Clarify the purpose: characterising change, differentiating contributors, planning rehabilitation or answering another defined functional question. A diagnosis, legal capacity or malingering judgement is not supplied automatically by one score.

Gather baseline abilities, education/language, sensory/motor function, medical/neurological history, mood, sleep, substances and medication. Collateral everyday function helps establish whether an apparent deficit is new and meaningful. Testing during delirium, marked fatigue or acute distress may answer a different question from stable baseline performance.

## Sample appropriate domains

Attention/processing speed, learning and memory, executive function, language, visuospatial skills and relevant motor functions are common domains. Tasks such as trail-making, verbal fluency, list learning or figure copying measure overlapping processes; an error cannot be assigned to one region without considering other requirements.

Select instruments with suitable norms, language and purpose rather than copying a fixed battery for every patient. Standardised administration matters, while accommodations must be documented and interpreted. Normative difference is not the same as decline from a person's own previous level.

## Performance and symptom validity

Assess whether the obtained profile can be interpreted, including task comprehension, consistency and relevant validity measures. Noncredible or invalid performance and intentional deception are different claims. A failed validity measure alone must not be turned into a complete malingering diagnosis without the appropriate context and evidence.

## Integrate rather than overlocalise

Compare patterns across tasks, history and observed function, considering multiple low scores, practice effects and measurement uncertainty. Psychiatric state or medication can affect performance without a progressive structural disease. Conversely, a plausible depression explanation does not eliminate neurological assessment when the history suggests it.

Communicate findings, limits and practical recommendations to the person and referral team. Review whether recommendations improve real-world functioning, not simply the test score. APA describes evaluation as history, testing, integration and feedback; complete instrument manuals and jurisdiction-specific legal questions remain separate specialist work.
chunks.title: Formal neuropsychological assessment: indications, domains and interpretation

# Remember

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Classical labels: describe the phenomenon before assigning a diagnosis

## Cotard and shared delusional content

Cotard describes nihilistic delusions, for example believing that the body, organs, self or world no longer exist. The theme can accompany severe depression or other illness; it is not an independent explanation of cause. Assess associated psychosis/mood symptoms, self-neglect and suicide risk rather than treating recognition of the name as completion of the evaluation.

Folie à deux is a historical label for shared/induced delusional phenomena. DSM-5-TR includes delusional symptoms in a relationship with an individual with prominent delusions as an example within other specified schizophrenia-spectrum/psychotic disorder. That is not an automatic diagnosis for two people agreeing on an unusual belief. Establish delusional quality, cultural context, relationship and each person's broader syndrome.

## Confabulation versus fantastic false narratives

Confabulation involves false accounts associated with impaired memory/reconstruction, not necessarily deliberate lying. Evaluate cognition, neurological/substance history, confidence and consistency. A plausible story does not establish intact memory, and an inaccurate one does not establish conscious deception.

Pseudologia fantastica describes elaborate false/fantastic narratives, with variable insight or investment in the story and no single universally accepted definition. It should not be equated automatically with a delusion, factitious disorder or malingering. Those conclusions require their own evidence, including motive and intentionality where relevant.

## Ganser-type approximate answers

Ganser's historical description includes conspicuously near-miss answers alongside other altered-state phenomena. Apparent knowledge of the right answer or occurrence in a forensic setting does not prove malingering. Evaluate consciousness, cognition, dissociation, psychosis and medical/substance causes rather than diagnosing intentional deception from one arithmetic error.

## Current formulation matters more than the eponym

Document the actual thought content, memory process, awareness and behaviour, then the supporting and conflicting evidence. A descriptive label, historical syndrome and current classification category are different levels. Collateral and repeat assessment can clarify uncertain presentations without hostile confrontation or false certainty.

No eponym supplies a treatment, legal responsibility conclusion or diagnostic shortcut. Preserve stable phenomenological distinctions while checking the applicable current manual and clinical risk; unfamiliar or theatrical behaviour alone does not establish fabrication.
chunks.title: Classical psychopathological labels: Cotard, shared delusions and false narratives

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Safeguarding: assess danger and coercion without erasing autonomy

## Recognise vulnerability and harm

Consider physical, sexual, psychological or financial abuse, neglect, exploitation and coercive control. Dependence, cognitive difficulty, severe illness, isolation or insecure housing may increase vulnerability, but no diagnosis alone proves abuse or inability to decide. A person can face harm without identifying themselves as a victim.

Enquire privately where safe, using accessible communication and avoiding a suspected perpetrator as the interpreter or sole informant. Changes in behaviour, unexplained injuries, withheld resources or fearful interactions require assessment, not an automatic allegation. Distinguish direct observation, the person's account and inference.

## Safety and medical care come first

Assess immediate danger, injury, intoxication, self-neglect and urgent medical/psychiatric needs. Consider children or other adults exposed to the situation as well as the identified patient. A community support plan cannot substitute for emergency care or protection when it is not feasible.

## Choice, coercion and capacity differ

Ask what the person wants and whether they can communicate freely. Apparent agreement under threats may not represent a voluntary choice. Decision-specific capacity, risk acceptance and an unwise preference are different questions; disagreement or dependence must not be used as a substitute for assessment.

Involve appropriate safeguarding, social, clinical and legal support with attention to confidentiality and the governing Greek duties. Do not promise absolute secrecy before explaining possible limits. Nor should all information be broadcast on the assumption that safeguarding overrides every privacy consideration.

## Record, coordinate and review

Document the account, findings, immediate actions, consent/concerns, consulted services and accepted follow-up responsibilities. Avoid repeated interviewing that increases distress or compromises evidence. A referral needs an identified receiving route and a plan for further danger.

NICE care-home guidance and Oxford's domestic-abuse discussion support recognition and coordinated response, not Greek statutory thresholds. English local-authority/Mental Capacity Act procedures must not be copied as Greek law. Current Greek reporting, disclosure, emergency and protective-measure rules remain to verify. The educational framework supplies clinical questions and proportionate coordination, not an automatic reporting checklist or authority to override autonomy.
chunks.title: Adult safeguarding: vulnerability, abuse, exploitation and clinical responsibility

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Brief depressive presentations: duration and symptom count must be stated separately

## Use the supplied DSM-5-TR framework explicitly

Other specified depressive disorder communicates the reason a clinically significant presentation does not meet a named depressive-disorder category, with relevant exclusions. Unspecified is different: the clinician does not state the reason, including when information is insufficient. Neither label means distress is trivial or removes the need to assess risk.

The supplied manual examples separate three patterns. Recurrent brief depression has depressed mood plus at least four other symptoms for 2–13 days at least monthly for twelve consecutive months, unrelated to the menstrual cycle. Short-duration depressive episode has depressed affect plus at least four of the other eight major-episode symptoms with distress/impairment and a shorter duration. Insufficient-symptom depression has depressed affect plus at least one other symptom with distress/impairment for at least two weeks.

## Preserve a source ambiguity rather than invent precision

The short-duration heading says 4–13 days, while its prose says more than four and fewer than fourteen days. A presentation lasting exactly four days therefore requires original-manual/erratum clarification; do not silently decide that the heading or prose overrides the other. The supplied examples also carry prior depressive/bipolar and current active/residual psychotic-disorder exclusions; short-duration excludes recurrent brief depression, and the insufficient-symptom example has its own mixed-anxiety/depression exclusion.

## History determines the differential

Assess prior full episodes, hypomania/mania, substances/medication, medical causes, menstrual linkage, stressor-related adjustment, grief and persistent mood symptoms. A duration below two weeks is not automatic evidence of bipolarity, and an intense short episode cannot be classified by severity alone.

Establish functional change, recurrence, safety and the actual symptom timeline using collateral where helpful. Past qualifying episodes can change how the current presentation is formulated; do not assign a supplied residual example while ignoring its exclusions.

## Follow-up is part of formulation

Brief presentations may resolve, recur or develop into another syndrome. Review longitudinal evidence rather than treating a provisional category as permanent. ICD and DSM categories should not be combined into a synthetic threshold. This study records supplied-manual teaching and its unresolved boundary, not clinical approval of a four-day rule or a complete current coding protocol.
chunks.title: Brief and other specified depressive presentations: classification and differential

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Bipolarity indicators: suspicion guides history, not an automatic diagnosis

## Look for a longitudinal syndrome

A depressive presentation can be part of unipolar or bipolar illness. The decisive history concerns episodes of mania/hypomania and their duration, symptoms, change from baseline and consequences—not a single atypical symptom. Ask about reduced need for sleep, increased activity/energy, disinhibition and observable episodic change, with collateral where possible.

Family history, earlier onset, recurrent episodes or psychotic/mixed features may increase concern, but do not individually establish bipolar disorder. A screening score or mood-instability description cannot replace a full episode assessment. Temperament, ADHD, substances, personality-related reactivity and situational excitement can create superficially similar accounts.

## Preserve important phenomenological distinctions

Reduced sleep need with sustained energy is different from insomnia with fatigue. Irritability or agitation alone is not hypomania. A depressive episode with some activation requires framework-specific mixed-feature assessment rather than an invented hybrid diagnosis or assumption that all agitated depression is bipolar.

Psychotic symptoms and atypical neurovegetative changes occur in more than one disorder. Their presence should prompt a careful differential and severity/risk review, not a deterministic prediction of later mania. The association between family history and risk likewise does not tell the outcome for one person.

## Treatment-emergent change and competing causes

New activation after an antidepressant may reflect an adverse effect, substance/medication exposure or a qualifying mood episode. Establish persistence, full syndrome and temporal relation; feeling briefly energised is not sufficient. Medical/neurological contributors and changes in sleep or substances should be assessed.

## Follow uncertainty prospectively

Document what supports bipolarity, what is absent and which missing history could change the formulation. Review future episodes and give appropriate warning-sign/contact advice without declaring conversion inevitable. Treatment choices and risks should reflect the degree of evidence and require their own phase-specific guidance; this unit does not prescribe a universal augmentation or antidepressant prohibition.

Use the applicable DSM/ICD criteria separately and avoid converting predictor literature into diagnostic criteria. Current safety, functioning and suicide assessment remain necessary regardless of the eventual polarity label. A coherent longitudinal account is more informative than collecting a maximum number of suggestive features.
chunks.title: Depression with bipolarity indicators: predictors and later mania

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Beyond monoamines: test pathways without making a universal disease story

## Glutamatergic and plasticity hypotheses

NMDA/AMPA signalling contributes to activity-dependent plasticity and interacts with inhibitory and monoamine networks. Proposed rapid-antidepressant pathways link NMDA-related disinhibition with downstream AMPA and trophic signalling. Receptor pharmacology, cellular change and clinical improvement are separate observations; their compatibility does not establish one necessary mediator.

BDNF and other growth-factor pathways support synaptic functions, but blood levels or imaging changes do not directly count newly repaired synapses. Animal neurogenesis and human symptom response cannot be treated as the same outcome. A reduced group marker does not prove that every depressed patient has irreversible neuronal loss.

## Immune and inflammatory associations

Some depressive groups show altered inflammatory markers, and proposed mechanisms involve immune–brain communication, microglial activity, oxidative/metabolic pathways and neurotransmission. These possibilities do not make depression identical to a general inflammatory disease or establish a CNS mechanism from one peripheral assay.

Obesity, infection, chronic disease, smoking, activity, sleep and treatment can affect the measured association. These can be causes, consequences or shared influences. Distinguish subgroup findings from an individual classification and evaluate timing and comparator before declaring mediation or treatment resistance explained.

## Integrate stress and environment

HPA, circadian and psychological/social processes interact with biological pathways rather than competing as mutually exclusive explanations. A plausible stress-to-plasticity diagram is not proof that a patient's brain has permanently degenerated. Environmental change and established treatment remain relevant even when a biological risk factor is present.

## Clinical translation requires more evidence

To select an intervention from a biomarker, establish reliable measurement, target-population validation, incremental decision value and evidence that the strategy improves outcomes with acceptable harm. Association with poor response does not by itself prove that blocking the pathway will restore it.

The inspected textbook models generate research questions; their optimistic language is not an approval for an anti-inflammatory or neuroprotective prescription. No CRP/BDNF threshold or new biologic dose is supplied. Meaningful symptoms, function, safety and conventional medical differential assessment remain central while specialised targeted-treatment evidence and current guidelines are reviewed separately.
chunks.title: Depression neurobiology: glutamate, plasticity and immune-model limits

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Complex PTSD: all core PTSD requirements plus disturbances in self-organisation

## Apply the ICD-11 framework, not trauma history alone

WHO CDDR describes complex PTSD (6B41) after extremely threatening/horrific exposure, most commonly prolonged or repeated events from which escape is difficult. That common pattern is not a requirement that only childhood or prolonged interpersonal trauma can qualify. Exposure alone cannot establish the diagnosis.

The syndrome includes all three PTSD core elements lasting at least several weeks: re-experiencing in the present, deliberate avoidance and a persistent sense of current threat. Rumination about an event is not necessarily here-and-now re-experiencing. Do not substitute DSM symptom counts or its duration threshold for this ICD framework.

## Additional self-organisation domains

Severe/pervasive affect-regulation difficulties, enduring negative self-concept with shame/guilt/failure, and persistent difficulty sustaining relationships or closeness must be assessed. These are three distinct domains, not any one general description of complexity. Significant functional impairment—or function maintained only with substantial extra effort—is also relevant.

Dissociation, substance use, depressive symptoms or self-harm may coexist but do not alone replace these requirements. Evaluate their timing and whether a separate disorder's full requirements are met rather than assigning every possible label to overlapping symptoms.

## Distinguish PTSD, BPD and classification systems

ICD complex PTSD and ordinary PTSD are differentiated by the additional domains, not simply trauma severity. BPD-pattern difficulties can overlap in affect and relationships. WHO describes complex PTSD as more often involving a stable negative self-view and relational avoidance/disconnection, compared with unstable identity, abandonment fears and volatile relationships in borderline-pattern presentations. These are differential clues, not exclusive rules. Assess both full frameworks rather than treating them as synonyms or declaring overlap impossible.

DSM-5-TR does not provide an identically named independent complex-PTSD category. A broader DSM PTSD/dissociation/personality formulation is not an exact crosswalk. Historical enduring personality change after catastrophic experience is also not mechanically interchangeable with the current ICD diagnosis.

## Formulate care and uncertainty

Assess safety, ongoing adversity, functioning, preferences and comorbidity. Greater symptom complexity does not prove that trauma-focused treatment is automatically contraindicated or that one mandatory phase sequence suits everyone. This unit defines the diagnostic architecture and boundaries, not a full psychotherapy protocol. Independent clinical/manual comparison remains required before approved use.
chunks.title: Complex PTSD: ICD-11, PTSD/BPD boundaries and historical concepts

questions.modelAnswer: Depersonalisation is detachment from self, body, actions or emotions; derealisation is an unreal/distant quality of surroundings. # Depersonalisation/derealisation: diagnostic boundaries and care

## The experience and the diagnosis
Depersonalisation is detachment from one's self, body, actions or emotional experience; derealisation is an unreal or distant quality of the surroundings. Emotional numbing, altered time and perceptual distortion can be intensely distressing. The defining distinction is retained reality testing: the world feels unreal, rather than being accepted as literally replaced or fabricated. An unusual description alone does not establish a delusion.

DSM-5-TR requires persistent or recurrent depersonalisation, derealisation or both, significant distress or impairment, intact reality testing during the experiences, and the relevant exclusions. It does not specify a minimum number of months. A transient experience during fatigue, panic or intoxication is not automatically the independent disorder. Where another disorder better explains the experience, formulate it within that syndrome.

## Exclude by chronology and phenomenology
Ask about onset, duration, triggers, awareness, memory, panic physiology and the meaning attributed to the experience. Review cannabis, hallucinogens, dissociative drugs, alcohol and prescribed medicines. PTSD, acute stress, depression, panic and other dissociative syndromes can include these symptoms. Psychosis requires assessment of convictions and the wider syndrome, not an inference from the word unreal.

Stereotyped brief spells, impaired awareness, automatisms, neurological signs or a new atypical presentation warrant medical/neurological assessment, including consideration of seizures. Testing follows the history and examination; neither an indiscriminate scan nor a purely psychological attribution is the default. Subjective difficulty owning memories differs from objectively demonstrated amnesia or cognitive decline.

## Care without a premature mechanism claim
Explain the distinction between an altered subjective experience and loss of reality testing, while acknowledging disability. Address precipitating substances, sleep disruption and qualifying comorbid disorders. Psychological work can target distress, attentional fixation and avoidance; treatment choice requires an individual formulation rather than a universal trauma explanation. The inspected classification establishes diagnosis, not a drug regimen. Medication evidence and a disorder-specific psychotherapy plan require further review; do not present an anxiolytic or antipsychotic as an established cure for the primary disorder.
chunks.title: Depersonalisation/derealisation: diagnostic boundaries and care

# Dissociative amnesia and identity disorder: careful differential assessment

## Two different centres of gravity
Dissociative amnesia concerns inability to recall important autobiographical information, usually stressful or traumatic, beyond ordinary forgetting. Localised and selective gaps are more typical than loss of the entire life history. DSM-5-TR additionally requires significant distress or impairment and exclusion of substances, neurological/medical conditions and better explanatory disorders. Fugue is a specifier: travel or wandering associated with amnesia for identity or other important autobiographical material, not every unexplained journey.

Dissociative identity disorder requires disruption of identity involving two or more distinct personality states, with marked discontinuity in self and agency, alongside recurrent memory gaps beyond ordinary forgetting. Distress/impairment and exclusions remain necessary. Symptoms may be reported or observed; dramatic named identities or overt switching are not compulsory. Broadly accepted cultural/religious practices and children's fantasy play must not be pathologised.

## Establish the pattern before interpreting it
Construct a timeline from the patient's account, contemporaneous records and consented collateral. Distinguish retrospective autobiographical gaps from impaired encoding during intoxication, delirium or seizures. Consider transient global or epileptic amnesia, head injury, neurocognitive disorder, PTSD, mood disorder and psychosis. Voice hearing alone cannot decide between psychotic and dissociative formulations; assess delusions, thought disorder, agency, chronology and overall function.

Reported trauma supports neither automatic diagnosis nor certainty about the historical accuracy of a newly recalled event. Use neutral, open questions. Avoid coaching identity elaboration or presenting suggestive memory-recovery procedures as factual verification. Apparent inconsistencies are a reason to investigate, not proof of deception; factitious disorder or malingering needs its own evidence and context.

## Clinical priorities
Assess self-harm, exploitation, current safety and functional disruption. Stabilise urgent medical or psychiatric problems and maintain continuity of care while uncertainty is resolved. A collaborative formulation can acknowledge the experiences without prematurely committing to their cause. Specialist psychological care and treatment of comorbidity may be needed. These diagnostic descriptions do not validate a recovered memory, prescribe a universal treatment sequence, or substitute for neurological investigation when red flags are present.
chunks.title: Dissociative amnesia and identity disorder: careful differential assessment

# Impulse-control disorders: pattern, motive and classification

## Failed control is not sufficient by itself
An impulse-control diagnosis describes a characteristic recurrent pattern after competing explanations have been assessed. Establish the act, antecedent tension, gratification or relief, motive, consequences and control attempts. Mania, intoxication, neurological disinhibition, developmental limitations and instrumental offending can produce superficially similar behaviour. A psychiatric label does not establish criminal responsibility or remove the need for safeguarding.

Intermittent explosive disorder concerns disproportionate, impulsive/anger-based aggression rather than planned aggression for money, power or intimidation. DSM-5-TR permits either non-injurious/non-destructive verbal or physical aggression averaging twice weekly for three months, or three destructive or injury-producing outbursts within twelve months. Distress, impairment or financial/legal consequences are required; minimum chronological age is six years or equivalent developmental level. Exclusions matter, including adjustment-related outbursts in ages six to eighteen. These DSM thresholds must not be silently attributed to ICD.

## Motive distinguishes stealing and fire setting
WHO ICD-11 kleptomania involves recurrent uncontrolled stealing without an apparent personal-use or monetary motive, with preceding tension and subsequent gratification/relief. Ordinary theft is not kleptomania. Pyromania involves repeated fire setting or attempts, fascination with fire, preceding arousal and gratification, without an apparent motive such as revenge or profit. Fire setting for another purpose, or secondary to mania/intoxication/cognitive impairment, needs a different formulation. Pyromania can include planning: lack of an external motive is not synonymous with absence of preparation.

## Sexual behaviour and addiction boundaries
ICD-11 places compulsive sexual behaviour disorder among impulse-control disorders. Loss of control and repetitive behaviour must extend over time (the WHO example is six months or more), with impairment or marked distress and relevant mental, medical and substance exclusions. High sexual interest alone and distress entirely from moral disapproval are insufficient. It is not a DSM-5-TR diagnosis or simply a synonym for paraphilia. Gambling and gaming disorders belong to ICD disorders due to addictive behaviours, not this grouping.

Care begins with safety, comorbidity, triggers and a disorder-specific behavioural formulation. Do not infer a single effective medicine, a shared cause or legal exculpation from the category name.
chunks.title: Impulse-control disorders: pattern, motive and classification

# Dual diagnosis: chronology and integrated treatment

## A service problem as well as a diagnostic problem
Dual diagnosis commonly denotes a substance-use disorder coexisting with another mental disorder, especially psychosis, mood disorder or anxiety. It is not itself one uniform diagnosis. Substance exposure may cause symptoms, exacerbate an independent illness, be used in response to symptoms, or share vulnerabilities with that illness. Several relationships can coexist in the same person and change over time.

Map intoxication, withdrawal, periods of reduced use, prescribed treatment and psychiatric episodes on one timeline. Ask about quantity, frequency, route, last use and combinations, including medicines taken outside their prescription. Establish symptoms predating exposure or persisting outside its expected effects, but do not use a single universal abstinence interval to decide every substance-related differential. Collateral and toxicology may help; a positive result does not establish causation, and a negative result does not exclude every exposure.

## Treat the person across both pathways
Acute priorities include overdose, dangerous withdrawal, delirium, suicidality, violence, exploitation and physical complications. Reassess diagnoses made during an emergency after stabilisation. Withdrawal can imitate anxiety or mood deterioration; agitation or suspiciousness can reflect intoxication, primary psychosis or both. A crisis diagnosis should not become a permanent unexplained label.

An integrated plan gives both conditions named treatment goals, responsible clinicians and coordinated follow-up. Include motivational work, harm reduction, relapse prevention, indicated psychiatric treatment and housing/physical-health support. Readiness to change is a treatment variable, not an admission criterion requiring perfect abstinence. For psychosis, NICE CG120 advises access to both mental-health and substance-use services rather than exclusion by either diagnosis; this is UK guidance, not a claim about Greek service entitlement.

## Prescribing and continuity
Consider additive sedation, overdose risk, altered exposure and adherence. A long-acting antipsychotic can address an appropriate adherence problem but is not a specific treatment for substance use. Discuss interactions without moralising. Transitions need accepted responsibility, a shared crisis plan and arrangements for both conditions. Reduction in psychiatric symptoms does not prove substance recovery; reduced use does not remove the need to follow an independent mental illness.
chunks.title: Dual diagnosis: chronology and integrated treatment

# Substance use in pregnancy: exposure, withdrawal and coordinated care

## Distinguish exposure from a deterministic prediction
Assess alcohol, opioids, cannabis, stimulants, tobacco and prescribed/non-prescribed medicines together. Establish gestational timing, route, amount, dependence, combinations, nutrition, infection and access to antenatal care. A punitive interview can impede disclosure; explain confidentiality and the limits of local safeguarding procedures before testing or sharing information. Foreign mandatory-reporting rules are not Greek law.

Alcohol can cause fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, including neurodevelopmental impairment. CDC states that no safe amount, timing or type of alcohol in pregnancy is established. This is prevention advice, not evidence that every exposure causes an affected child. A dependent pregnant person may require medically supervised withdrawal: abruptly stopping heavy use without assessment can introduce maternal and fetal danger. Obstetric and addiction teams must coordinate that decision.

## Opioid dependence needs treatment, not an unsupported detoxification target
ACOG recommends opioid agonist treatment for pregnancy-associated opioid-use disorder in preference to medically supervised withdrawal because of relapse-related harms. Methadone or buprenorphine selection and dosing require specialist care. Neonatal opioid withdrawal is a possible consequence of exposure, including treatment exposure; it does not by itself show that effective maternal treatment was a mistake. Plan neonatal observation and continuing maternal support rather than abruptly withdrawing treatment to avoid neonatal symptoms.

## Cannabis and stimulants
Cannabis is not an established safe treatment for pregnancy-related nausea or anxiety. CDC describes potential adverse fetal growth and later developmental associations; confounding and exposure measurement limit precise individual predictions. Do not translate observational associations into a guaranteed developmental deficit.

Stimulant exposure raises concern about maternal cardiovascular toxicity and adverse obstetric outcomes; intoxication, chest pain, severe hypertension or altered consciousness requires urgent assessment. Substance-specific, timing-specific risks differ and should not be compressed into one generic neonatal abstinence syndrome.

## The continuing plan
Combine antenatal care, addiction treatment, psychiatric assessment, nutrition, infection prevention and practical support. Review prescribed medicines separately for pregnancy and lactation; a prenatal exposure discussion is not a breastfeeding recommendation. Prepare delivery/neonatal handover and postpartum relapse and overdose prevention. Avoid numerical risk estimates or drug-switching instructions unsupported by current product and obstetric guidance.
chunks.title: Substance use in pregnancy: exposure, withdrawal and coordinated care

# MDMA, dissociative drugs and volatile inhalants: toxidrome distinctions

## Exposure identity is provisional
A street name does not establish composition, dose or purity. Ask about timing, combinations, environment and route; examine physiology rather than waiting for a toxicology label. Mixed exposures can obscure the expected syndrome. Agitation or unusual perception may be toxicological, and apparent psychiatric symptoms do not remove the need for emergency medical assessment.

## MDMA: serotonergic/stimulant effects and competing fluid hazards
MDMA produces stimulant and perceptual/emotional effects through monoaminergic mechanisms, prominently serotonergic. The acute presentation can include autonomic activation, anxiety, agitation and altered perception. Hyperthermia, seizures and systemic complications require urgent recognition. Hot crowded environments and exertion can increase risk, but their absence does not establish safety.

Hyponatraemia is a different emergency from dehydration. Excessive water intake can contribute to severe hyponatraemia; giving unrestricted water to someone who is confused after MDMA is not a safe default. Assess temperature, consciousness, cardiorespiratory status, electrolytes and complications according to the presentation. No universal fluid or sedation regimen is encoded here.

## PCP and ketamine: dissociation is not the same as a classic psychedelic state
Both antagonise NMDA-mediated neurotransmission. Analgesia, dissociation and altered perception can coexist with impaired judgement. PCP intoxication can include nystagmus, hypertension, agitation, psychotic-like symptoms and impaired consciousness; severe cases may include rigidity or seizures. Ketamine exposure and supervised anaesthetic/antidepressant use differ in indication, dose, monitoring and context. Therapeutic use does not validate the safety of an unknown recreational preparation.

## Volatile inhalants: the chemical and the heart matter
Solvents, fuels and aerosols can produce alcohol-like disinhibition followed by CNS depression, incoordination and reduced consciousness. Cardiovascular toxicity and sudden death may occur; the specific chemical changes the risk. Hypoxia, injury and co-exposure are important competing explanations for deterioration. A generic positive drug screen may not identify the inhalant.

## Initial clinical approach
Prioritise airway/breathing, circulation, temperature, seizures and consciousness, minimise injury and seek toxicology/emergency support. Reassess psychiatric symptoms after acute stabilisation. Persistent symptoms, dependence and recurrent exposure need follow-up; neither a frightening drug experience nor a single intoxication establishes a chronic primary psychotic disorder.
chunks.title: MDMA, dissociative drugs and volatile inhalants: toxidrome distinctions

# Dementia carers: needs, skills and safeguarding

## Assess the carer as a person
Carer burden includes sleep loss, emotional distress, restriction of work and relationships, physical strain and practical or financial demands. Burden is not interchangeable with hours of care, and apparent competence does not exclude exhaustion. Ask about depression, anxiety, health, sleep, willingness to continue and the availability of backup. Identify multiple carers and disagreement about responsibilities rather than assuming one relative can provide unlimited care.

The person's dementia subtype, functional needs, communication and behavioural changes influence care demands. Sudden deterioration should prompt assessment for pain, delirium, infection or medication effects, not simply advice to tolerate progression. A carer's account is valuable longitudinal evidence; it is not automatically identical to the patient's preferences or capacity.

## Education must become usable skills
Explain the expected course and the limits of prediction. Teach communication adapted to comprehension, recognition of triggers and practical responses to distress. Discuss routines, meaningful activity, eating/drinking, medication organisation and what should prompt urgent help. Demonstration and rehearsal are more useful than handing over a leaflet without checking understanding. NICE NG97 recommends psychoeducation and skills training; its UK assessment/respite entitlements are not statements of Greek law.

Support may include respite, peer contact, psychological treatment for the carer and practical assistance. Match it to the dyad and access barriers. Goals include tolerable burden, safer care and sustained participation, not a promise to prevent institutional care. Track the carer's outcomes separately from the patient's symptoms and function; improvement in one does not necessarily imply improvement in the other.

## Safeguarding and transitions
Ask privately where appropriate about coercion, neglect, violence, financial exploitation and unsafe exhaustion. Risk can affect either member of the dyad, and deterioration in care may arise without deliberate abuse. Immediate danger needs escalation through local procedures; do not postpone protection until a training programme is completed.

Plan contingencies for illness or absence of the main carer, deterioration in function and discharge transitions. Involve the patient as far as possible and clarify consent, capacity and information-sharing boundaries. Supporting carers complements professional care; it must not become an unexamined transfer of service responsibility to a family.
chunks.title: Dementia carers: needs, skills and safeguarding

# Neuroimmunology: research associations and actionable red flags

## Three levels of evidence
Peripheral inflammation can signal to the brain through humoral, endothelial and neural pathways; CNS immune activity involves glia and other cells. Infection, systemic illness and autoimmune disease may produce neuropsychiatric symptoms. Group-level associations between inflammatory markers and psychiatric diagnoses do not establish an immune cause in every patient, a diagnostic blood test, or an indication for immunotherapy.

Separate mechanistic plausibility, an observed association and a clinically validated action. A raised inflammatory marker is nonspecific and must be interpreted with infection, metabolic illness, medicines and the physical examination. A psychiatric diagnosis is neither proof against encephalitis nor evidence for a primary inflammatory lesion.

## Recognise a syndrome requiring neurological assessment
Rapidly evolving psychiatric symptoms with memory change, altered mental status, seizures, focal findings or movement disorder merit medical/neurological evaluation. Autonomic instability or reduced consciousness increases urgency. Consider infectious encephalitis, intoxication, metabolic disturbance and other neurological disorders alongside autoimmunity. Absence of fever alone is not reassuring enough to close the differential.

The 2016 Graus possible-autoimmune-encephalitis framework requires all three elements: progression in less than three months of working-memory deficits, altered mental status or psychiatric symptoms; at least one new focal CNS finding, seizure unexplained by a known seizure disorder, CSF pleocytosis above five cells/mm³ or suggestive MRI finding; and reasonable exclusion of alternatives. It is an entry framework, not permission to label isolated anxiety or an incidental serum antibody as definite encephalitis. MRI, EEG and CSF address different questions; specialist selection and interpretation of antibody testing matter.

## Antibody results are conditional evidence
A positive result needs a compatible phenotype, appropriate specimen, assay interpretation and attention to false positives. A negative antibody panel does not alone exclude immune-mediated disease. Clinical evolution and conventional investigations remain central; neither response to steroids nor a single test substitutes for differential assessment.

## What changes practice
Recognised inflammatory neurological syndromes require timely specialist management, including exclusion/treatment of infection and consideration of immune therapy. Research on immune contributions to depression or psychosis must not be converted into routine cytokine screening or unsupervised anti-inflammatory prescribing. Preserve the distinction between a promising therapeutic hypothesis and a current individual indication. Exact encephalitis criteria, antibody algorithms and treatment protocols require their own full source review.
chunks.title: Neuroimmunology: research associations and actionable red flags
