# Psychosomatic medicine and psychological factors affecting medical illness

## Integration rather than an unexplained-symptom category
Psychosomatic medicine examines interactions among physical disease, psychological processes, behaviour and social conditions. Consultation-liaison practice uses this perspective for assessment and care in medical settings. It does not require that symptoms lack a medical explanation, and it does not imply that disease is imaginary or deliberately produced. A physical diagnosis and a clinically relevant psychological process can both be present.

Differentiate the medical condition, the person's experience of it and any independently diagnosable mental disorder. Depression, delirium, anxiety, substance use and medication effects may complicate care. A formulation should specify how the proposed factor affects disease or treatment rather than merely state that stress is important.

## A specific DSM construct
DSM-5-TR psychological factors affecting other medical conditions requires a medical symptom or condition other than a mental disorder. Psychological/behavioural factors must adversely influence its course, interfere with treatment, constitute an additional established health risk, or influence pathophysiology in a way that precipitates/exacerbates symptoms or necessitates care. The factors must not be better explained by another mental disorder.

Temporal association, adherence behaviour and disease mechanisms are evidence to examine, not interchangeable proofs of causation. Assess barriers such as cost, misunderstanding, adverse effects or inaccessible services before labelling non-adherence as psychologically driven. The inspected DSM severity descriptors concern increasing medical risk, aggravation, hospital/emergency care and severe life-threatening risk; they are not a scale of how emotional the patient appears.

## Boundaries and practical work
Somatic symptom disorder concerns the qualifying symptom-related cognitive, emotional and behavioural pattern; it does not require medically unexplained symptoms. Illness anxiety emphasises illness preoccupation with absent or mild somatic symptoms. Neither diagnosis follows simply from a negative investigation. Intentional symptom falsification and external incentives require separate evidence for factitious or malingering formulations.

Care addresses the identified interaction: clear illness information, workable adherence plans, treatment of qualifying psychiatric illness, coping strategies and coordination with the medical team. Maintain diagnostic openness when physical findings change. Psychological intervention is not a substitute for necessary medical treatment, and medical treatment alone may leave an important behavioural obstacle untouched.

# Chronic pain, fatigue and functional somatic syndromes: formulation and care

## Formulate without denying disease
Describe the symptom pattern, time course, functional consequences and red flags before choosing a diagnostic framework. Pain and fatigue may accompany established disease, a recognised syndrome, psychiatric illness or more than one of these. A negative test does not prove psychological causation. Reassess new focal findings, systemic deterioration or a changed pattern rather than preserve an old functional label at all costs.

A biopsychosocial formulation connects relevant mechanisms and maintaining conditions: physical pathology, sleep, medication effects, threat interpretation, avoidance, activity patterns, work demands and social support. It must distinguish observed relationships from hypotheses. Assess depression, anxiety, suicidality and substance use on their positive features; these are not obligatory explanations for chronic symptoms.

## Match the plan to the condition
For chronic pain, separate primary from secondary pain and recognise coexistence. Treat identified disease and clarify realistic functional goals. NICE NG193's chronic-primary-pain recommendations include appropriately supported activity and psychological approaches; they are not a rule to withdraw all analgesia from every secondary pain condition. Selected antidepressants may be considered for adults with primary pain after discussion of benefits and harms, including when depression is absent. Analgesic benefit does not prove depressive causation.

Review opioid, sedative and other medicine exposure, actual benefit, adverse effects and dependence. A medication review is collaborative and must account for withdrawal risk, not simply replace one unexplained-symptom label with abrupt discontinuation. Coordinate care to reduce contradictory messages and repeated investigations lacking a clinical indication.

## Fatigue is not one treatment target
Assess sleep disorder, anaemia/endocrine disease, infection, medicines and mood alongside the history. ME/CFS requires its own diagnostic and management assessment, particularly post-exertional malaise. Its activity response cannot be assumed equivalent to uncomplicated deconditioning. Current NICE NG206 advises individual energy management and rejects programmes using fixed incremental exercise increases. The older textbook's activity-increase discussion is historical, not the current ME/CFS prescription.

## Outcomes and communication
Validate the symptoms, explain what is known and uncertain, and agree measures of participation, sleep, symptom interference and quality of life. Psychological support can help coping without promising a cure or requiring acceptance of a psychogenic cause. Follow-up should identify worsening medical risk and whether the agreed plan is workable.
chunks.title: Chronic pain, fatigue and functional somatic syndromes: formulation and care

# Adult autism after diagnosis: support, adjustments and comorbidity

## The diagnosis begins a support formulation
Discuss what the diagnosis explains, the person's strengths and the difficulties they want help with. Needs vary with communication, sensory environment, executive demands, intellectual ability and available support; diagnostic labels do not determine identical needs or incapacity. Consent and decision-making must be assessed for the actual decision, with appropriate communication support.

Assess coexisting depression, anxiety, ADHD, sleep problems, substance use and physical illness without attributing every change to autism. Pain, sensory overload, disrupted routine or inaccessible communication can look like psychiatric deterioration. Establish baseline and time course, especially for marked regression, catatonic features, self-harm or loss of function. An autism diagnosis does not exclude a new treatable disorder.

## Adjust the encounter before judging engagement
Use clear concrete language, an explicit agenda, predictable arrangements and enough processing time. Offer written/visual information and check the person's preferred communication method. Reduce sensory demands or arrange breaks and a quieter setting where feasible. Non-standard eye contact or literal answers must not be treated as non-cooperation. Accommodations should improve access rather than reward performance that conceals distress.

Plan practical support around daily living, relationships, education or employment and the person's own goals. Involve family or supporters with agreement and clarify their role. Neither independence nor family involvement is a universal outcome requirement. UK reasonable-adjustment/service recommendations inform clinical practice here; Greek legal entitlements and local availability require separate verification.

## Treat the qualifying problem
For coexisting mental disorders, use disorder-specific interventions adapted to communication and learning style. NICE CG142 recommends structured, concrete cognitive/behavioural work, explicit rules and supportive written/visual material. Psychotropics do not routinely treat the core features of adult autism. When severe behaviour that challenges leads to medication consideration, identify its function and physical/environmental triggers first; specialist review, a defined target and benefit/harm monitoring are necessary, not an indefinite response to a vague behaviour label.

## Review access and benefit
Measure meaningful function and quality of life, not only outward conformity. Check adverse effects, sensory/communication barriers and whether the person can use the plan in daily life. Support needs can change with context; a post-diagnostic plan should be revisited rather than regarded as a one-time referral.
chunks.title: Adult autism after diagnosis: support, adjustments and comorbidity

questions.modelAnswer: DSM-5-TR learning disorder requires relevant academic-skill symptoms for at least six months despite targeted intervention, skills substantially below age expectations with meaningful interference, school-age onset and exclusions. # Remember

- Adult access problems and acquired decline require different assessments.

# Learning, language and communication disorders: adult recognition

## Specify the impaired skill
Specific learning disorder concerns persistent difficulty acquiring or using academic skills: reading, written expression or mathematics. Dyslexia describes a reading/decoding pattern; dyscalculia describes a numerical/arithmetic pattern. They are not synonyms for low general intelligence or poor effort. Specify the affected domain and subskills rather than use an undifferentiated learning-problem label.

DSM-5-TR requires relevant symptoms for at least six months despite targeted intervention, skills substantially below age expectations with meaningful interference, school-age onset and exclusions. Difficulty may become visible only when demands exceed compensation. For people aged seventeen or older, documented impairing history may substitute for standardised achievement assessment; history, reports and clinical synthesis still matter. Inadequate instruction, language proficiency, uncorrected sensory problems and other disorders must be evaluated rather than folded into the diagnosis.

## Language is not speech, and speech is not all communication
Language disorder concerns persistent comprehension/production difficulties across modalities, including vocabulary, sentence structure and discourse. Speech sound disorder concerns intelligibility and sound production; childhood-onset fluency disorder concerns fluency. Social pragmatic communication disorder concerns social use of communication, conversational rules, contextual adaptation and inference/nonliteral language.

For the pragmatic disorder, examine current and historical restricted/repetitive behaviours before distinguishing autism. Reduced eye contact or literal language alone does not settle that differential. Developmental disorders differ from acquired aphasia, dysarthria or new cognitive decline. Sensory assessment and culturally/linguistically appropriate evaluation are essential; difficulty in a second language is not sufficient evidence of a developmental disorder.

## Why the adult psychiatrist needs the distinction
Unrecognised reading, numerical or language limitations may affect work, treatment information, medication instructions and clinical interviews. Apparent disorganisation or non-adherence can reflect an inaccessible task rather than a psychiatric symptom. ADHD, autism, anxiety and depression can coexist but do not replace domain-specific assessment.

Obtain a developmental/educational history and relevant records, clarify current functional barriers and consider specialist learning or speech-language assessment. Adapt instructions, written material and time demands while the formulation is clarified. Do not infer incapacity from a learning diagnosis; assess understanding and the actual decision with suitable support.
chunks.title: Learning, language and communication disorders: adult recognition

questions.modelAnswer: Pica is persistent nonfood/nonnutritive ingestion for at least one month, developmentally inappropriate and outside culturally normative practice; DSM suggests age two to avoid infant-mouthing misclassification. Rumination is repeated regurgitation for at least one month, potentially rechewed/reswallowed/spat out, not medically explained or exclusively within anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating disorder or ARFID. In another relevant condition, either must warrant additional attention.

For regurgitation, clarify meal relation, nausea/retching, swallowing and observed behaviour, considering reflux/structural/motility disease. Weight/shape-motivated intentional purging differs; involuntary/habitual regurgitation is not proof of deception or completed GI exclusion.

Atypical anorexia meets anorexia requirements except low weight despite substantial loss; serious risk can occur at normal/higher weight. Purging disorder involves recurrent weight/shape-driven purging without binges. Night eating involves awareness/recall, unlike some sleep-related eating. Unspecified does not state the shortfall reason.

- Normal/higher weight does not exclude serious restrictive-eating complications.

# Pica, rumination and other specified eating disorders

## Pica: ingestion outside developmental and cultural norms
DSM-5-TR pica requires eating non-food, non-nutritive substances persistently for at least one month, inappropriate to developmental level and outside a culturally supported/socially normative practice. When present with another mental disorder or a medical condition, including pregnancy, severity must warrant additional clinical attention. Ordinary infant mouthing is not sufficient; the manual suggests a minimum age of two to avoid this confusion.

Identify the material, quantity, pattern and access. Poisoning, gastrointestinal obstruction/injury, infection and nutritional deficiency are relevant complications. A nutritional association does not exclude other causes or justify treating every presentation with an assumed supplement. Assess the consequences and the associated developmental/psychiatric context.

## Rumination: repeated regurgitation, not a generic vomiting label
Repeated regurgitation for at least one month can involve re-chewing, swallowing again or spitting out. It is not attributable to a gastrointestinal/medical condition and does not occur exclusively during anorexia, bulimia, binge-eating disorder or ARFID. In another mental-disorder context it must warrant additional attention.

Clarify relation to meals, retching/nausea, intentional purging, swallowing difficulty and observed behaviour. Consider reflux, structural or motility problems and nutritional effects. Habitual or apparently involuntary regurgitation should not be presumed deceptive. The label does not establish a completed gastrointestinal investigation or a behavioural treatment protocol.

## OSFED identifies a specified diagnostic shortfall
Other specified feeding or eating disorder applies when clinically significant eating symptoms do not meet a named disorder's full criteria and the reason is stated. Examples include atypical anorexia, low-frequency/limited-duration bulimia or binge-eating disorder, purging disorder and night-eating syndrome. It is not a shorthand for mild disease.

In atypical anorexia, all anorexia requirements except low weight are met despite significant weight loss; serious physiological complications can occur at normal or higher weight. Purging disorder involves recurrent weight/shape-motivated purging without binge eating. Night eating involves awareness and recall, unlike some sleep-related eating presentations. If the reason for unmet criteria is not specified or information is insufficient, an unspecified category differs from OSFED.

Across categories, assess medical instability, nutrition, self-harm and functional impairment. Risk and treatment intensity cannot be inferred solely from BMI or the word atypical.
chunks.title: Pica, rumination and other specified eating disorders

questions.modelAnswer: DSM-5-TR restriction requires at least one: significant weight loss/faltering growth, nutritional deficiency, reliance on enteral feeding/oral supplements or marked psychosocial interference, with relevant exclusions. There is no universal BMI cutoff or minimum month duration; low BMI is not required. Low-interest, sensory and feared-consequence patterns are not compulsory coexisting subtypes, and the disorder is not child-only.

Directly assess weight/shape beliefs and compensatory behaviour: ARFID lacks disturbed body-weight/shape experience and cannot occur exclusively within anorexia/bulimia. Sensory dislike alone does not exclude another eating disorder.

questions.modelAnswer: Assess actual intake/repertoire, weight/growth trajectory, hydration, vital signs, deficiencies and physiological instability, considering refeeding risk. Urgency and care setting cannot be chosen by BMI or absence of weight/shape concerns alone. Coordinate medical/nutritional rehabilitation with a developmental and avoidance formulation; fear, sensory sensitivity and low appetite need different approaches. Track nutritional adequacy, eating ability and participation, not weight alone.
questions.prompt: How do nutritional state and maintaining avoidance guide urgency and the initial multidisciplinary formulation?

# Remember

- One qualifying consequence is enough; low weight is not compulsory.
- Sensory avoidance, low interest and fear are patterns, not mandatory combined criteria.
- Medical/other-disorder exclusions and weight/shape assessment remain essential.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# ARFID: qualifying restriction, differential and medical risk

## Restriction without the anorexia weight/shape mechanism
Avoidant/restrictive food intake disorder can involve low interest in eating, sensory avoidance or fear of adverse consequences such as choking/vomiting. These are common presentation patterns, not three compulsory subtypes or requirements that must coexist. DSM-5-TR applies across the lifespan; it is not confined to children or autistic people.

Qualifying restriction is associated with at least one consequence: significant weight loss/faltering expected growth, significant nutritional deficiency, reliance on enteral feeding or oral nutritional supplements, or marked psychosocial interference. Low BMI is not required and a stable weight does not exclude nutritional deficiency or severe interference. The manual does not impose a universal BMI cutoff or minimum month duration.

## Preserve the exclusions
Food scarcity or a culturally sanctioned practice must not better explain the pattern. The disturbance does not occur exclusively within anorexia or bulimia, and there is no disturbance in the experience of body weight/shape. Ask directly about feared weight gain, compensatory behaviour and the meaning of restriction; stated sensory dislike alone does not exclude another eating disorder.

Medical conditions, swallowing problems, gastrointestinal symptoms, medicines and other mental disorders need evaluation. If restriction accompanies another condition, it must exceed the expected disturbance and warrant additional attention. Autism-related selectivity does not automatically meet ARFID, nor does autism rule it out. Ordinary preference without a qualifying consequence differs from a disorder.

## Risk assessment and formulation
Assess the actual nutritional intake and repertoire, weight/growth trajectory, hydration, vital signs and symptoms of deficiency. Severe malnutrition can produce physiological danger even when the narrative lacks weight/shape concerns. Medical evaluation determines urgency and the need for supported nutritional rehabilitation; BMI alone cannot choose the setting. Consider refeeding risk where intake and nutritional state warrant it.

The initial multidisciplinary plan combines medical/nutritional care with assessment of the maintaining avoidance pattern and developmental context. Expansion of intake must be safe and feasible; fear, sensory sensitivity and low appetite may need different approaches. A complete psychological or feeding protocol and medicine regimen are not supplied by diagnostic criteria. Track nutritional adequacy, social participation and the person's ability to eat, rather than weight change alone.
chunks.title: ARFID: qualifying restriction, differential and medical risk

questions.modelAnswer: Delayed phase has late onset/waking with difficulty meeting earlier demands, often satisfactory sleep on the preferred schedule. Advanced phase has undesired early sleepiness/waking. Shift-work problems track work overlapping biological sleep. A late/early chronotype alone is not a disorder: recurrent/persistent misalignment must cause insomnia/sleepiness and meaningful distress/impairment; insufficient sleep opportunity is a separate possible contributor.
questions.prompt: Contrast delayed phase, advanced phase and shift-work presentations, including the boundary with normal chronotype.

questions.modelAnswer: Obtain sleep/work/light history and a diary across work/free days, with actigraphy where useful. Record naps, caffeine, alcohol, medicines and actual sleep opportunity. Distinguish stable phase shift from drifting non-24-hour or irregular patterns; assess relevant mood illness, apnoea, restless legs and primary insomnia. Sleep studies investigate competing disorders rather than automatically prove circadian phase.
questions.prompt: What longitudinal sleep data and competing explanations are needed before a circadian formulation?

questions.modelAnswer: Light and melatonin are phase-directed: timing relative to biological phase can shift/stabilise rhythm, while mistiming may shift it wrongly. Agree feasible schedules, sleep opportunity and adherence, addressing driving/hazardous-work safety and environmental adjustments. Monitor sleepiness, function and mood; the 2015 AASM intrinsic-disorder guidance is qualified, not a universal shift-work protocol or arbitrary clock-time prescription.
questions.prompt: Why does treatment timing matter, and how should safety, feasibility and response guide the plan?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Chronotype becomes disorder only with qualifying disruption and impairment.
- Work/free-day patterns distinguish phase disorder, restricted sleep opportunity and other sleep disease.
- Light and melatonin act by timing; bedtime sedation is not phase correction.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Circadian sleep–wake disorders: timing, impairment and treatment logic

## Diagnose misalignment, not an inconvenient preference
Circadian sleep–wake disorders involve recurrent/persistent disruption from altered circadian timing or misalignment with required schedules, producing insomnia, excessive sleepiness or both and meaningful distress/impairment. A late or early chronotype without impairment is not automatically a disorder. Insufficient opportunity for sleep can coexist but is a different explanation.

Delayed sleep phase presents with late sleep onset and awakening and difficulty meeting an earlier required schedule. Sleep may be satisfactory when the preferred schedule is permitted. Advanced phase presents with early sleepiness and waking relative to the desired schedule. Shift-work presentations arise in relation to working hours that overlap the usual biological sleep period; establish the relationship rather than label every tired shift worker.

## Measure the pattern across ordinary life
Use a sleep/work/light-exposure history and a diary spanning work and free days; actigraphy can support assessment where appropriate. Record naps, caffeine, alcohol, medicines and actual sleep opportunity. Assess mood disorder, sleep apnoea, restless legs and primary insomnia when their features are present. Sleep study testing may address a suspected competing disorder; it is not the default proof of circadian phase.

Distinguish a stable delayed/advanced phase from a progressively drifting non-24-hour pattern or an irregular fragmented sleep–wake pattern. Context, neurological illness and visual impairment can matter. Daytime risk assessment includes driving, hazardous work and error-prone duties; a sedative prescription does not resolve schedule mismatch.

## Treatment is timed, not merely sedating
Agree a feasible target schedule with attention to sleep opportunity and adherence. Consistent timing and appropriately scheduled light exposure aim to alter or stabilise circadian alignment. Melatonin's timing relative to biological phase matters, not simply whether it is taken at bedtime. Mistimed light or melatonin can shift the rhythm in the wrong direction; specialist assessment may be needed rather than an arbitrary universal clock time.

The AASM 2015 intrinsic-disorder guideline supports selected strategically timed interventions with qualified recommendations; it is not a blanket current protocol for all shift-work disorders. Medication licensing, formulations and precise light/melatonin schedules require separate review. Monitor function, sleepiness and mood as well as clock times. Necessary work/environmental adjustments and safe transport may be as important as an attempt to move biological phase.
chunks.title: Circadian sleep–wake disorders: timing, impairment and treatment logic

questions.modelAnswer: RBD combines recurrent REM-related vocalisation/complex movement with loss of normal atonia; obtain timing, dream recall, waking alertness, injuries and partner history. Video-polysomnography evaluates REM without atonia, but asymptomatic atonia loss alone is insufficient. The inspected DSM-5-TR permits suggestive history plus established synucleinopathy as an alternative to the polysomnographic element, not a universal lab requirement across classifications.
questions.prompt: What clinical and sleep-state evidence supports RBD, and what alternative does the inspected DSM allow?

questions.modelAnswer: NREM arousals tend to occur early at night with confusion/incomplete recall; stereotyped spells suggest seizures. Assess apnoea-related arousals, medication/substance timing and neurological baseline, using suitable video-polysomnographic/EEG/physiological evidence where needed. Dream enactment alone is not diagnostic, and a needed antidepressant should not automatically be stopped without weighing temporal evidence and risks.
questions.prompt: How would NREM arousals, seizures, sleep apnoea and medication effects be distinguished?

questions.modelAnswer: Explain the strong longitudinal association of isolated RBD with Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy as reason for neurological follow-up, not inevitable conversion or an exact individual date/probability. Cohort estimates depend on age, comorbidity, case definition and follow-up. Symptom treatment does not establish prevention of neurodegeneration.
questions.prompt: How should synucleinopathy risk be discussed without an individual deterministic prediction?

questions.modelAnswer: Remove hazardous objects, reduce furniture-related injury and consider separate sleeping arrangements. Assess sleep apnoea, falls, cognition and vulnerability before medication. The 2023 AASM recommendations for clonazepam/immediate-release melatonin are conditional and setting/formulation-specific; clonazepam sedation, falls and respiratory risks matter. Specialist dosing/product review remains necessary, targeting harmful enactment rather than promised neuroprotection.
questions.prompt: What bedroom safety measures and treatment-risk considerations precede a specialist medicine plan?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Dream enactment, REM without atonia and a competing sleep disorder must be related, not assumed.
- DSM includes an established-synucleinopathy/history alternative; do not erase it.
- Safety is immediate; symptomatic treatment does not prove neurodegeneration prevention.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# REM sleep behaviour disorder: confirmation, safety and prognosis

## Dream enactment requires a sleep-state explanation
REM sleep behaviour disorder (RBD) involves recurrent vocalisation or complex movement during REM sleep, associated with impaired normal muscle atonia. Punching or shouting during sleep is not sufficient by itself. Obtain the person's and bed partner's descriptions, timing, injuries, medication history and neurological baseline. Dream recall and alertness after waking support the pattern, but do not replace a differential.

Video-polysomnography assesses REM without atonia and whether the observed behaviour belongs to REM. Isolated REM without atonia can be an asymptomatic finding, so laboratory and clinical evidence must be combined. The inspected DSM-5-TR criteria also allow a suggestive history with an established synucleinopathy as an alternative to the polysomnographic element; this must not be misrepresented as universal sleep-laboratory confirmation in every classification.

## Important mimics and associated conditions
NREM arousal disorders more often involve early-night episodes with confusion and incomplete recall. Stereotyped nocturnal seizures, sleep apnoea-related arousals, medication/substance effects and other sleep behaviours need assessment. Polysomnography with suitable EEG/physiological recording can clarify competing explanations. Do not automatically stop a necessary antidepressant solely because dream enactment is reported; review the temporal relationship and risks.

Isolated RBD has a strong longitudinal association with later synucleinopathies, including Parkinson disease, Lewy body dementia and multiple system atrophy. This supports neurological follow-up and a careful prognostic discussion, not a guarantee of conversion or an exact forecast for one individual. Age, comorbidity, case definition and follow-up horizon affect interpretation of cohort estimates.

## Reduce injury while reviewing treatment
Make the sleeping environment safer: remove hazardous objects, reduce injury from nearby furniture and consider separate sleeping arrangements when needed. This is important even before a medicine decision. Evaluate sleep apnoea, falls, cognition and other vulnerabilities.

The AASM 2023 guideline makes conditional recommendations for clonazepam and immediate-release melatonin in defined adult RBD settings; formulations and indications are not interchangeable. Clonazepam's sedative/fall and respiratory risks matter, particularly in older or vulnerable people. Treatment aims to reduce harmful dream enactment, not to claim prevention of neurodegeneration. Specialist selection, dose and monitoring require a full current protocol and local product review.
chunks.title: REM sleep behaviour disorder: confirmation, safety and prognosis

questions.modelAnswer: Map menstrual/vasomotor and sleep changes alongside psychiatric history, medicines, physical illness and life context. Assess persistence, anhedonia, impairment, suicidality and past depressive/manic episodes; menopausal timing does not explain every syndrome. Consider thyroid/sleep disease and independent mood illness. Subjective cognitive complaints may reflect sleep/distress, while progressive decline or neurological signs need separate evaluation.
questions.prompt: How would chronology and syndrome assessment distinguish menopausal symptoms from independent depression, bipolar illness or cognitive disease?

questions.modelAnswer: NICE NG23 considers HRT for depressive symptoms below depression criteria beginning around other menopausal symptoms; specified vasomotor-associated depressive/sleep problems may also warrant menopause-related CBT. Suspected or diagnosed depression needs menopause and depression guidance together. HRT is not a universal substitute for disorder-specific antidepressant/psychological treatment, and preparation-specific risks/contraindications need individual medical review.
questions.prompt: What is the NICE boundary for considering HRT for mood symptoms, and how does diagnosed depression change the plan?

questions.modelAnswer: Assign each intervention a target and coordinate menopause, sleep and psychiatric care. Review adherence, exposure, illness and adverse effects before changing psychotropics rather than escalating solely because of menopause. Monitor mood, sleep, cognition, function and harms separately. NICE advises against HRT for dementia prevention; better concentration after sleep/vasomotor improvement is not disease modification.
questions.prompt: How should coordinated treatment and follow-up avoid automatic psychotropic escalation or dementia-prevention claims?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Transition-associated depressive symptoms and diagnosed depression require distinct treatment reasoning.
- HRT and psychiatric treatment may coexist; neither replaces an individual assessment.
- HRT is not a dementia-prevention prescription.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Menopause and mental health: symptoms, depression and treatment boundaries

## Establish the transition and the clinical syndrome
Perimenopausal hormonal fluctuation can coincide with vasomotor symptoms, sleep disruption, mood symptoms and subjective cognitive difficulty. Assess menstrual/vasomotor chronology alongside psychiatric history, medicines, physical illness and psychosocial circumstances. Not every symptom during midlife is caused by menopause; thyroid disorder, sleep disease and an independent mood disorder remain relevant differentials.

Ask about persistence, anhedonia, function, suicidality and past episodes. Depressive symptoms associated with the transition and a qualifying depressive disorder are different clinical targets. Previous bipolar disorder or new manic symptoms changes assessment and treatment; reproductive timing does not justify treating activation as simple low mood. Cognitive complaints can reflect poor sleep, distress or other disease and do not themselves establish dementia.

## Coordinate menopause and psychiatric care
Explain the interaction of vasomotor disturbance, sleep and daytime function without claiming a single hormonal cause. Support sleep and coping, review alcohol/caffeine and assess relevant physical contributors. The person may need both menopause treatment and disorder-specific psychiatric care. Document which outcome each intervention targets.

NICE NG23 recommends considering HRT for depressive symptoms that do not meet depression criteria and begin around the same time as other menopausal symptoms. It also recommends considering menopause-related CBT for specified depressive/sleep problems associated with vasomotor symptoms. For suspected or diagnosed depression, menopause and depression guidance should be used together. HRT is therefore not a universal replacement for antidepressant/psychological treatment of established depression.

## Prescribing boundaries and review
HRT choice depends on the individual's medical history, symptom burden, contraindications and preferences, with appropriate medical/menopause expertise. Different preparations and routes have different benefit–risk profiles; this chunk does not prescribe a universal regimen. Changes in psychotropic response should prompt an individual review of adherence, exposure, illness and adverse effects, not automatic dose escalation based on menopause alone.

NICE advises against HRT for dementia prevention. Improvement in concentration after better sleep or relief of vasomotor symptoms is not proof of disease modification. Follow mood, sleep, cognition, function and adverse effects separately. New neurological signs, persistent cognitive decline or severe psychiatric symptoms warrant their own evaluation, even when menopausal symptoms are also present.

# Antipsychotic switching and discontinuation: transition risks

## Define the decision before the schedule
Switching for adverse effects, inadequate response or formulation preference differs from stopping an unnecessary medicine or discontinuing maintenance after recovery. Reassess diagnosis, adherence, exposure, indication and previous relapse before interpreting apparent failure. Agree the target benefit, unacceptable harms and follow-up responsibilities. An adverse-effect improvement is not sufficient if psychotic control deteriorates.

## Compare pharmacokinetics and receptor effects
Cross-titration reduces one agent while introducing another, balancing under-treatment against additive adverse effects. A direct switch or a slower overlap can be appropriate in selected circumstances; there is no universal schedule. Long half-lives, active metabolites and depot absorption mean that the final dose date is not the disappearance date. Oral-to-depot, depot-to-oral and depot-to-depot transitions require product-specific initiation and residual-exposure checks.

Routine drug-free gaps when switching treatment for psychosis can increase relapse risk. Overlap can also increase sedation, hypotension, QT or other harms. A change in metabolic interactions or smoking can alter exposure independently of the nominal prescribed dose. Emergency toxicity may require a different approach from a planned tolerability switch.

## Withdrawal, rebound and relapse are related but distinct
Reduction of antimuscarinic effects can produce cholinergic withdrawal symptoms such as gastrointestinal disturbance, sweating and insomnia. Dopaminergic changes can include movement symptoms. Rebound describes symptom return exceeding the previous level or occurring with withdrawal dynamics; relapse denotes recurrence of the underlying illness. Timing and associated symptoms inform interpretation, but do not reliably separate every case.

Chronic receptor adaptation and dopamine supersensitivity are proposed contributors to withdrawal-associated psychosis. They are not a proven explanation for every relapse or a justification to assume maintenance has no benefit. Hyperbolic taper proposals reflect nonlinear dose–occupancy relationships; they are not a single validated percentage or duration for every agent/person.

## Make the transition observable
Document the last effective regimen, planned changes, monitoring and what happens if sleep, agitation, movement symptoms or psychosis worsens. Clozapine interruption has additional rebound and restart hazards requiring its dedicated protocol. Gradual reduction with close review is the usual planned-discontinuation principle; abrupt changes, intolerance or urgent toxicity require specialist decisions. An apparently successful first week does not establish long-term stability.
chunks.title: Antipsychotic switching and discontinuation: transition risks

# Classical antipsychotics and depots: formulation-specific distinctions

## Similar class, different preparation
Zuclopenthixol and flupentixol are thioxanthenes; fluphenazine is a phenothiazine. Their dopamine-antagonist effects can control psychosis while producing extrapyramidal and prolactin-related harms. A classical-versus-atypical label is a poor substitute for the individual drug's receptor profile, dose, patient vulnerability and prior tolerability. No class label guarantees absence of sedation, metabolic harm or QT effects.

Oral forms and oil-based long-acting esters differ in absorption and persistence. Flupentixol, fluphenazine and zuclopenthixol decanoate are maintenance depot formulations; milligrams and intervals are not interchangeable across agents or preparations. Peak concentration is not the same as therapeutic onset or steady state. A recent dose can continue contributing to exposure after a switch or missed appointment.

## Acetate is not decanoate
Zuclopenthixol acetate (Clopixol Acuphase) is a short-term intramuscular preparation, distinct from maintenance zuclopenthixol decanoate. The inspected UK SmPC describes a desired effect over two to three days and explicitly limits Acuphase treatment to two weeks, a maximum cumulative 400 mg and no more than four injections. These are UK product limits, not a Greek emergency protocol or a justification to extrapolate decanoate intervals to acetate.

The same SmPC excludes circulatory collapse, depressed consciousness from any cause and coma. It should not be treated as a universally suitable response to undifferentiated agitation or intoxication. The patient's medical state and the precise formulation must be established first.

## Choose and monitor the actual medicine
Consider dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia, prolactin-related symptoms, orthostasis and sedation alongside metabolic/cardiac risk. Akathisia can be mistaken for worsening agitation. Routine indefinite anticholinergic prophylaxis is not a solution to all movement effects and can add burden. Serious reactions can persist with a depot because the injected medicine cannot simply be removed.

The inspected UK Depixol low-volume SmPC restricts its use to people stabilised on oral therapy. Other products require their own tolerability, initiation and injection instructions. Check concentration, units, dose, volume, site and interval; do not copy a remembered depot recipe across brands. Greek availability, licensed indications and dose schedules remain to be verified before clinical use.
chunks.title: Classical antipsychotics and depots: formulation-specific distinctions

# Pregabalin and other non-benzodiazepine anxiety choices

## Start with the anxiety disorder and treatment goal
Non-benzodiazepine is not a diagnosis-specific efficacy or safety category. Distinguish GAD, panic, social anxiety, OCD/PTSD-related symptoms and anxiety secondary to substances or medical illness. Psychological treatment and disorder-appropriate antidepressants remain central options. Buspirone, beta-blockers, sedating antihistamines and gabapentinoids have different targets and limitations; reduced autonomic symptoms or sedation is not equivalent to treating the full syndrome.

## Pregabalin: mechanism and a specific indication
Pregabalin binds the alpha-2-delta auxiliary subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels; it is not a benzodiazepine-site or direct GABA-receptor agonist. Its adult GAD indication is established in EU product information. Gabapentin is not automatically an interchangeable licensed GAD treatment because of the shared gabapentinoid label.

NICE CG113 considers pregabalin for GAD when SSRIs/SNRIs cannot be tolerated. That UK sequencing statement differs from the existence of an EU licence and should not be generalised to every anxiety disorder. The inspected EU Lyrica SmPC gives a 150–600 mg/day adult GAD range in two or three divided doses, with regular reassessment. This is a product reference for patients without a required renal reduction, not a dose target for every person.

## Renal, respiratory and dependence risks
Renal elimination means dosing must be individualised to creatinine clearance; severe impairment and dialysis require the actual product table. Dizziness/somnolence, functional impairment and additive CNS-depressant effects matter. Opioids, other sedatives, respiratory vulnerability and older age can increase serious respiratory risk. Assess misuse/diversion and dependence, including at therapeutic doses, without equating physical adaptation with addiction.

The UK MHRA strengthened gabapentinoid dependence/addiction/withdrawal/tolerance warnings in January 2026. Discuss a stopping plan before treatment. EU information specifies gradual withdrawal over at least one week; this is a minimum, not proof that one week suits long-term treatment. MHRA advice allows individual tapers taking weeks or months when necessary.

## Evaluate benefit rather than accumulate sedatives
Measure anxiety and function, review adverse effects and avoid automatic escalation when tolerance, withdrawal or misuse could explain the change. Other non-benzodiazepine choices need their own efficacy/contraindication review, not substitution by name. Pregnancy/lactation, Greek product implementation and combinations require separate current checks.
chunks.title: Pregabalin and other non-benzodiazepine anxiety choices

# Choosing psychotherapy: target, format and suitability

## Choose an intervention for a defined problem
Begin with the clinical syndrome, formulation and the person's goals. Clarify whether the immediate target is symptoms, behaviour, relationships, coping with illness or functional recovery. Diagnostic assessment and safety planning precede an elective therapy choice when there is acute medical danger, severe intoxication, mania or another destabilising problem. Suitability is a clinical decision, not a judgement of whether someone deserves psychological care.

Match the evidence to the disorder, population, severity and outcome. An intervention's benefit for one problem does not establish superiority for all distress. Distinguish a treatment package with outcome evidence from its proposed mechanism and from the therapist's preferred explanatory model. A workable alliance matters, but shared therapeutic factors do not make every approach interchangeable.

## Format changes the work
Individual therapy permits detailed personal formulation and private disclosure. Group therapy can use shared learning, interpersonal feedback and practice, but requires attention to group composition, participation and confidentiality. Family or couple work may address interaction, care burden or communication; it is not automatically appropriate when there is coercion or when one member's safety or privacy cannot be protected. These formats can be combined when their targets are explicit.

Ask about preference, prior experience, language, cognitive/communication needs, disability, time, transport and treatment availability. Apparent non-engagement may reflect an inaccessible format. Adapt pacing and materials without assuming that every modification preserves the tested treatment. Therapist competence, supervision and the capacity to deliver the intended intervention are part of selection.

## Negotiate an observable plan
Explain expected tasks, duration, possible distress, alternatives and limits of confidentiality. Agree how progress will be assessed and what would trigger review. Symptom change, participation, functioning and the person's goals are related but distinct outcomes; attendance alone does not establish benefit.

For non-response, check the formulation, whether the treatment was actually delivered, engagement barriers, comorbidity and adverse effects before declaring the model ineffective. Consider modification, another appropriate therapy or combined treatment. The choice is revisable and should not require the patient to adopt an unverified causal theory. Disorder-specific session counts and comparative efficacy require their own current guideline review.
chunks.title: Choosing psychotherapy: target, format and suitability

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# DBS, VNS and psychiatric neurosurgery: role and safeguards

## Distinguish three interventions
Deep brain stimulation (DBS) uses implanted electrodes and a pulse generator to modulate selected brain targets. Vagus nerve stimulation (VNS) delivers stimulation through a peripheral nerve, with effects mediated through connected central systems. Ablative psychiatric neurosurgery creates a targeted lesion. They are not different names for ECT or transcranial magnetic stimulation, and evidence for one technique, target or disorder cannot be transferred automatically to another.

Stimulation parameters can be adjusted, but an implanted treatment is not risk-free or completely reversible in every consequence. Surgery, infection, hardware, maintenance and ongoing specialist follow-up matter. Lesion procedures have an irreversible anatomical component. Reduced symptoms do not alone establish preserved cognition, agency or long-term quality of life.

## Historical context is not current endorsement
Historical broad leucotomy was associated with serious cognitive, affective and behavioural harms. Modern target selection and stereotactic techniques differ, but technical precision does not by itself demonstrate clinical effectiveness. Historical enthusiasm, an uncontrolled responder series and a plausible circuit model are weaker evidence than a reliable indication-specific comparison.

Severe treatment-resistant depression and OCD are among the conditions studied in specialist invasive programmes. Establish diagnosis, adequate prior treatment, adherence, comorbidity and the actual residual disability before considering a resistant-illness pathway. The existence of a programme or a device indication in another jurisdiction does not establish Greek approval, reimbursement or access.

## Governance is part of the clinical decision
Selection requires multidisciplinary expertise, meaningful consent, independent safeguards and a plan for continuing treatment and device care. Explain uncertainty, alternatives and the possibility of adverse effects or limited benefit. A psychiatric diagnosis does not itself invalidate consent, and desperation is not a substitute for understanding. Coercive use to control socially inconvenient behaviour is not a therapeutic indication.

NICE's VNS depression guidance moved from IPG679 to HTG551 in January 2026; renumbering is not evidence of a new efficacy conclusion. Direct current recommendation pages were unavailable in this pass. DBS/VNS indication-specific evidence, current governance wording and Greek implementation remain review gates. Do not present these procedures as routine rescue treatments or encode an invasive-treatment eligibility recipe from older textbook practice.
chunks.title: DBS, VNS and psychiatric neurosurgery: role and safeguards

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Receptors and intracellular signalling: channels, cascades and adaptation

## A receptor is the first step, not the whole response
Ionotropic receptors are ligand-gated channels: binding changes ion conductance through the receptor complex. Metabotropic receptors act through intracellular signalling; many are G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs). A GPCR's seven-transmembrane architecture differs from an ion-channel pore. These categories describe signalling machinery, not whether the eventual clinical effect is beneficial or whether every response is simply excitatory or inhibitory.

Examples matter: nicotinic acetylcholine, GABA-A and ionotropic glutamate receptors are channel complexes, whereas muscarinic receptors are GPCRs. Ion flux changes membrane potential according to the channel, electrochemical gradients and cellular context. Fast electrical effects can also trigger calcium-dependent biochemical changes; ionotropic does not mean that all downstream effects are brief.

## Follow a signal through the cell
In a GPCR cascade, ligand binding changes receptor conformation and interaction with a G protein, which regulates effectors and second messengers. The inspected Stahl example links cAMP to protein kinase activity; calcium can also act as an intracellular messenger. Kinases phosphorylate proteins and phosphatases remove phosphate groups. Phosphorylation does not invariably activate a target: the consequence depends on the protein.

Targets include channels, enzymes and transcriptional regulators. Changes in gene expression and protein production can outlast the initial receptor event. Multiple cascades converge and interact, so one transmitter cannot be assigned one inevitable behavioural outcome. A downstream model is useful for understanding possible actions, not a direct biomarker of a particular psychiatric disorder.

## Adaptation changes the input–output relation
Receptor response can alter with sustained exposure. Desensitisation means reduced response despite agonist presence; it differs from simple loss of ligand or competitive blockade. Channel resting, open, closed, desensitised and inactive states are distinct. Changes in receptor availability and coupling are other regulatory possibilities requiring mechanism-specific evidence.

Do not equate receptor binding affinity, occupancy, intrinsic efficacy and clinical response. They answer different questions. Nor does delayed clinical improvement prove one specific transcriptional cascade caused it. Use receptor/cascade knowledge to formulate pharmacological hypotheses while checking the actual medicine's mechanism, exposure and outcome evidence.
chunks.title: Receptors and intracellular signalling: channels, cascades and adaptation

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# The cholinergic system: receptor families, cognition and clinical effects

## Two receptor families, distributed functions
Acetylcholine acts at nicotinic ligand-gated ion channels and muscarinic GPCRs. Nicotinic subtypes differ by their subunit composition; muscarinic subtypes differ in signalling and location. Presynaptic regulation and postsynaptic effects both matter. A cholinergic action is not automatically a global increase or decrease in cognition.

Acetylcholinesterase and butyrylcholinesterase hydrolyse acetylcholine; choline can be taken up and recycled. Inhibiting breakdown differs from directly stimulating a receptor or blocking one subtype. Peripheral autonomic and neuromuscular effects must be distinguished from central cognitive and behavioural effects when interpreting a medicine.

## Attention and memory are not one transmitter score
Cholinergic signalling contributes to attention and memory-related networks. The inspected Stahl discussion identifies central alpha-7 and alpha-4-beta-2 nicotinic subtypes and muscarinic regulation at cholinergic and other synapses. These are mechanisms within a network, not a diagnostic test for dementia or a reason to infer an acetylcholine deficiency from one forgetful response.

Delirium can involve impaired cholinergic function, but is a clinical syndrome with multiple causes. Attention/arousal change and acute course require a medical differential; no transmitter model replaces examination, medication review or investigation. Baseline dementia and an acute superimposed delirium need to be distinguished.

## Pharmacology connects central and peripheral risk
Medicines with antimuscarinic effects can impair cognition or contribute to delirium in vulnerable people. Dry mouth, constipation, urinary difficulties and other peripheral effects provide additional clues, but absence of these signs does not exclude central burden. Consider cumulative exposure across psychotropics and non-psychiatric medicines instead of counting only drugs explicitly called anticholinergics.

Cholinesterase inhibitors, nicotine-related interventions and muscarinic-targeted treatments have different indications and benefit–risk profiles. The mechanism does not establish a universal memory-enhancing prescription or a class-wide psychiatric indication. Anticholinergic treatment for a defined movement problem must be weighed against cognitive and peripheral harm.

When function changes, compare baseline, timing, dose changes and interacting illness. A drug-related hypothesis should lead to an appropriate supervised review, not an unsupported abrupt-stop instruction. Current prescribing, subtype-specific treatment claims and toxicity management require their own source checks.
chunks.title: The cholinergic system: receptor families, cognition and clinical effects

# Neuroendocrinology: thyroid, gonadal, prolactin and growth-hormone axes

## Feedback axes and clinical interpretation
The hypothalamus integrates signals and regulates pituitary secretion, while target hormones provide feedback. A hormone concentration must be interpreted with sampling conditions, medicines and the relevant axis. Endocrine illness can affect mental state; a psychiatric presentation does not make endocrine testing either universally necessary or universally unhelpful.

In the hypothalamic–pituitary–thyroid axis, TRH promotes TSH secretion, which supports thyroid hormone production; circulating thyroid hormones provide negative feedback at pituitary and hypothalamic levels. Consider thyroid disease when the clinical picture or treatment monitoring warrants it. Anxiety, depressive or cognitive symptoms alone do not identify a specific thyroid disorder, and a single test needs the appropriate clinical/biochemical interpretation.

## Reproductive signalling and dopamine inhibition
Pulsatile GnRH stimulates pituitary LH and FSH, which regulate gonadal function. Sex steroids and other signals feed back into the system. Reproductive transitions and endocrine disturbance can interact with mood, sleep, sexual function and fertility, without establishing a universal hormonal cause for a psychiatric syndrome.

Prolactin differs from a simple releasing-hormone cascade: hypothalamic dopamine provides important inhibition. Dopamine-blocking medicines can therefore raise prolactin. Assess menstrual/sexual symptoms, galactorrhoea, fertility concerns, medicines and other endocrine causes rather than assume every elevation is antipsychotic-induced. A laboratory abnormality and its clinical consequences should be documented separately. Thresholds for endocrine imaging or treatment require current specialist guidance.

## Growth hormone and timing
Growth hormone secretion is pulsatile, with hypothalamic GHRH stimulation and somatostatin inhibition; IGF-1 participates in downstream actions and feedback. A random GH value is not a direct readout of a psychiatric trait. Physiological timing and endocrine diagnostic protocols matter before interpreting an apparent abnormality.

## Historical challenge tests are not current psychiatric diagnostic criteria
Neuroendocrine challenges were used to investigate transmitter/axis function, including hormone responses to pharmacological stimulation. Group differences or an altered response do not prove a specific individual mood-disorder mechanism. Historical findings must not become a compulsory test panel or a treatment-selection biomarker. The HPA axis has its own chunk; this unit concerns the other axes and the distinction between endocrine disease assessment, treatment effects and psychiatric research measures.
chunks.title: Neuroendocrinology: thyroid, gonadal, prolactin and growth-hormone axes

questions.modelAnswer: Episodic explicit memory supports events/context; semantic explicit memory supports facts/meanings. Nondeclarative systems support skills, conditioning and priming without conscious recollection, so performance can improve despite no memory of practice. Working memory temporarily maintains/manipulates information. Specify task and delay: ambiguous short-term memory may refer to span or later recall and cannot itself locate a deficit.

questions.modelAnswer: Assess initial learning before interpreting delayed recall: attention, arousal, language and motivation affect encoding. Delayed loss, cueing and recognition help characterise possible encoding/storage/retrieval problems but behaviour rarely uniquely identifies the failed stage. Medial-temporal, diencephalic/frontobasal, executive and other distributed systems overlap; one score or lateralised item is not an infallible lesion map.
questions.prompt: How do encoding, delayed recall, cueing and recognition inform a memory formulation without uniquely localising a deficit?

Integrate baseline, attention/arousal, course, collateral function, medicines/substances and multiple tasks. Distinguish amnestic syndrome from delirium, broader decline and subjective complaints; account for education, language, senses and mood before inferring cause, dementia, deception or capacity.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Memory systems: declarative, procedural and working-memory distinctions

## Define the task before localising it
Memory is not a unitary faculty. Declarative or explicit memory concerns consciously accessible information. Episodic memory concerns events and their context; semantic memory concerns knowledge and meanings. Non-declarative memory includes skills, conditioning and priming, which can influence performance without conscious recollection of the learning episode. A person can improve at a task while not remembering having practised it.

Working memory supports temporary maintenance and manipulation of information during an ongoing task. Immediate span, learning across trials, delayed recall and recognition are different measures. The clinical phrase short-term memory is ambiguous: it may mean immediate storage or recall after minutes/days. Specify the operation and delay rather than attach a lesion inference to the phrase.

## Stages and networks
Encoding, consolidation/storage and retrieval are separable analytical stages, although behaviour alone may not uniquely identify the failed stage. Attention, arousal, language and motivation affect acquisition; a low delayed-recall score is uninterpretable without considering what was initially learned. Cueing and recognition can help characterise the pattern, not deliver an infallible anatomical diagnosis.

Episodic learning depends on a network including medial temporal structures and diencephalic/frontobasal connections. Working-memory/executive processes engage prefrontal and parietal systems. Semantic knowledge has partly distinct distributed associations, while skills and other implicit functions depend on their own task-specific networks. These are overlapping systems rather than one store per brain region. Lateralised verbal/nonverbal patterns are useful tendencies, not deterministic localisation from one item.

## Clinical interpretation
Anterograde difficulty concerns learning after the onset of illness; retrograde difficulty concerns retrieval of previously acquired information. Neither is synonymous with being disoriented or with loss of personal identity. An amnestic syndrome should be distinguished from delirium, broader neurocognitive decline and subjective memory complaints with preserved measured performance.

Use history, collateral and tasks sampling more than one memory operation. Establish baseline, course, functional consequences, medicines and substance exposure. Formal neuropsychological assessment addresses questions beyond a brief bedside screen. Interpretation must account for sensory, educational, linguistic and mood-related factors; a memory score does not by itself establish dementia, deception, capacity or the cause of impairment.
chunks.title: Memory systems: declarative, procedural and working-memory distinctions

questions.modelAnswer: A p-value evaluates incompatibility of observed or more extreme results with a specified model under its assumptions. It is not the probability that the null is true, that chance caused the finding, or the effect’s magnitude. Prespecification, multiplicity and selective reporting matter; a significance threshold proves neither clinical importance, reproducibility nor freedom from bias.
questions.prompt: What does a p-value condition on, and which common probability/effect interpretations are incorrect?

questions.modelAnswer: A frequentist interval comes from a procedure with long-run coverage, not posterior probability that this realised interval contains the fixed target. Examine width and effects compatible with the data against a clinical threshold, using appropriate absolute/relative scales and baseline risk/horizon. Nonsignificance may permit important benefit and harm; it does not establish equivalence, which needs a prespecified margin/design/analysis.
questions.prompt: How should a confidence interval and effect scale be interpreted when a result is nonsignificant?

questions.modelAnswer: Alpha is the planned type-I error probability: rejecting a true null. Beta is type-II error for a specified alternative: failing to reject; power is 1−beta, depending on effect, sample, variability, design and alpha. These control sampling error under assumptions, not confounding/selection/measurement bias. Neither low p nor nonsignificance proves equivalence or rescues a biased estimate.
questions.prompt: Distinguish alpha, beta and power, and explain why none repairs bias or proves equivalence.

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- A p-value is not the probability the hypothesis is true or a measure of effect size.
- Confidence coverage concerns a procedure; precision does not eliminate bias.
- Power is 1−beta for a specified alternative; nonsignificance is not equivalence.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Statistical inference: p-values, intervals, errors and effect size

## A p-value is conditional on a model
A p-value quantifies how incompatible the observed result, or a more extreme one, is with a specified statistical model under its assumptions. It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, the probability that chance caused the findings, or the size of the treatment effect. A threshold decision discards information and does not establish clinical importance or reproducibility.

State the estimand, test and analysis plan. Multiple outcomes, repeated analyses and selective reporting alter the interpretation of a small p-value. A result chosen because it was significant is not equivalent to a prespecified confirmatory test. Statistical inference does not repair confounding, measurement problems or biased recruitment.

## Precision and magnitude answer other questions
A confidence interval describes an estimation procedure with a specified long-run coverage under assumptions. For a 95% frequentist interval, repeated applications would cover the fixed target in about 95% of comparable samples; it is not a 95% posterior probability for that particular realised interval. Width reflects precision, not protection from systematic bias.

Interpret the interval's plausible effect range alongside a clinically meaningful threshold. A nonsignificant comparison may remain compatible with important benefit and harm. It does not establish equivalence: an equivalence/non-inferiority claim needs its own design, margin and analysis.

Effect size describes magnitude on an appropriate scale. Absolute risks, relative measures and standardised differences are not interchangeable. A small average difference may matter at population level; an apparently large relative change may accompany a small absolute change. Context, baseline risk and time horizon are necessary for interpretation.

## Error control and power
Type I error is rejection of a true null under the testing procedure; its planned probability is alpha. Type II error is failure to reject when a specified alternative is true; its probability is beta. Power is one minus beta and depends on the proposed effect, sample size, variability, design and chosen alpha. It is not the observed p-value expressed as confidence in a result.

Report estimates, uncertainty, assumptions and relevant outcomes rather than a significance badge. Clinical decisions combine magnitude, precision, benefits/harms, evidence quality and patient priorities. A statistically precise biased estimate remains biased.
chunks.title: Statistical inference: p-values, intervals, errors and effect size

questions.modelAnswer: Match population, intervention/exposure, comparator and outcome to the question. Randomised comparisons help causal treatment inference, while prognosis, diagnostic accuracy, rare/long-term harms and experience may require other designs. Assess allocation concealment separately from blinding, missing data, measurement and selective reporting; observational work additionally needs confounding/selection appraisal. A design hierarchy label does not guarantee direct or reliable evidence.
questions.prompt: How does the clinical question determine the useful study design and its major bias threats?

questions.modelAnswer: Check review question/eligibility, search, selection, extraction and appraisal, then duplicate populations, compatible outcomes/horizons, clinical and methodological heterogeneity and publication bias. A systematic review need not pool; meta-analysis is a statistical combination. Random effects allows differing underlying effects but cannot remove bias or make incompatible studies answer one meaningful question. Inspect individual effects as well as the pooled estimate.
questions.prompt: What must be checked before pooling a systematic review, and what does a random-effects model not solve?

questions.modelAnswer: GRADE rates an outcome-specific evidence body using bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias; symptom, harm and function certainty can differ. Recommendation strength also considers benefits/harms, values, resources and implementation, not just certainty. Licensing and reimbursement answer regulatory/funding questions separately. Check scope, conflicts, methods, updates and jurisdiction; imported guidance is not Greek law.
questions.prompt: How do outcome-specific GRADE certainty and guideline recommendations differ from licensing or reimbursement?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Evidence design must fit the question; labels do not remove bias.
- Systematic review and meta-analysis are different concepts.
- Certainty, recommendation strength, licensing and reimbursement are distinct.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Evidence hierarchy, systematic reviews and guideline appraisal

## The question determines the relevant design
Randomised comparisons are valuable for causal treatment effects, but hierarchy labels do not make every trial reliable. Long-term/rare harms, prognosis, diagnostic accuracy, experience and service implementation may require other designs. Ask whether the population, intervention/exposure, comparator and outcome answer the clinical question. A large irrelevant study is not direct evidence for the decision.

Separate risk of bias within a result, certainty across a body of evidence and a guideline recommendation. Randomisation and allocation concealment differ from blinding. Missing data, outcome measurement and selective reporting can undermine a trial despite its randomised label. Observational associations need their own confounding and selection assessment.

## Systematic review is a method, not a guarantee
A review should state its question, eligibility, search and selection methods, data extraction and appraisal. A meta-analysis is a statistical combination and may be part of a review; a systematic review need not pool data. Identify duplicate populations, incompatible outcomes, follow-up differences and publication bias before trusting a pooled number.

Fixed-effect and random-effects models make different assumptions about underlying effects. A random-effects model does not make methodological or clinical heterogeneity disappear. Inspect the studies and the spread of effects, not only the summary diamond. Inappropriate pooling can create a precise answer to no meaningful common question.

## Certainty is outcome-specific
Cochrane uses GRADE to assess certainty across a body of evidence, including risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias. Certainty can differ between symptom improvement, serious harm and long-term function for the same intervention. A review's publication date alone does not show that its search is current or its evidence applicable.

## Read the recommendation as a decision
Guidelines combine evidence with benefits/harms, values, resources and implementation considerations. Recommendation strength is not identical to evidence certainty or proof of comparative superiority. Check scope, methods, conflicts of interest, update process and jurisdiction. A regulator's licence, a professional recommendation and a reimbursement decision are distinct.

When applying evidence, preserve absolute effects, uncertainty, follow-up horizon and applicability. Do not treat an imported guideline as Greek law or an older review as a complete current evidence synthesis.
chunks.title: Evidence hierarchy, systematic reviews and guideline appraisal

questions.modelAnswer: Impulsive action has impaired withholding or inadequate consequence consideration. Goal-directed action tracks outcomes and their current value. Habits are stimulus–response cued and relatively outcome-insensitive; they can be adaptive. Compulsivity is persistent/repetitive action despite harm or reduced goal relevance. Impulsivity and compulsivity can coexist, and repetition alone does not diagnose a disorder.

questions.modelAnswer: The teaching model links reward/motivational impulsive action with ventral-striatal/prefrontal loops and habitual/compulsive action with dorsal-striatal/orbitofrontal loops. Repetition may shift control toward entrenched habit across cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical networks. This is a proposed account, not inevitable linear progression in every addiction/OCD presentation or proof of one shared lesion, cause or treatment.
questions.prompt: What does the ventral-to-dorsal loop model propose, and why is it not a universal disease progression?

Behavioural work can target cues, alternatives and goal control, but medication needs diagnosis-specific efficacy/safety evidence. Clinical benefit neither validates the circuit hypothesis nor provides an individual biomarker; aim at agency, function and reduced harm.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Impulsivity–compulsivity circuits: reward, habits and control

## Phenomena first, circuits second
Impulsivity includes difficulty withholding an action and acting without adequate consideration of consequences. Compulsivity concerns repetitive, persistent action despite adverse consequences or reduced relevance to the current goal. Neither is one diagnosis, and the same person may show both. Habitual action can be efficient and adaptive; repetition alone is not a compulsive disorder.

Goal-directed behaviour is sensitive to what an action achieves and whether that outcome is currently valued. A habit is more strongly cued by learned stimulus–response associations and can become relatively insensitive to outcome value. This behavioural distinction is more informative than assuming that every repeated act begins with a consciously experienced urge.

## Parallel loops and a proposed shift
Stahl's teaching model relates reward/motivation and impulsive action to ventral-striatal loops with prefrontal control, and habitual/compulsive action to dorsal-striatal loops involving orbitofrontal systems. These are cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical networks, not isolated striatal switches. Learning, salience, inhibition and environmental context interact.

A ventral-to-dorsal shift with repeated behaviour is a proposed account of how initially rewarding actions become entrenched habits. It should not be read as a universal linear progression in every addiction, OCD presentation or impulse-control disorder. Symptom dimensions can cut across classifications without proving that the disorders share one lesion, cause or treatment.

## Translate the model cautiously
Assess the actual action, antecedents, expected reward/relief, consequence, control attempts and context. Distinguish an impulsive act during mania or intoxication from a longstanding repetitive pattern. A compulsive action can be maintained by avoidance or relief as well as positive reward; multiple formulations may be relevant.

Behavioural interventions can target cues, alternative actions and goal-directed control. Medication decisions require diagnosis-specific evidence and safety assessment rather than selection from a schematic circuit diagram. Benefit from an intervention does not prove that it reversed a particular ventral-to-dorsal mechanism.

Network models help organise hypotheses and research tasks; they do not provide routine individual diagnostic biomarkers. Preserve the gap between a behavioural construct, a circuit association and a demonstrated causal treatment mechanism. The clinical objective is reduced harm and improved agency/function, not suppression of all habits or impulses.
chunks.title: Impulsivity–compulsivity circuits: reward, habits and control

questions.modelAnswer: Cardiometabolic disease, smoking, substances, infection, unequal care access, social disadvantage and treatment harms interact; antipsychotics are not the whole explanation. Group mortality differences do not predict individual lifespan. Diagnostic overshadowing prematurely assigns physical symptoms to mental illness: new chest pain, neurological change, fever or weight loss warrants normal medical assessment with communication/access support.

questions.modelAnswer: Review established disease, BP, weight/metabolic trajectory, indicated glucose/lipids and cardiovascular history, plus smoking, diet/activity, infection exposure, sexual/dental/respiratory health and substances. Review cardiac, endocrine, sedative and metabolic medication effects/interactions. Integrate prevention, vaccination/screening and disease treatment with psychiatric care, weighing relapse if switching medicines and exposure changes when smoking changes.
questions.prompt: What should a broad physical-health review include beyond antipsychotic metabolic measurements?

questions.modelAnswer: NICE adult-schizophrenia antipsychotic anchors include baseline assessment; weight weekly for six weeks, then twelve weeks, one year and annually; pulse/BP and glucose/lipids at twelve weeks, one year and annually. These UK anchors are not every illness/drug’s schedule, and risk may require earlier checks. Name who obtains/interprets results, treats abnormalities and confirms follow-up/access: completed tests alone do not complete care.
questions.prompt: State the qualified NICE monitoring anchors and explain how responsibility and abnormal-result follow-up complete the pathway.
