# Remember

- Mortality disparity involves disease, exposure, treatment and access; it is not an individual forecast.
- Avoid diagnostic overshadowing and assess established disease as well as risk.
- Monitoring requires interpretation, action and accepted responsibility.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Physical health in severe mental illness: risk, access and follow-through

## Excess mortality is not only a medication problem
Severe mental illness is associated with avoidable physical morbidity and premature mortality. Cardiometabolic disease, smoking, substance exposure, infections and unequal access to effective care contribute alongside treatment-related harms and social disadvantage. A population mortality gap does not predict one person's life expectancy. Do not attribute every risk to antipsychotics or regard physical illness as inevitable.

Diagnostic overshadowing occurs when symptoms are attributed prematurely to mental illness. New chest pain, neurological change, fever or weight loss needs appropriate medical assessment. Distress, communication barriers or difficulty organising appointments should lead to support, not a lower diagnostic standard.

## Assess risks and existing disease together
Review blood pressure, weight/metabolic trajectory, glucose/lipids where indicated, smoking, activity, diet and family/personal cardiovascular history. Assess infection exposure, sexual health, dental problems, respiratory symptoms and substance use according to need. Medication review includes metabolic, cardiac, endocrine and sedative effects and relevant interactions. A screening result is not a completed treatment pathway.

Offer prevention and treatment adapted to the person's circumstances. Smoking cessation, nutrition/activity support, appropriate vaccinations/screening and treatment of established physical disease should be integrated with psychiatric care. Avoid replacing one necessary psychiatric medicine solely to improve a marker without weighing relapse and other harms. Changes in smoking can also change some psychotropic exposures, requiring medicine-specific review.

## Monitoring needs an owner
NICE CG178 specifies baseline and follow-up metabolic/cardiovascular assessment during antipsychotic treatment. Its adult schizophrenia schedule includes weight weekly for the first six weeks, then twelve weeks, one year and annually; pulse/BP and glucose/lipids at twelve weeks, one year and annually. These are UK guideline anchors, not one schedule for all severe mental illness or every medicine. Additional clinical risk can justify earlier assessment.

Agree who obtains results, interprets them, treats abnormalities and confirms follow-up. Coordinate primary, psychiatric and specialist services, including practical help accessing appointments. Monitor benefit, adherence and equity as well as test completion. The desired outcome is appropriate prevention and treatment of physical illness, not a form marked reviewed while abnormalities remain unaddressed.
chunks.title: Physical health in severe mental illness: risk, access and follow-through

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# The Greek mental-health system: national network and local pathways

## Distinguish organisational law from available care
Law 5129/2024 established the National Network of Mental Health Services (EDYPSY), organised through Regional Networks (PeDYPSY) in the competent Health Regions (DYPE). The Ministry's 2025 implementation account describes seven regional networks corresponding to the seven Health Regions. The inspected first-Health-Region decision documents transfer/interconnection arrangements from 1 February 2025; a file's older upload path must not override its displayed document date.

The enacted framework retains sectorisation and community-care principles, continuity, deinstitutionalisation and rehabilitation. Sectorisation links responsibility to a population/area; it does not mean every person can obtain every intervention locally. Administrative integration, clinical coordination and actual service capacity are different questions. The original 2024 text is not a certified October 2026 legal consolidation.

## Map functions rather than memorise an institution list
Community mental-health centres and outpatient services support assessment, treatment and continuity. Day services, mobile units, early-psychosis services and rehabilitation/residential structures address different needs; emergency and inpatient care remain distinct functions. The appropriate destination depends on age, clinical urgency, need and the current local remit. A network name is not a complete referral rule or an involuntary-admission authorisation.

The official May 2025 First Intake announcement describes digital first-appointment requests to participating mental-health structures. A submitted request is not evidence of acceptance, a guaranteed appointment time or an emergency response. Confirm the current service and alternative access route where digital use is impractical.

## A safe referral has a receiving clinician/service
Identify the relevant regional/local structure, clarify eligibility and urgency, and confirm acceptance and interim responsibility. Transfer the clinical question, current risks, treatment information and follow-up plan with lawful information sharing. A discharged patient must not be assumed supported simply because a community unit appears in a directory.

Current amendments, duty arrangements, staffing, catchment exceptions and digital availability require local verification. This is a bounded organisational overview; it does not certify current legal procedure, transport arrangements or an operational nationwide referral map.
chunks.title: The Greek mental-health system: national network and local pathways

questions.modelAnswer: Primary prevention reduces new illness before onset; secondary reduces emerging illness consequences through early recognition/treatment; tertiary reduces disability/complications of established illness, including rehabilitation and relapse work. Promotion strengthens wellbeing, resources and supportive conditions beyond named-disorder prevention. State the intended outcome/stage: wellbeing, incidence, early access and disability measures are not interchangeable.
questions.prompt: Contrast primary, secondary and tertiary prevention with mental-health promotion.

questions.modelAnswer: Universal programmes reach a whole defined population without risk selection; selective programmes reach an elevated-risk group; indicated programmes reach early signs/symptoms below the relevant disorder boundary. These describe coverage/selection, not another primary–secondary–tertiary stage ladder. A programme may serve several purposes, but risk enrichment does not mean inevitable illness.
questions.prompt: How do universal, selective and indicated approaches differ, and why are they not a second disease-stage ladder?

questions.modelAnswer: Check accuracy, false positives, stigma/overdiagnosis and accessible diagnostic assessment/effective follow-up; a positive screen is not diagnosis. Define population, denominator, outcome and horizon, evaluating reach, equity, implementation and harms. Increased service use may mean better access, increased detection is not failed prevention, and symptom improvement is not necessarily reduced incidence. Aspirational programme labels do not establish net benefit.
questions.prompt: What evidence, follow-up and outcome distinctions determine whether screening or prevention provides net benefit?

- Prevention level concerns stage/outcome; universal/selective/indicated concerns population selection.
- Promotion, screening and treatment are distinct.
- Evaluate incidence, access, disability and equity separately.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Prevention and mental-health promotion: levels, populations and outcomes

## Specify what is being prevented
Primary prevention aims to reduce new illness before it develops. Secondary prevention concerns early recognition and treatment to reduce the consequences of emerging illness. Tertiary prevention reduces disability and complications in established illness, including rehabilitation and relapse-related work. An intervention can serve more than one purpose, but its intended outcome and stage should be stated.

Mental-health promotion aims to strengthen wellbeing, resources and supportive conditions; it is not limited to preventing a named disorder. The distinction matters when choosing an outcome: improved wellbeing, fewer incident diagnoses, earlier access and reduced disability are not interchangeable measures of success.

## Population coverage is a different dimension
Universal prevention addresses an entire defined population without selecting individuals by elevated risk. Selective prevention targets a group with increased risk; indicated prevention targets people with early signs or symptoms who do not yet meet the relevant disorder boundary. These terms describe whom the programme reaches, not a simple replacement for primary/secondary/tertiary levels.

Examples can clarify the target: supportive school environments may promote wellbeing broadly; an intervention for a high-risk group may seek to reduce incident illness; early access for emerging psychosis may reduce delayed treatment; rehabilitation in established illness may reduce disability. Each needs its own evidence and does not guarantee prevention in every participant.

## Screening requires a care pathway
Earlier detection is not automatically a net benefit. Consider test accuracy, false positives, stigma, overdiagnosis, access to assessment and whether effective follow-up exists. A positive screen is not a diagnosis, and risk enrichment does not predict inevitable illness. An education campaign, screening programme and therapeutic intervention are distinct activities.

Assess reach, acceptability, equity, implementation and unintended harms alongside effectiveness. Programmes that depend on resources unavailable to disadvantaged groups may widen disparities despite average benefit. Structural measures and individual care need not compete; the appropriate combination depends on the problem and population.

When evaluating prevention, define the population, outcome, denominator and time horizon. Changes in service use may reflect improved access rather than increased disease. Reduced symptoms are not proof of reduced incidence, and increased detection is not proof of failed prevention. Clinical/public-health claims should follow the measured outcomes, not the programme's aspirational title.
chunks.title: Prevention and mental-health promotion: levels, populations and outcomes

questions.modelAnswer: Descriptive psychopathology characterises experiences/signs; nosology groups syndromes. Biological approaches examine mechanisms, while psychological approaches investigate meaning/learning/relationships and social approaches examine context/institutions. They address different levels that can inform each other without equivalence. Specific biopsychosocial links are more useful than a list of three labels or one supposedly complete theory.
questions.prompt: How do descriptive, biological, psychological and social approaches differ in the questions they address?

questions.modelAnswer: Kraepelin-associated course-based classification helped distinguish syndromic trajectories, not prove timeless discrete biological entities. Freud’s unconscious/developmental, interpretation/transference tradition and later learning/cognitive approaches contributed different therapeutic models and research questions. Package efficacy does not validate every explanatory claim, just as drug efficacy does not prove a simple transmitter-deficiency cause.
questions.prompt: What did course-based classification and psychological treatment traditions contribute without proving complete causal theories?

questions.modelAnswer: History includes changing classifications/theories/services and coercive or exclusionary harms; popularity never guaranteed efficacy or ethical legitimacy. Judge community reform by real access, continuity and support, not bed closure alone. Ask what each claim addresses, how it can be tested and its limits, combining experience and scientific explanation without obsolete-treatment revival, diagnostic eponyms or treating present consensus as permanent certainty.
questions.prompt: How should historical change and institutional harms inform present-day formulation and evidence judgement?

chunks.rememberMarkdown:
# Remember

- Description, classification, causal explanation and treatment evidence are different tasks.
- Historical/model-specific theories are not universal established mechanisms.
- Institutional and rights history matters alongside scientific ideas.
chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Modern psychiatry: historical approaches and present-day integration

## Historical schools answer different questions
Psychiatry's development involves changes in classification, causal theories, institutions and treatment, not one orderly replacement of false ideas by a complete final model. Descriptive psychopathology characterises experiences and signs; nosology groups syndromes; biological research investigates mechanisms; psychological and social approaches examine meaning, learning, relationships and context. These levels can inform one another without becoming interchangeable.

The nineteenth-century medical tradition combined observation of individual illness with somatic and psychological theories. The inspected Oxford account describes Esquirol's predisposing/precipitating factors and Griesinger's somatic approach. Course-based classification associated with Kraepelin helped distinguish syndromic trajectories, but contemporary diagnoses are not simply unchanged copies of historical entities.

## Psychological and biological traditions
Freud proposed unconscious and developmental explanations and developed a therapeutic tradition using interpretation and transference. These are historical/model-specific claims, not demonstrated universal causes of mental disorder. Learning and cognitive approaches address behaviour, appraisal and information processing with different assumptions and research methods. Evidence for a therapy package does not validate every part of its explanatory theory.

Biological psychiatry developed through neurological, pharmacological, genetic and other research. Drug efficacy does not establish a simple transmitter-deficiency cause, and a group-level brain association does not identify an individual lesion. More operational classifications improved consistency in describing syndromes without automatically proving that each category is a discrete biological disease.

## Institutions and rights belong in the history
Asylum care, hospital treatment and community services reflect social organisation as well as clinical ideas. The history includes coercion, exclusion and serious abuses; an intervention's contemporary popularity was not proof of benefit or ethical legitimacy. Community reform must be evaluated by access, continuity and actual support rather than the mere closure of beds.

## Use history to improve judgement
Ask which claim a theory addresses, what evidence could test it and where its limits lie. A biopsychosocial formulation should connect specific relevant factors rather than list three labels. Scientific explanation and understanding the person's experience are complementary tasks. Avoid using historical names as diagnostic shortcuts, treating current consensus as permanent certainty, or reviving obsolete treatment simply because an older theory once justified it.
chunks.title: Modern psychiatry: historical approaches and present-day integration

questions.modelAnswer: Bowlby framed attachment as a central protection/security process supporting exploration, not merely feeding’s consequence. Ainsworth’s Strange Situation observes separation/reunion behaviour to characterise attachment patterns. Harlow’s rhesus surrogate experiment showed contact comfort beyond milk under experimental conditions. The animal result does not prescribe one human caregiving form or determine adult psychopathology; method/coding comparisons still require review.
questions.prompt: Compare Bowlby, Ainsworth and Harlow by their question, method and main contribution.

questions.modelAnswer: Separation distress alone does not classify attachment: reunion and wider observation matter. Secure/avoidant/resistant/disorganised patterns are descriptive relationship patterns, not permanent personality or abuse diagnoses. Insecurity is not reactive attachment disorder/disinhibited social engagement disorder, which have their own developmental/care requirements. chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Development and attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth and Harlow

## Attachment as a developmental relationship
Attachment theory concerns the child's use of a familiar caregiver for protection and security, with exploration possible when the relationship supports it. Bowlby treated attachment as a central developmental process rather than simply a secondary consequence of feeding. A relationship can change with circumstances; a pattern is not a permanent personality label or a destiny for adult illness.

Development must be understood through temperament, caregiving, learning, maturation and context. Separation can have different effects depending on age, previous relationships, the reason and handling of separation and care available during it. The older maternal-deprivation label should not become a universal mother-blaming explanation. Fathers, other caregivers and the quality of continuity matter.

## Observe reunion, not just separation distress
Ainsworth's Strange Situation observes behaviour around separation and reunion with an attachment figure. Secure, avoidant, resistant/ambivalent and disorganised are commonly used attachment-pattern labels. Distress at separation alone does not classify attachment: reunion behaviour and the wider observation matter. Different measures and coding schemes must not be assumed equivalent; the original-method comparison remains a source-review task.

Attachment insecurity is not itself reactive attachment disorder or disinhibited social engagement disorder. Those are separate diagnostic constructs with specific developmental/care-context requirements. A strange-situation classification is not a standalone diagnosis of abuse or an adult psychiatric screening tool.

## Harlow's experiment and its limits
Harlow's rhesus-monkey surrogate-caregiver work showed the importance of contact comfort beyond provision of milk under the experimental conditions. This challenged an exclusively feeding-based account of attachment. It does not prove that human caregiving has one necessary form, that feeding is irrelevant to infant health, or that an animal experiment determines an individual adult's psychopathology. The experimental separation/deprivation context also raises substantial ethical concerns.

## Clinical use without determinism
Explore relational security, separation experiences, caregiving consistency and current support when relevant to formulation. Associations between attachment patterns and later problems do not establish inevitable outcomes or one causal explanation for every symptom. Avoid reading an adult's current relationship difficulty backward as certain evidence of infant attachment type. Developmental history can guide understanding and support, while diagnostic and intervention decisions still need their own evidence.
chunks.title: Development and attachment: Bowlby, Ainsworth and Harlow

# Rapid tranquillisation: selection, reassessment and physical monitoring

## Calm safely while retaining a medical differential
Rapid tranquillisation uses urgent parenteral medication when oral treatment is not possible or appropriate. Its aim is safe calming that permits assessment, not punishment or routine unconsciousness. Continue de-escalation where feasible, assess immediate danger and consider delirium, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia, intoxication/withdrawal, pain and medication effects. Agitation is not a drug-specific diagnosis.

Prepare trained staff, monitoring and resuscitation capability before administration. Review preferences/advance plans, prior response, pregnancy, physical illness, current medicines and total recent doses. Record what was actually administered, not only what was prescribed. A regular depot or prior PRN can remain active and contribute to cumulative exposure.

## A jurisdiction-specific selection example
NICE NG10 recommends adult IM lorazepam alone or IM haloperidol with IM promethazine. It favours lorazepam when information is insufficient or there has been no prior antipsychotic exposure, and advises against the haloperidol/promethazine combination with cardiovascular/QT concerns or no ECG. These are UK recommendations, not permission to ignore respiratory vulnerability or a Greek product-specific regimen. Dose, formulation and route require the actual local protocol and product information.

The inspected Maudsley discussion distinguishes zuclopenthixol acetate from a rapidly acting tranquillisation agent; its prolonged/delayed action is not a substitute for immediate calming. Do not extrapolate a maintenance depot schedule into an emergency. Oral, IM and IV use have different onset, accumulation and staffing implications.

## Reassess before repeating
NICE specifies an initial single-dose prescription and review of its effect before repetition. Lack of immediate calm does not prove a dose has had time to work. Assess response, respiratory state, consciousness and other adverse effects rather than automatically stacking injections.

After administration, NICE requires at least hourly monitoring of pulse, BP, respiratory rate, temperature, hydration and consciousness until physical concerns resolve. Fifteen-minute monitoring applies when the BNF maximum is exceeded or the person is sedated/asleep, has taken alcohol/illicit drugs, has pre-existing physical illness or has suffered restrictive-intervention harm. Local risk may require closer observation.

Respiratory compromise, cardiovascular deterioration, severe dystonia, reduced consciousness or hyperthermia requires prompt medical escalation. Reversal drugs are not universally safe antidotes. Document intervention, response, injuries, clinical cause and the prevention plan after the emergency.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Psychiatric bioethics: principles, conflicts and justified decisions

## Four principles identify obligations, not automatic answers
Respect for autonomy requires taking the person's values and choices seriously, supporting understanding and avoiding coercion. Beneficence concerns clinically meaningful benefit; non-maleficence concerns avoiding or minimising harm. Justice concerns fair treatment, access and distribution of resources. None is a blanket permission to disregard the others. A treatment can offer benefit while creating harm, burden or an unacceptable intrusion.

Psychiatric diagnosis, disagreement and an unwise choice do not independently establish lack of decision-making capacity. Assess the relevant decision and support communication. Informed consent is a process involving information, understanding and voluntary choice, not merely a signature. Emergency or involuntary pathways require applicable legal authority as well as an ethical argument; foreign legal rules are not Greek rules.

## State the conflict concretely
Specify whose interests are affected, which facts are established, what remains uncertain and the available alternatives. A refusal may create a tension between autonomy and expected benefit. Disclosure may create a tension between confidentiality and protection. Scarce-resource allocation may involve justice as well as individual benefit. Identify the actual expected consequences rather than write principle names as a substitute for analysis.

## Justify proportionate action
Compare alternatives, including less restrictive options, foreseeable harms and whether the proposed action can achieve its aim. Explain why a restriction or disclosure is necessary, what it is limited to and when it will be reviewed. Confidentiality has limits, but neither concern nor professional convenience justifies unlimited sharing. Distinguish legal requirements, ethical duties and the person's preferences.

Document the reasoning, supported decision-making efforts, consultation and the responsible decision-maker. Seek additional clinical, ethics or legal advice for difficult conflicts without transferring responsibility into an unexplained committee label. After an emergency, revisit the person's understanding, preferences and account of the intervention.

The WMA code supports dignity, autonomy, competent care and confidentiality; it is professional ethical guidance, not a statutory compulsory-treatment test. Ethical quality is shown by a defensible decision and continuing accountability, not by citing all four principles or assuming that beneficent intention makes an intervention harmless.
chunks.title: Psychiatric bioethics: principles, conflicts and justified decisions

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Family intervention in schizophrenia: psychoeducation and relapse prevention

## Help the family without making it the cause
Family intervention addresses understanding of illness, communication, coping, problem solving and crisis planning. Families can be a major source of support and can themselves experience distress, uncertainty and practical burden. The formulation should identify what this family needs rather than assume that every relative is available, safe or willing to provide care.

Expressed emotion describes aspects of the family emotional climate, including criticism, hostility and emotional overinvolvement. Higher expressed emotion has been associated with relapse in research settings; it is not proof that a relative caused schizophrenia or that warmth can replace treatment. Symptoms and burden can affect relationships, and simplistic blame obstructs collaboration.

## Education is one component
Explain symptoms, course uncertainty, treatment benefits/harms and early warning signs in accessible language. Distinguish illness-related experiences from deliberate misconduct without excusing dangerous behaviour. Practise communication, negotiated problem solving and responses to a crisis. Support the carer's own health and practical needs rather than offer only more duties.

Psychoeducation can improve knowledge and coping, but a leaflet or one information meeting is not necessarily the full family-intervention package. Intervention effects vary with what was delivered, outcome and setting. Do not promise elimination of relapse, or infer that every effective component works through expressed-emotion reduction alone.

## Delivery anchors and safeguards
NICE CG178 recommends family intervention for families living with or in close contact with the person. Its delivery description includes the patient where practical, three months to one year, at least ten planned sessions and preference-sensitive single-family or multi-family formats. These are UK delivery anchors, not a universal guarantee or a Greek service entitlement.

Negotiate the person's involvement and information-sharing boundaries. Relatives can provide observations without being given unrestricted confidential information. Coercion, abuse or conflict may require separate meetings or a different plan; joint work should not expose someone to danger.

## Keep it connected to care
Integrate the intervention with psychiatric treatment, physical-health and substance-use review, social support and a shared relapse/crisis plan. Assess knowledge, coping, burden, relationships, patient functioning and relapse separately. A successful meeting is not evidence of reduced admissions. Review access, actual delivery and outcomes when progress stalls, and preserve the person's agency rather than assigning relatives an enforcement role.
chunks.title: Family intervention in schizophrenia: psychoeducation and relapse prevention

# Secondary mania: medical, medication and substance causes

## Establish an elevated-state syndrome, then explain it
Manic features include abnormal elevated, expansive or irritable mood with increased activity/energy and associated changes such as reduced sleep need, pressured speech, grandiosity and risky behaviour. Agitation, insomnia or disinhibition alone does not establish mania. Assess severity, psychosis, function and immediate danger while obtaining the longitudinal history.

Secondary mania is a clinical shorthand, not one uniform DSM diagnosis. Separate substance/medication-induced bipolar presentations from bipolar disorder due to another medical condition and from an independent bipolar disorder with coincidental illness. A temporal sequence suggests a hypothesis; it does not prove physiological causation.

## Exposures and medical differential
Review prescribed and non-prescribed substances, recent initiation, dose changes and withdrawal. Corticosteroids, stimulants and other activating exposures may be relevant, but the actual agent, timing and capability to produce the syndrome matter. Antidepressant activation is not automatically a full switch or lifelong bipolar diagnosis.

Consider endocrine disease, neurological injury/disease, encephalitis and other medical causes according to the findings. DSM discusses examples including Cushing disease, multiple sclerosis, stroke, TBI and anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. A list of possible causes is not a mandatory identical investigation panel for every patient.

## Red flags change the investigation
First late-life onset, abrupt atypical change, altered attention/arousal, cognitive decline, seizures, focal signs, autonomic disturbance or close exposure chronology should strengthen medical assessment. Consider delirium: manic-like symptoms occurring exclusively in delirium do not meet the relevant independent DSM secondary-bipolar diagnosis. Neurological and systemic examination guide testing.

DSM medical-condition attribution requires history, examination or laboratory evidence of a direct pathophysiological relationship, relevant exclusions and significant consequences. For substance/medication attribution, establish exposure chronology and the agent's capability, then examine evidence for an independent course. The manual's examples of persistence are not a universal pharmacokinetic washout rule.

## Treat risk and revisit attribution
Stabilise dangerous behavioural or medical states, review the implicated exposure with appropriate specialists and treat the established syndrome alongside its cause. Do not delay urgent care until attribution is certain. After recovery, revisit prior spontaneous episodes, residual symptoms and the need for continuing treatment. Reversible contribution, acute treatment response and long-term bipolar diagnosis are separate conclusions.
chunks.title: Secondary mania: medical, medication and substance causes

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Adjustment disorder: stressor, timing and diagnostic exclusions

## Stress-linked distress is not automatically a disorder
Adjustment disorder concerns a clinically significant response to an identifiable stressor that does not meet a better explanatory disorder. The stressor need not meet the trauma threshold for PTSD or acute stress disorder. Relationship, occupational, medical and continuing social stressors can be relevant; assess what happened, its meaning and the context rather than diagnose from the event name.

## DSM-5-TR precision
Emotional or behavioural symptoms begin within three months of stressor onset. Clinical significance can be disproportionate distress, taking external/cultural context into account, significant functional impairment, or both. The response must not meet another mental disorder's criteria or merely exacerbate an existing disorder. Exclude normal bereavement and a better prolonged-grief explanation.

After the stressor or its consequences end, symptoms must not persist for more than another six months. This is not a rule that every adjustment disorder ends six months after its first symptom. Continuing stressors or enduring consequences can support a longer course; DSM specifies acute duration below six months and persistent/chronic duration of six months or longer. Record which clock is being used.

Depressed mood, anxiety, mixed emotional symptoms and conduct-related presentations are DSM specifier possibilities, not different causal mechanisms. The inspected criteria are DSM; they must not be silently merged with ICD wording or timing.

## Differential and risk
A full depressive disorder after a stressor is not downgraded to adjustment disorder solely because its cause seems understandable. PTSD/ASD need their own trauma and symptom patterns. Grief, anxiety, substance effects and exacerbation of pre-existing illness also require assessment. An apparently modest stressor can be highly consequential in its social context, while ordinary distress is not necessarily pathology.

Adjustment disorder does not mean low suicide risk. Assess self-harm, hopelessness, ongoing threat, substance use, supports and functioning. Avoid treating a residual diagnostic category as a reason for minimal follow-up.

## Care follows the maintaining problem
Address practical stressors where possible, support coping and relationships, and monitor symptom/function change. Reassess the diagnosis if a different syndrome emerges or the course no longer fits the timing conditions. A brief supportive approach can be useful, but a universal drug regimen or guaranteed spontaneous recovery is not established by the diagnostic label. Continuing adversity and evolving illness deserve distinct documentation.
chunks.title: Adjustment disorder: stressor, timing and diagnostic exclusions

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# OCPD versus OCD: pervasive control and symptom-related rituals

## Personality pattern rather than a synonym for OCD
Obsessive-compulsive personality disorder (OCPD) is a pervasive preoccupation with order, perfectionism and mental/interpersonal control at the expense of flexibility, openness and efficiency. DSM-5-TR requires onset by early adulthood, presence across contexts and at least four of eight features. General personality-disorder requirements and contextual exclusions still apply. Being conscientious or organised is not sufficient.

## Preserve the eight-feature map
The features are: detail/rule/list preoccupation that loses the activity's purpose; perfectionism that prevents completion; excessive work/productivity at the expense of leisure/friendships, beyond economic necessity; overconscientious rigid morality/values beyond cultural or religious identification; inability to discard worthless/worn items without sentimental value; delegation only on exact compliance with one's method; miserly spending to hoard for feared future catastrophe; and rigidity/stubbornness.

These features describe consequences and inflexibility, not a requirement to be successful, tidy in every domain or unemotional. Poor completion can be the direct result of perfectionistic standards. Evaluate longstanding function and relationships rather than count context-appropriate work habits as pathology.

## The OCD distinction needs phenomenology
OCD involves qualifying obsessions, compulsions or both, with its own distress/time/impairment requirements and exclusions. OCPD does not require either symptom. OCD intrusions/rituals and the personality pattern can coexist, so the diagnoses are not mutually exclusive.

Ego-dystonic versus ego-syntonic is a useful tendency, not an absolute rule. OCD insight can vary, and an individual with OCPD may recognise harms or experience distress. Ask what the person fears, why an act must be done, whether it neutralises an intrusive concern and how the pattern changes across settings. Repeated checking alone cannot settle the diagnosis.

## Broader differential and care implications
Hoarding disorder has its own discarding, accumulation and impairment pattern; one OCPD criterion is not enough to establish it. Consider depression, anxiety, autism-related inflexibility, occupational demands and cultural norms when interpreting the presentation.

Assess treatment goals collaboratively, including task completion, tolerating uncertainty, flexibility and interpersonal impact. Do not automatically prescribe an OCD regimen for a personality diagnosis or attribute a lifetime pattern to a brief symptomatic episode. Independent treatment evidence and the actual coexisting syndrome should determine the intervention plan.
chunks.title: OCPD versus OCD: pervasive control and symptom-related rituals

# Chronic systemic alcohol complications: organs, nutrition and assessment

## Several mechanisms, not one alcohol-damage syndrome
Chronic alcohol exposure can cause direct tissue injury, nutritional deficiency and complications mediated through trauma, infection or coexisting disease. Dependence severity, current intoxication and organ damage are different constructs: substantial medical harm can exist without an obvious withdrawal presentation. Establish amount/pattern, duration, nutrition, other exposures and previous complications without attributing every abnormal result to alcohol.

## Liver and pancreas
Alcohol-associated liver disease includes steatosis, inflammatory injury and fibrosis/cirrhosis. Portal-hypertension and synthetic-function complications can include bleeding, ascites and other serious decompensation. Jaundice, haematemesis/melaena, acute confusion or rapidly worsening function requires medical assessment. Hepatic encephalopathy is not simply intoxication; compare attention/arousal, liver context and competing causes, including withdrawal and infection.

Acute and chronic pancreatitis are distinct problems. Chronic pancreatic injury may affect digestion and endocrine function; abdominal pain, vomiting or nutritional deterioration needs assessment rather than a psychiatric explanation. Alcohol is an important exposure, not proof of the cause in every pancreatic presentation. Do not use normal appearance or the absence of current drunkenness to exclude medical disease.

## Cardiovascular, blood and cancer risks
Hypertension, cardiomyopathy, arrhythmia and vascular complications can accompany exposure. Dyspnoea, chest pain, syncope or a new neurological deficit warrants urgent medical evaluation. Haematological abnormalities may involve poor nutrition, bleeding, liver disease or direct effects; anaemia is not synonymous with one vitamin deficiency.

Alcohol causes cancer at several sites. IARC identifies oral/pharyngeal/laryngeal, oesophageal, liver, colorectal and breast cancers; WHO states that no safe alcohol level is established for cancer risk. This is a risk statement, not a deterministic prediction for an individual. Older observational cardiovascular-protection claims do not cancel cancer or other harm and should not become advice to drink for health.

## Nutrition and coordinated care
Assess actual intake, weight trajectory, vitamin deficiency and electrolyte/metabolic problems. Thiamine-related neurological emergencies require their own treatment pathway, not a generic multivitamin recommendation. Management connects organ-specific care, nutritional rehabilitation and alcohol-use treatment. In dependence, stopping alcohol may introduce withdrawal risk and needs a planned safe pathway. Follow organ function and recovery separately from reduced consumption or improved mood.
chunks.title: Chronic systemic alcohol complications: organs, nutrition and assessment

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Stimulant crash and withdrawal: risk and continuing treatment

## Withdrawal is not merely being tired
After prolonged stimulant use is stopped or reduced, dysphoria, fatigue, disturbed sleep, appetite change and altered psychomotor activity can emerge. A crash can follow a period of intense use, but presentation and course vary with agent, exposure, co-use and baseline illness. Reduced autonomic activation does not establish that all danger has passed.

DSM-5-TR stimulant withdrawal requires cessation/reduction of prolonged use, dysphoric mood and at least two of five changes developing within hours to several days: fatigue, vivid unpleasant dreams, insomnia/hypersomnia, increased appetite, or psychomotor slowing/agitation. Distress/impairment and exclusions are required. Craving and anhedonia can occur but are not substitutes for this criterion structure. Stimulant-use disorder instead requires at least two of eleven features within twelve months. Tolerance/withdrawal under appropriate prescribed treatment do not alone establish it.

## Assess safety across the transition
Suicide risk, severe depression, psychosis, dehydration, sleep loss and concurrent medical/substance problems need active assessment. The ASAM/AAAP guideline highlights possible increased suicidality as intoxication wanes and acute withdrawal begins. Chest pain, seizures, abnormal temperature or marked cardiovascular disturbance still requires medical evaluation rather than reassurance that the person is detoxifying.

Distinguish expected withdrawal from independent mood/psychotic illness and another substance's withdrawal. Use a longitudinal timeline and reassess after stabilisation. Post-acute depression, anxiety, insomnia or suspiciousness may last weeks to months; persistence does not automatically prove either permanent stimulant damage or an independent psychiatric disorder.

## Continuing care is the main treatment task
Support nutrition, sleep, safety and engagement while treating qualifying medical and psychiatric problems. Build a plan for triggers, craving, harm reduction and return-to-use risk. ASAM/AAAP recommends contingency management as a primary component alongside other psychosocial treatment; CBT/community reinforcement approaches can contribute. This is US guidance and requires feasible local implementation.

No single universally effective withdrawal-substitution medicine is established here. Selected pharmacotherapies for stimulant-use disorder require indication-specific evidence, specialist oversight and safety review rather than a general detoxification recipe. Follow participation, substance use, mental state and function separately. A resolved crash is not evidence of sustained recovery.
chunks.title: Stimulant crash and withdrawal: risk and continuing treatment

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Primary progressive aphasia: three clinical variants and pathology limits

## Establish the language-led syndrome first
Primary progressive aphasia (PPA) has insidious progressive language difficulty that dominates the early illness and its functional impact. Exclude non-degenerative causes such as stroke or tumour and a better psychiatric explanation. Prominent early non-language memory, visuoperceptual or behavioural disturbance may point elsewhere. A poor verbally loaded cognitive score does not alone establish generalised dementia.

The 2011 consensus separates clinical, imaging-supported and definite-pathology levels. A phenotype is not a protein diagnosis. Frontotemporal and Alzheimer pathology associations are probabilistic, and mixed/unclassifiable cases can occur. Assess speech, grammar, naming, comprehension, repetition, object knowledge and reading/writing rather than classify from fluency alone.

## Retain the variant-defining pattern
**Nonfluent/agrammatic:** at least one core feature—agrammatism or effortful/apraxic speech—plus two of impaired complex-syntax comprehension, spared single-word comprehension and spared object knowledge. Speech-planning errors differ from simple word-finding pauses.

**Semantic:** both impaired naming and single-word comprehension, plus at least three of impaired object knowledge, surface dyslexia/dysgraphia, spared repetition and spared grammar/motor speech. Failure to know a word's meaning differs from failure to retrieve its name.

**Logopenic:** both word-retrieval and sentence/phrase-repetition impairment, plus three of phonological errors, spared single-word/object comprehension, spared motor speech and absence of frank agrammatism. Slow output is not automatically the nonfluent variant.

Expected imaging patterns support, rather than replace, the clinical pattern. Structural investigation also addresses competing causes. Do not assume every progressive aphasia belongs to one frontotemporal subtype or infer definite Alzheimer pathology from a logopenic presentation alone.

## Assessment and support
Obtain collateral, functional history and an appropriately adapted language/neuropsychological assessment. Hearing, language background, education and other cognitive domains affect interpretation. Assess ability using accessible communication; aphasia does not by itself establish incapacity or absence of understanding.

Speech-language support, alternative communication, practical planning and support for close others can address disability while neurological assessment clarifies the cause. Track progression across language and other domains. Medicine selection and pathology-directed treatment need their own contemporary specialist evidence; a variant name is not an automatic prescription.
chunks.title: Primary progressive aphasia: three clinical variants and pathology limits

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Psychosis beginning in older age: differential and treatment boundaries

## Age of onset is a clue, not an aetiology
New psychosis in older age requires assessment of the syndrome, baseline and medical context. Historical consensus terminology distinguishes late-onset schizophrenia after forty years and very-late-onset schizophrenia-like psychosis after sixty; these are descriptive conventions, not proof of an independent primary illness. Previous symptoms and overlooked earlier episodes can change the apparent onset date.

Clarify hallucinations, delusions, mood, attention/arousal, cognition and everyday function. Obtain collateral and examine the timeline of medicines, substances, physical illness and sensory change. Hearing/visual impairment and isolation can influence experience and interpretation without themselves proving the cause. Do not equate unusual beliefs with a fixed delusion without understanding context.

## Medical and neurocognitive differential
Acute fluctuation, inattention or altered arousal raises concern for delirium. Progressive cognitive/functional change suggests a neurocognitive assessment; Lewy-body features include recurrent formed visual hallucinations, fluctuation and parkinsonism, with important antipsychotic sensitivity. Structural, vascular, seizure, infectious and metabolic explanations should be evaluated according to findings. Depression or mania with psychosis remains a distinct possibility.

Symptoms can precede a clear dementia syndrome; absence of impairment on one brief screen does not guarantee absence of evolving neurological illness. Conversely, older age or a memory complaint does not automatically make psychosis dementia-related. Repeated assessment may be necessary while treating immediate danger and distress.

## Care must match the established problem
Address pain, illness, sensory needs, medicines, sleep and environmental stressors. Use supported communication and involve close others with appropriate information-sharing boundaries. Antipsychotic choice requires attention to frailty, orthostasis, movement effects, cardiac/metabolic risks and interactions; a young-adult prescription is not a default geriatric regimen.

For dementia-associated presentations, NICE NG97 limits antipsychotic use to risk of harm or severe distress from qualifying agitation/hallucinations/delusions, with low-dose/short-duration principles and reassessment at least every six weeks. This UK dementia guidance is not an automatic duration rule for every primary psychotic illness. Lewy-body/Parkinson dementia needs particular caution.

Document the target symptom, benefit, harms and ongoing need. A calmer patient is not proof of a correct diagnosis, and discharge should retain medical follow-up and a plan to reconsider the attribution.
chunks.title: Psychosis beginning in older age: differential and treatment boundaries

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Rapidly progressive dementia and prion disease: urgent differential

## A tempo requiring action
Rapidly progressive dementia (RPD) describes cognitive/functional decline over a much shorter course than typical slowly evolving neurodegeneration. Establish the actual chronology with collateral; an apparently sudden presentation can reflect late recognition of a longer illness. Delirium, seizures, depression and other conditions may imitate or complicate the picture.

Do not equate RPD with Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD). Autoimmune/inflammatory, infectious, toxic/metabolic, vascular and structural causes can be treatable. Rapid change with seizures, focal findings, movement disorder, fever, autonomic instability or reduced consciousness needs urgent neurological/medical assessment. Search for reversible causes while considering neurodegeneration, rather than defer treatment until a prion label is resolved.

## Investigations answer different questions
MRI with diffusion-sensitive sequences, EEG, CSF and targeted systemic investigations support different parts of the differential. Select them with specialists based on time course, examination and exposure history. A normal or nonspecific initial test does not close every diagnosis. Medical instability and suspected infection require their own immediate care.

## CJD: certainty levels and test limits
The inspected CDC sporadic-CJD framework allows probable disease with a neuropsychiatric syndrome and positive RT-QuIC. Its alternative route requires rapid dementia, at least two of myoclonus, visual/cerebellar signs, pyramidal/extrapyramidal signs or akinetic mutism, a qualifying EEG/CSF/MRI result and no routine alternative explanation. Definite disease requires tissue-based pathological evidence. These are classification routes, not an instruction to biopsy every suspected case.

RT-QuIC is distinct from CSF 14-3-3, which is not independently disease-specific. In the CDC alternative route, qualifying EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes; 14-3-3 applies with illness under two years; qualifying MRI shows caudate/putamen signal or at least two temporal/parietal/occipital cortical regions on DWI/FLAIR. These findings are supportive within the required syndrome, not proof from one result. Classic sporadic/familial/iatrogenic CJD and variant CJD have different contexts; do not apply one exposure narrative to all prion illness. Operational specimen/test interpretation still needs specialist confirmation.

## Safety and continuing care
Coordinate diagnostic testing and specialist specimen/instrument precautions when prion disease is suspected. Use procedure- and tissue-specific precautions rather than assumptions based only on the word transmissible. Explain uncertainty, offer symptomatic/supportive care and attend to patient/family needs. A rapidly fatal prognosis must not be assigned to every RPD presentation or used to abandon assessment for a treatable cause.
chunks.title: Rapidly progressive dementia and prion disease: urgent differential

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Bulimia nervosa treatment: psychological care, medicines and medical risk

## Treat the maintaining eating pattern and its consequences
Establish binge eating, loss of control, compensatory behaviour and weight/shape overvaluation, while distinguishing anorexia, binge-eating disorder and other specified presentations. Record frequency, methods, intake, weight trajectory, psychiatric comorbidity and actual functional impact. Normal-range weight does not establish medical safety, and reduced binge frequency does not alone demonstrate nutritional or psychological recovery.

## Psychological treatment is central
NICE NG69 recommends considering bulimia-focused guided self-help for adults. If unacceptable, contraindicated or ineffective after four weeks, consider individual eating-disorder-focused CBT. The described adult CBT-ED course can include up to twenty sessions over twenty weeks. These UK delivery anchors are not proof that four weeks without recovery equals global treatment resistance.

Early work supports engagement and regular eating, then addresses restrictive patterns, binge/purge cycles, weight/shape concerns and relapse prevention. Explore triggers and context without presenting one theoretical mechanism as established in every case. Children/young people have a different family-treatment pathway; an adult self-help plan must not be transferred automatically.

## Medication complements, not replaces, care
NICE advises against medication as the sole bulimia treatment. The inspected UK fluoxetine SmPC describes an adjunct to psychotherapy to reduce binge/purge activity and recommends 60 mg/day for adults. This is a specific UK product reference, not an automatic prescription or a universal dose for younger patients, pregnancy, hepatic impairment or interacting medicines. Its long-term-efficacy limitation beyond three months is not a mandatory discontinuation date.

## Detect risk independently of weight
Assess fluid/electrolyte disturbance from vomiting, laxatives, diuretics and other compensatory behaviours; consider cardiac risk and the need for ECG. Syncope, palpitations, weakness, severe dehydration or gastrointestinal bleeding requires medical assessment. Severe electrolyte imbalance, malnutrition, dehydration or impending organ failure can require emergency admission. Do not wait for an underweight BMI or completion of psychotherapy before treating danger.

Review dental complications and medical/psychiatric comorbidity, including self-harm and substance exposure. Correcting an electrolyte result does not remove the maintaining behaviour. Coordinate nutrition, psychological and medical care; measure binge/purge frequency, nutritional adequacy, weight/shape preoccupation, function and treatment harms separately. Revise the formulation and level of support when the plan is not safe or usable.
chunks.title: Bulimia nervosa treatment: psychological care, medicines and medical risk

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Restless legs and periodic limb movements: diagnosis and augmentation-aware care

## RLS is a waking symptom pattern
Restless legs syndrome (RLS) involves an urge to move, usually with unpleasant leg sensations, beginning/worsening at rest, relieved by movement and worse in the evening/night. Distinguish cramps, positional discomfort, neuropathic symptoms and akathisia. DSM-5-TR additionally specifies at least three times weekly for three months, impairment/distress and exclusions. These DSM frequency/duration anchors are not a universal definition across every sleep-classification or research framework.

## A sleep-recording finding is not PLMD by itself
Periodic limb movements of sleep (PLMS) can accompany RLS and other sleep disorders or occur without qualifying impairment. PLMD requires frequent recorded movements, meaningful sleep/daytime disturbance and no better explanation. The AASM 2025 description uses more than fifteen events/hour in adults and more than five in children, with exclusion of relevant disorders such as RLS, untreated OSA, RBD and narcolepsy. An elevated count alone is not an indication to treat a disorder.

## Check contributors and iron before escalating medicines
Assess iron indices, renal disease, pregnancy, medicines and sleep-disordered breathing. AASM prioritises aggravating-factor review and regular ferritin/transferrin-saturation assessment. Its adult iron consensus suggests supplementation when ferritin is at most 75 ng/mL or saturation below 20%, with IV-only iron in the 75–100 ferritin interval. These thresholds are consensus guidance, not empirically validated universal normal-range cutoffs or an infusion order. Borderline/discordant results require clinical interpretation.

## Augmentation changes long-term treatment reasoning
Dopaminergic treatment can initially help but can produce augmentation—treatment-associated worsening rather than simple loss of benefit. Earlier onset, broader symptom spread or increasing burden can raise concern; investigate the pattern before increasing a dose. AASM now strongly recommends selected alpha-2-delta ligands for adult RLS and conditionally advises against standard use of several dopamine agonists because of long-term augmentation. This is not an instruction to abruptly stop an established agonist; rebound can be severe.

Select treatment with the person, accounting for sedation, falls, renal function, misuse/respiratory risks and pregnancy-specific safety. RLS treatment evidence cannot automatically be applied to isolated PLMD. Greek availability/licensing and specific dosing require separate verification. Track symptom timing, sleep, daytime function and adverse effects rather than only a movement count.
chunks.title: Restless legs and periodic limb movements: diagnosis and augmentation-aware care

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# Therapeutic drug monitoring: sampling and clinically useful interpretation

## Start with a clinical question
Therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) measures drug or metabolite concentration to inform an exposure-related decision. Useful questions include suspected toxicity, inadequate response, adherence uncertainty, an interaction or altered clearance. It is particularly useful where an exposure–response/toxicity relationship and interpretable reference conditions exist. A measurable concentration does not mean every medicine needs routine monitoring.

## A result needs a sampling context
Record the medicine/formulation, dose pattern, recent dose changes, last-dose and sample times, missed doses, clinical state and interacting illness/exposures. Specify whether the assay measures parent, metabolite, active moiety, total or free concentration and check units. A reference interval developed for one measurement cannot be transferred to another without justification.

Trough means immediately before the next dose; a standardised twelve-hour post-dose sample is a specific convention and is not the trough of every dosing schedule. Steady state concerns recurring peak–trough exposure, not constant concentration. Under first-order conditions, four to five half-lives is a common approximation for near steady state, but clearance changes, active metabolites and long-acting absorption can alter timing. Suspected toxicity requires timely assessment; do not wait for a routine steady-state appointment.

## Interpret clinically, not as an automatic dose order
A therapeutic reference range summarises population evidence under particular conditions. Response can occur below it and toxicity within it. A single low level may reflect sampling, recent missed doses, increased clearance or other factors; a detectable level does not establish continuous adherence. Compare like-timed prior samples and repeat an unexpected value when appropriate without delaying urgent care.

Clinical toxicity, symptoms, function and tolerability determine what the result means. Neither a normal level nor a falling concentration excludes an independent cardiac, neurological or medical emergency. Document the hypothesised explanation, action and follow-up through the exposure change.

TDM complements prescribing judgement; it does not diagnose addiction, prove a metabolic genotype or measure clinical competence. Medicine-specific target, timing and decision rules require checked laboratory/product guidance, not transfer of a familiar lithium or clozapine number to another drug.
chunks.title: Therapeutic drug monitoring: sampling and clinically useful interpretation

# Clozapine plasma concentrations: sampling, units and ratios

## Measure exposure under comparable conditions
Record actual dose, schedule, formulation, recent adherence, last-dose/sample times and time on the unchanged regimen. Clozapine monitoring commonly uses a standardised approximately twelve-hour post-dose sample, before a morning dose where applicable; record the schedule rather than call every sample a true trough. A sample taken soon after a dose or after intermittent use can mislead comparisons.

Check units: 350 micrograms/L equals 350 ng/mL and 0.35 mg/L. The Maudsley/SPS reference window is approximately 350–600 micrograms/L (0.35–0.6 mg/L), interpreted with response and tolerability. This is not a guarantee, mandatory target for every responder or toxicity-free ceiling. The target concerns clozapine, not the sum of parent and norclozapine. Clinical toxicity needs review regardless of whether the number falls inside the reference window.

## A stable prescription can conceal changing clearance
Combustion smoking, relevant enzyme-inducing/inhibiting medicines and illness can alter exposure. Smoking cessation and serious infection can raise levels; recovery or resumed smoking can change them again. Confirm actual exposure history and current clinical signs rather than infer an interaction from a concentration alone. A neutrophil result is a separate safety measurement, not evidence of therapeutic exposure.

## Ratios support hypotheses, not verdicts
The concentration-to-dose ratio divides the measured concentration by daily dose. Specify units, sample timing and stable-state conditions. Compare within the person when conditions are comparable; a changed ratio can reflect altered clearance, sampling or adherence, not necessarily one cause. There is no universal ratio cutoff proving non-adherence, poor metabolism or resistance.

The clozapine:norclozapine ratio is different. It is sensitive to sampling, metabolism and recent dosing and should not be treated as a stand-alone adherence test. Different ratio directions need a clinical/exposure explanation rather than a memorised accusation.

Unexpected concentrations prompt review of dose history, illness/interactions, timing and toxicity, with repeat sampling where appropriate. Urgent sedation, delirium, seizure or cardiovascular/respiratory concern cannot wait for a confirmatory routine sample. Document the action and follow-up when the exposure context reverses; if treatment is interrupted, restart dosing and blood-monitoring rules are separate checks.

# Clozapine interruption and restart: dose tolerance and monitoring are separate

## Confirm the interruption and its cause
Establish the last actually taken dose, dose history, duration of interruption, reason, prior tolerability and current illness. Prescription records alone do not prove recent ingestion. Loss of tolerance to cardiovascular/sedative effects makes resuming a familiar full dose potentially dangerous. Assess urgent toxicity, infection, bowel, cardiac or haematological concerns before a restart decision.

A stop for suspected serious adverse reaction differs from a missed-dose interruption. Restart instructions are not permission to re-expose after a contraindicating reaction. The inspected UK SmPC prohibits re-exposure after clozapine-induced myocarditis/cardiomyopathy; haematological and other stop reasons need their own current rules and specialist assessment.

## An explicitly attributed dose anchor
For UK Clozaril adult treatment-resistant schizophrenia, the inspected SmPC states that when the interval since the last dose exceeds two days, restart with 12.5 mg once or twice on day one. Faster subsequent titration may be feasible if tolerated, but is not compulsory. This is the source's greater-than-two-days wording, not an invented boundary for exactly forty-eight hours or a universal rule for Parkinson psychosis.

Retitration depends on current risk, interruption length, setting, previous adverse effects and observed dose tolerance. Monitor orthostatic/cardiovascular state, consciousness and other adverse effects with an appropriate clinical team. Do not copy a rapid dose-doubling schedule or compensate for missed tablets with catch-up doses. A past therapeutic level does not establish today's safe dose.

## Blood-monitoring eligibility uses a separate clock
The September 2025 EU-aligned HPRA safety letter revised ANC monitoring. Its interruption bullets say stable patients treated for at least two years without neutropenia can resume their prior monitoring irrespective of interruption duration; another says interruptions of at least four weeks require weekly monitoring and retitration regardless of prior duration/neutropenia. Their overlapping wording is not silently harmonised here. Clarify the current Greek product/service rule before applying an operational monitoring schedule. Continuing a prior blood schedule never authorises a full-dose restart.

## Withdrawal also needs follow-up
Abrupt cessation can produce cholinergic rebound, worsening psychosis, movement symptoms or catatonic presentations. Treat urgent symptoms and their differential rather than assume every deterioration is ordinary relapse. Planned discontinuation and emergency stopping have different constraints. Coordinate supply, prescriber, laboratory and receiving service, and document a safe continuing plan.

chunks.studyMarkdown:
# ECT medical safety: pre-assessment, anaesthesia and recovery

## A joint psychiatric and anaesthetic decision
Modified ECT induces a therapeutic cerebral seizure under general anaesthesia and muscle relaxation. Confirm the indication, expected benefit, alternatives, consent/capacity and applicable legal process. Document baseline cognition and the person's understanding of memory risks; anaesthetic clearance alone is not treatment consent or proof that the indication is appropriate.

Assess cardiovascular, respiratory, neurological and relevant endocrine/metabolic illness, airway/dentition, aspiration risk, previous anaesthetic reactions and recovery after earlier ECT. Physical examination and investigations should answer actual risks rather than become an identical panel for every patient. Recent unstable illness, intracranial pathology or significant cardiorespiratory vulnerability may require optimisation and specialist planning.

## Prepare the individual procedure
Review all medicines with psychiatrist and anaesthetist. Lithium, anticonvulsants, benzodiazepines and other exposures can affect seizure/recovery or medical risk, but a blanket stop-all-medicines rule is unsafe. Specify fasting and diabetes management, not an unsupervised patient instruction.

The inspected 2023 Indian guideline gives a fasting example of two hours for clear liquids, six for milk/light meals and eight for fatty/fried food or meat. This is an attributed protocol, not a universal Greek rule; current anaesthetic policy and individual aspiration/medical factors govern. The older Oxford five-hour blanket wording is not adopted as current practice.

## Anaesthesia and muscle relaxation have different jobs
Induction provides unconsciousness; muscle relaxation reduces musculoskeletal injury and motor expression without replacing anaesthesia or the cerebral seizure. Agent selection balances haemodynamics, seizure effects and recovery. A short visible convulsion under relaxation does not itself establish an inadequate seizure.

Succinylcholine is commonly used, but previous prolonged paralysis, pseudocholinesterase deficiency, neuromuscular injury or malignant-hyperthermia risk can change relaxant choice. Anaesthetic expertise determines the individual plan and appropriate alternatives; this chunk supplies no induction or relaxant dosing recipe.

## Monitor through recovery
Have airway/oxygenation, suction, resuscitation and trained staffing available. Observe ECG, haemodynamics, oxygenation, ventilation and seizure activity, then recovery of breathing, consciousness and function. Early bradycardia and later sympathetic activation are relevant physiological phases; neither justifies ignoring an arrhythmia or severe blood-pressure change.

Prolonged seizure/apnoea, cardiovascular instability or delayed/confused recovery requires assessment and a response plan. Discharge criteria and escort/support depend on the setting and current policy. Record complications, cognition and changes required before the next treatment; a completed stimulus is not a completed safety pathway.
